en: Vāgbhaṭa: *Rasaratnasamuccaya*,
with the commentary *Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī* by Āśubodhavidyābhūṣaṇa and Nityabodhavidyāratna.

2) [Salutation] to that [Goddess], who, by means of the nectar of perfected mercury— whose splendor flashes forth, which is produced from the arising of bliss, which is endowed with the digits of auspiciousness, and who is an ocean of the nectar of her compassionate glance— [bestows grace].
Salutations to that Supreme One, the foremost physician of the world, by whom the diseases of birth, destruction, old age, passion, and the like of his devotees are instantly pacified.
Ādima, Candrasena, the confident Laṅkeśa,
Kapālī, Mattamāṇḍavya, Bhāskara, and Śūrasenaka.
Ratnakośa, Śambhu, Sāttvika, Naravāhana,
Indrada, Gomukha, Kambali, and Vyāḍi.
Nāgārjuna, Surānanda, Nāgabodhi, Yaśodhana,
Khaṇḍa, Kāpālika, Brahmā, Govinda, Lampaka, and Hari.
There are twenty-seven [deities] who bestow the accomplishment of mercury (rasasiddhi):
Rasāṅkuśa, Bhairava, Nandin, and Svacchandabhairava; // VRrs_1.5 //
Manthānabhairava, Kākacaṇḍīśvara, Vāsudeva, the sage Śṛṅga, and the compiler of the Kriyātantrasamuccaya.
The Yogin Rasendratilaka, Bhālukī, he who is called Maithila,
Mahādeva, Narendra, Vāsudeva, and Harīśvara.
Having examined other tantras, this compendium is now being composed for the sake of medical treatment regarding these perfected elixirs (rasas) that are useful for healing.
The *Rasaratnasamuccaya* was composed by the son of Siṃhagupta;
it treats mercury, secondary minerals, and metals, as well as the construction of apparatus and other such instruments.
For the purpose of purifying metals, the methods for making crucibles and so forth will be taught;
furthermore, purification, the extraction of essence, liquefaction, and the production of ash will be explained.
In the northern direction, there is a great mountain, a dwelling of frost,
whose mass of lofty peaks surpasses the clouds.
Exhausted by the intense fatigue of traversing the path through the sky,
the host of autumnal clouds descended, as it were, to the earth for rest.

It shines forth, exceedingly lofty, as if it had emerged from the earth after piercing through it— the radiance of the hoods of the lord of the serpent-king, who is the presiding deity of the zodiac signs.
The gem-studded grounds of its slopes, where medicinal herbs blaze at night, imitate clouds of unrestrained lightning.
Upon the feet of the kinnara women wandering in his mountain fastness,
the application of red lac was accomplished by means of mineral pigments.
Adorned with the moon as his crest-jewel, veiling the sky-clad quarters of space,
he who dwells within the cave is celebrated by the world as Girīśa.
Upon whose peaks the sages, with eyes perpetually closed,
perceive Giriśa, who is beyond the reach of speech and mind.
Because of the spray from the waterfalls striking against the surfaces of the rocks,
even during the day the Yakṣas behold the sky marked by stars.
In that place, men, unable to endure the excess of frost and wind,
constantly seek the warmth of their own wives' breasts.
As he wandered through the mountain fastness, even in the heat of summer, the sun’s fierce warmth was blocked by intense snowdrifts so that it could not distinguish itself from the cool-rayed moon.
In mountain caves fragrant with the musk of the kastūrī deer,
where kinnarīs sing of the wedding festival of Gaurī.
There shines Maheśvara, the primordial god of the worlds;
for he was born as the Great Essence (Mahārasa) in the form of aesthetic flavor (rasa) in order to protect the universe.
The merit that men obtain by performing a hundred horse-sacrifices, by giving ten million cows, or by the gift of a thousand pieces of gold,
or by bathing at all sacred fords, is obtained simply by beholding the birth of a son.
Whoever, endowed with devotion, having fashioned a *rasaliṅga*, should worship it,
shall obtain the fruit of worshipping the *liṅgas* of the three worlds.
Consuming, touching, giving, meditating, and fully worshipping—
this fivefold worship of the essence (rasapūjā) is said to destroy even the greatest sins.
Merely by eating it, one destroys the entire multitude of diseases arising from the sins of previous births for all men; of this there is no doubt.
The sins committed by embodied beings in previous lives perish instantly if Śambhu is anointed with fragrant ground paste.
"Whoever causes even a mere *truṭi* of mica to be fully digested by the mercury, for him there shall be the fruit of a hundred sacrifices; thus spoke Śiva."
And whoever reviles the Lord of the Sūtas, the supreme radiance of Śambhu,
shall fall into a terrible hell for as long as the duration of a kalpa-cycle.
He who gives medicinal juice, properly purified and processed, to the sick,
obtains the eternal fruit of the Tulā-dāna and the Aśvamedha sacrifices.
"Once the elixir is perfected, I shall make the world free from the disease of poverty.
This meditation on the elixir has been proclaimed as the remover of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. (VRrs 1.31)
For the consumption of mercury by the clouds is proclaimed as the sacrificial offering (naivedya) for the essence;
having performed this worship of the rasa, one shall obtain the fruit born of sacrifice.
When the child is situated in the womb and his life departs,
he is liberated from terrible evil and proceeds to the supreme state.
Having fainted, it removes disease; having experienced bondage, it becomes the giver of liberation;
indeed, when dead, it turns one into an immortal—what other source of compassion is there besides mercury?

Since he pacifies even that leprosy— which is indeed incurable and arises from the mass of sins committed by harming the preceptor of the gods, cows, and the twice-born— who, then, could be more pure than the Sūta?
Only the binding of mercury is blessed, for one who constantly exerts effort at its commencement will succeed with mercury and shall make the earth free from old age and death. (VRs 1.36)

This birth in a noble family is, for now, the fruit of well-performed deeds; and even therein, there is intelligence, which has as its fruit the ability to weigh the entire surface of the earth; and the earth itself is easily governed.
The fruits of being subject to the earth are objects of desire, and those objects have various enjoyments as their fruit;
yet these enjoyments exist within the body, which is impermanent; therefore, everything is in vain.
Thus, considering wealth, the body, and enjoyments to be impermanent, one must always strive for liberation;
that [liberation] comes from knowledge, that [knowledge] from practice, and that [practice] when the body is stable.
No alchemical elixir whatsoever—such as mercury, base metals, and the like—is capable of ensuring stability therein;
for they are themselves unstable by nature, subject to burning, moistening, and drying.
Wooden plants dissolve into lead; lead into tin, and tin into copper;
copper into silver, silver into gold, and gold dissolves into mercury.
Just as yogins, when dissolved within the form of Hara, attain immortality,
so too do gold, iron, and other metals [attain it] when the sky is swallowed by the king of essences (rasarāja).
Just as in the Supreme Self, there occurs the constant dissolution of all beings therein;
this alone is the king of elixirs, which makes the body free from old age and death.
Having attained knowledge endowed with the eight qualities through the power of practice while the body is stable,
one reaches the state of Brahman and no longer experiences the sufferings of birth or dwelling in rebirth.
The supreme light stands pervading the entire world simultaneously with one quarter;
that immortal state is easily attained through three quarters, not by mere dispassion alone.
For indeed, that subtle Brahman cannot be worshipped by means of this body, which is in some way distressed by the sufferings of disease, old age, and death, and which perishes in an instant.
Who could grasp even the name of the perfected body without the body itself—
that reality which is accessible through yoga, stainless, and beyond the range of even the mind?
Through sacrifice, charity, austerity, study of the Vedas, self-restraint, and virtuous conduct,
self-realization is indeed said to arise most abundantly by the power of yoga.
Situated between the two eyebrows, that supreme light consisting of consciousness— which illuminates the world like a peacock, lightning, or the sun—
manifests for those whose vision is purified by merit.

It is the single essence of supreme bliss, the nature of supreme light, free from conceptual construction, with all afflictions completely dissolved; it is the object of knowledge, peaceful, and to be personally realized within oneself.
Fixing the mind upon that [Self], seeing the entire throbbing world as consisting of consciousness,
one whose bonds of karma are destroyed attains the state of Brahman even here in this very life.
Freed from passion and hatred, practicing truth and devoid of falsehood,
they become indistinguishable in all respects through contact with the consciousness of Brahman.
They remain endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā*, their bodies radiant, and ever-arisen in bliss;
having attained the immortal nature of Brahman, they have indeed accomplished all that was to be done.
Excluding this one body alone, which is the abode of all sciences and the root of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— what other supreme good could there be that is free from old age and death?
How shall he who does not know the birth-impurity by means of direct perception know the God whose form is unseen and who consists of pure consciousness?
That which is worn out by old age and rendered helpless by the sufferings of cough, asthma, and the like,
is unfit for meditative concentration, as the functioning of the intellect and the senses is obstructed.
How can a mortal man— first a youth of sixteen years, addicted to tasting the flavors of sensory objects,
and later an old man whose discernment has departed— attain liberation?
For those who have no realization of the Supreme Self within this very body,
that Brahman is even more remote for them after the abandonment of the body.
Brahmā and the other gods strive toward that [state], having assumed divine bodies;
so too do others who are liberated while living and sages who endure until the end of the kalpa.
Therefore, a yogi desiring liberation while living must first bring about a divine body through the union of the creation of Hara and Gaurī.
On this mountain, as the sexual union of Śiva and Śivā proceeded out of mutual affection and a desire to conquer one another— an act that caused the three worlds to tremble— *61*.
Desiring a son who would be the slayer of the asura Tāraka, the gods dispatched the Fire-god to prevent the union of those two.
He had assumed the form of a pigeon in a cave of the Himalayas;
though he was not a bird, he was agitated by that state, gazing with the playful movements of the god of love.
Seeing him, Śambhu was ashamed and desisted from the act of love;
the final element that had been discharged was then caught by the wielder of the trident.
He was cast into the mouth of the Fire-god, and he fell into the Gaṅgā as well;
she too, being scorched by him, cast him back out.
From the depositing of that impurity, the bodily constituents (dhātus) were produced, which are the causes of accomplishment;
this continued until the semen fell from the mouth of Agni, possessing abundant essence.
Having made five wells each one hundred yojanas deep,
from that time forward that semen remained within the wells, divided into five parts.
Rasa, Rasendra, Sūta, Pārada, and likewise Miśraka—
thus the fivefold [mercury] born of Śambhu arises according to the distinction of its source-places (kṣetra).
The essence was red and liberated from all defects; it was a rejuvenating elixir (*rasāyana*).
By means of it, the thirty gods were born free from disease, devoid of decay, and immortal.
The lord of mercury (rasendra), when freed from its impurities, is dark, dry, and extremely volatile;
by means of it, the practitioners of alchemy (rasāyinaḥ) became like serpents (nāgāḥ), abandoned by death and old age.
The gods and the nāgas filled those two wells with earth and stones;
from that time forward, they became exceedingly difficult for people to find.
Slightly yellowish in color, with a dry body and endowed with the [proper] qualities, that mercury (sūtaka),
perfected through the eighteen purificatory rites, transforms the body into iron.
Now, there is another [substance] produced from a well, which is mobile and white in color;
it is indeed mercury (pārada), which removes all diseases through various medicinal preparations.
That rasa, possessing the luster of a peacock’s eye, is considered *miśraka*;
when endowed with the eighteen refinements, it is exceedingly efficacious in granting success.
The three beginning with the Sūta—the Sūtas and others—are performers of all accomplishments;
through the manifestation of their own specific activities, they possess power in an extreme degree.
He who understands this production of tastes is righteous;
he attains longevity, health, progeny, and the perfection of tastes.
It is called "rasa" because it provides the essence (*rasa*) of all the bodily constituents;
or rather, it is considered "rasa" because it is tasted (*rasyate*) for the destruction of old age, disease, and death.
Because it is the king among juices (rasa) due to its superiority over other juices, it is celebrated as Rasendra;
because it produces the accomplishment of the body and of metals, it is therefore known as Sūta.
He is called *pārada* because he delivers those submerged in the mire and ocean of disease;
he is that in which the luster inherent in all metals resides, mingled with fire.
Therefore, that [elixir] is called "mixed," as it bestows fruits of various forms.
By the power of such a mercury— which severs the death and disease of mortals—
human beings have come to possess strength and lifespan equal to those of the gods.
Having seen them, Rudra was immediately entreated by Śakra;
and the king of essences (mercury) was then joined with the defects and the casings.
From that time forward, this Sūta was no longer perfected as long as he remained unrefined;
moving through the water in the form of water, he would swiftly become a goer of swans.
The impure becomes impure in form, and that which is smoky becomes smoky;
the movement of the living soul follows another divine course, as the soul emerges from the egg.

He gives life to those living beings; therefore, the vital essence (*rasa*) is known as "life" (*jīva*). *Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):* He describes the fivefold course of the mercury (*rasa*) with the verse beginning "jalaga" (VRrsBo 1.84ab).

In the form of water, by virtue of its fluidity, it becomes "water-going" (jalaga), meaning it has the nature of moving together with water; the sense is that it is an extremely subtle portion of the rasa, similar to fine powder. It is "swift" (tvarita) and "fickle" (cañcala), meaning it moves with instability; thus, it becomes "swan-going" (haṃsaga), having the nature of moving like a swan. And because it takes the form of impurity (mala) due to its state as dross, it becomes "impurity-going" (malaga), being mixed with impurity and conjoined with the bodily humors (doṣas).

Accompanied by smoke because fire is seen [therein], moving with the smoke—that is, having the nature of flying upward—there is another, a fifth, divine movement of the *rasa* (the vital essence), which is invisible in form; this is the sense. By that movement, the *jīva*, the self, would emerge from the *aṇḍa* (the egg-like sheath of the body), as it were; such is the meaning of "rasa. By what means? [By the power of the breath.]
The meaning is that just as the way the soul (jīva) departs from the body cannot be seen, so too the fifth movement of mercury (pārada) cannot be known. 2.

In the preceding verse, by the term "the movement of the soul" (jīvagati), the movement of the essence (rasagati) was indicated; he states the reason for the word "soul" (jīva) having the sense of "essence" (rasa) with the words "sa" [he]. 3.

That *rasa* would cause those living beings (*jīva*) to live—that is, it would bestow long life by means of destroying old age, death, and so forth—for that reason, *rasa* is traditionally known and declared to be the "giver of life" (*jīvanadāyaka*), based on the etymological derivation that "it causes the living to live" (*jīvayatīti jīvaḥ*). The four states of existence are visible; the fifth state of existence is invisible.
By means of mantra, meditation, and so forth, its fifth course is obstructed.
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā):
Now, he states the different names [of this element] according to its various courses, beginning with "jalaga" (the water-goer).*

That mercury which moves in the form of water, by virtue of its watery nature, is called "water-moving" (*jalaga*), meaning it possesses the specific quality of moving like water. (VRṢṬī 1.85;2) The metals such as gold and others are composed of that [mercury]. (VRṢṬī 1.85;3) Even the stable essences (*rasa*) and so forth are likewise composed of that. (VRṢṬī 1.85;4)
By means of the application of earth as dross (*malakiṭṭa*), their density and stability [are produced].
(VRṢṬī 1.85;5) For this very reason, their existence is possible only in the form of fluidity (*druti*). (VRṢṬī 1.85;6) The nature of water is characterized by downward movement. (VRṢṬī 1.85;7)

Even for metals that have attained a state of stainless fluidity, downward movement is indeed observed. (VRṢṬī 1.85;8) That mercury which moves swiftly with speed and force, yet does not go too high into the sky but rather in the space close to the earth and upon the ground itself, is called *haṃsaga*.
(VRṢṬī 1.85;9) It is called *haṃsaga* because it moves in the sky like a swan (*haṃsa*). (VRṢṬī 1.85;10)
But that [wind], when situated among peacocks, earthworms, and the like, is established as such. That which moves distinguished by a black-colored portion in the form of impurity is called *malaga*.
And that which is "with smoke" (*sadhūma*)—meaning it exists together with a movement through space accompanied by upward streaks and a color identical to smoke—is called *dhūmaga*.
But that [mercury] resides within yellow orpiment, cinnabar, realgar, vitriol, gaurī-pāṣāṇa, and so forth.
For it is observed that these indeed emerge after bursting through the obstruction of smoke.

Even when a smokeless digestion (*nirdhūmajāraṇā*) is performed using instruments such as the navel-machine, mountain-presses, iron crucibles, and the like, their stability must be examined with great effort to see whether it truly exists.
There is another, a fourth state of mercury;
it is called the "living state" (*jīvagati*).
The living state is the invisible movement of mercury, just like the movement of a living being (*jīva*).
For this very reason, it is also called "divine" (*daivī*).

Because its movement is invisible, like that of a deity, the mercury (*pārada*), when joined with it, emerges—that is, goes out—from the egg [of the body], just as the individual soul (*jīva*) departs from its own place by means of an invisible movement.
The emergence from the egg is seen in the case of the body, but the departure of the individual soul together with the body is not seen.
The sense is that, just as a child’s movement, inhalation, exhalation, and other such activities are inferred [to indicate life], so too it is with this [essence].

(VRṢṬī 1.85;23) Endowed with that movement, it alone sustains living beings (*jīva*); therefore, that essence is known by the name "life" (*jīvana*). (VRṢṬī 1.85;24) A king—or one equal to him—possessing wealth, should have that [essence] prepared by the hand of a physician skilled in the *saṃskāra* process, for the sake of protecting himself and his subjects. This is the intended meaning. (VRṢṬī 1.85;25)
Thus, because its course is so volatile, the processing of the king of elixirs is difficult to achieve;
nevertheless, a skilled physician should protect it with great care.
Seeing the bride, freshly bathed after her first menses, mounted upon a horse, well-adorned, and looking about, the water residing in the well desired to seize her.
Seeing him, she too rises up with speed and goes away with great velocity;
the charioteer follows her for a distance of one yojana to the boundary.

Then Śivasambhava returned to the well with speed; they caught the mercury as it rested in the hollows dug along the path. Having fallen into the region of Darada due to its weight, it emerged from the mouth of fire.
That essence, having dissolved into the surface of the earth, is extracted as mercury by those living in various regions who cast that clay into a distillation apparatus.
VRṢ, 2 [The Eight Great Metals]: Abhra, vaikrānta, mākṣika, vimala, ādrijas, and sasyaka;
Having understood that there are eight types of mercury, including the restless (capala) and the extractable (rasaka), one should collect them.
"The menstrual blood of the Goddess becomes *gandha*, and her seminal element (*dhātu*) likewise becomes *abhraka*. This is an interpolated verse.

*Abhra* is the supreme vital energy of Gaurī, an ambrosia that destroys wind, bile, and consumption; it awakens wisdom, pacifies disease, and is the foremost of aphrodisiacs and life-prolonging elixirs.
Light, unctuous, providing relish, not increasing *kapha*, digestive, and cold in potency—such is *vyoma* (mica), which, through various formulations, removes all diseases and binds mercury.
That mercury which is extracted from a mine located below the "king's cubit" (rājahasta) yields the results described; however, that which is devoid of essence is utterly fruitless. (VR 2.3)

*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* That very same abhraka which is found in the middle of the earth, situated one and a quarter cubits (*rājahasta*) below the surface, being a mineral ore (*khanija*) that is dense and known as "vajra" (thunderbolt)— that alone possesses the qualities previously mentioned.
But the other [earth] should be known as devoid of essence due to its connection with wind, water, urine, excrement, heat, and worms.
(VRṢṬī 2.3;2) This is an illustration [applicable] to all mineral substances.
(VRṢṬī 2.3;3) For, generally, those [substances] existing within the womb of the earth possess their full essential qualities. (VRṢṬī 2.3;4)

* Here, although the word "ghana" (cloud) denotes any kind of mica (*abhraka*), it refers specifically to "vajra-mica" (*vajrābhra*). // VRṣṭī 2.3;5 * This is because only that [vajra-mica] possesses the aforementioned qualities. // VRṣṭī 2.3;6 [Sub-types of Mica]
Pināka, Nāgamaṇḍūka, and Vajra— these are considered the types of *abhra* (mica).
According to the distinction of colors such as white and so forth, each of these is fourfold.
The Pināka bow, heated by fire, releases a mass of arrows;
having bound the impurity of one who has relied upon it, it surely kills that man.
The *nāga* should produce a sound like that of a serpent while remaining within the fire;
[such is the medicinal property of *nāga*.]
When consumed, that [meat] undoubtedly causes the skin disease known as maṇḍala-kuṣṭha.
The *maṇḍūka* falls repeatedly leaping up after being blown upon; and the *abhraka* [falls likewise].
[Regarding the medicinal properties of the *maṇḍūka*: it is used for healing.]
Otherwise, one should treat that disease of urinary calculi with surgical instruments, for it would otherwise become incurable.
Vajra,
when heated in fire, becomes like a diamond-cloud, freed from all defects; it produces a body of steel and is the supreme remover of all diseases.
It is of four kinds: white, red, yellow, and black.
White is prescribed for white rites; that which has a reddish luster is for red rites;
and that abhraka which has a yellow luster is excellent for yellow rites.
Although four kinds of excellent space are mentioned in the science of alchemy (rasāyana),
nevertheless, that which has the appearance of black clouds possesses millions upon millions times more qualities.
[Examination of Cloud-Quartz:
That cloud-quartz which is glossy, broad-leaved, endowed with excellent color, heavy in weight, and whose leaves can be easily detached is declared to be the most praiseworthy. 2.11.
The mercury shall not swallow the sky, which is unsuitable for consumption, accompanied by moonlight and resembling dross;
once swallowed, however, it may be employed both in metallurgy and in alchemy (*rasāyana*).

*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* "For if there is an absence of 'grasping' (the consumption of mercury), mercury would not be effective in its task, like one who has fasted; thus he says, 'sacandrikam' (with luster). *VRṣṬī_2.12;1* "Sacandrikam" means accompanied by brilliance (*cākacikya*). *VRṣṬī_2.12;2*
*Kiṭṭābha* is that which has abundant dross (*prabhūtakiṭṭa*).

And the *grasita* [iron], being of the nature of *grasitābhra*, is to be employed for the production of gold and other metals from iron, for the killing of iron, for the application of iron to ward off diseases,
and likewise in *rasāyana*— meaning in such *rasāyanas* as *Jvarāṅkuśa* and others, and in forms such as *Lakṣmīvilāsa* and *Vajrapañjara*, which will be described later.
By the etymological derivation that "rasa" is that by which one goes toward or attains [the goal], the word *rasa* here includes both mercury (*rasa*) and elixirs (*rasāyana*).
A sky devoid of moonlight is beneficial for all diseases when dead;
however, when served while joined with the moon, it causes urinary disorders and weak digestion.
Those who, devoid of reason, have spoken of leaf-minerals and elixirs,
by them has the poison known as *kālakūṭa* been seen for the sake of life.
For the sake of sentient beings and for the purpose of service, one should employ purified abhraka;
otherwise, having rendered it devoid of its qualities, it will certainly cause harm.
Abhra (mica) that has been heated and immersed in kāñjika seven times,
or even thrown into cow's urine, certainly becomes free from defects. (VR 2.16)
Furthermore, having specifically boiled cow's milk with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
one should then prepare *dhānyābhraka* (paddy-iron) and grind it with the juices of *matsyākṣikā*.
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* Matsyākṣikā, hilamocikā, or gaṇḍadūrvā.
Having formed it into a discus (cakrī) and dried it, one should then roast it in an ardhebhaka puṭa. @----------

*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Then, having made that mica into "grain-mica" (*dhānyābhraka*), one should grind it for the duration of one day with the juice of *matsyākṣikā*, form it into a thick, round pill (*cakrī*), dry it, enclose it in a pair of earthen lids (*śarāvasampuṭa*), and place it in a crucible (*puṭa*) containing half as much mica.

One should cook [the substance] in half an *abhraka*-puṭa; that is called an *ardha-gajapuṭa*. It becomes an *ardha-gajapuṭa* by filling half the space of a *gajapuṭa* with *vanopala* (natural pebbles). *Puṭet* means "one should cook."
Then, having ground the mica leaf by leaf and formed it into a pellet (cakrī), one should dry it and place it within a pair of earthen lids (*śarāva*).
One should thus roast it six times with the juice of *punarnavā*.
Having ground it even with a sixteenth part of ṭaṅkaṇa and formed it into pills,
one should indeed roast it seven times using the half-elephant (ardhebhaka) type of crucibles.

In this manner, one should also saturate it seven times with the juice of vāsā and the juice of taṇḍulīya, according to the previously described procedure. Thus perfected, the mercury (ghana) may be employed in all yogic applications.
Powdered *dhānyābhra* mixed with rice and bound in a cloth is placed in fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*). When it has emerged from the cloth after being rubbed out, it is called *dhānyābhra*.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):
[The author] states the procedure for "grain-mercury" (*dhānyābhra*) as "powdered mercury" (*cūrṇābhra*).

"Powdered mercury" means powdered mica mixed with rice. Although the quantity of rice has not yet been specified here, nevertheless, following other treatises, it should be understood as being accompanied by one-quarter part (*pāda*) of rice-grain. Thus...
And in the Rasendrasārasaṃgraha:
"One should place mica mixed with a quarter-part of rice inside a woolen blanket (*kambala*) in water for three nights; once it is soaked, one should grind it thoroughly."
"That which has fallen from a woolen blanket, being smooth and free of grit, is called dhānyābhraka for the purpose of accomplishing the extraction of the essence of the mineral.
Thus [it is said]. (VRrsBo 2.21)
"Niryāta" means emerged or gone out.

Having pulverized the mica (*abhra*), one should bind it with a portion of *śāli* rice in a coarse cloth and rub it in sour gruel (*kāñjika*) until it emerges through the openings of the cloth as something fine and free from grit; that is known as "mica-rice" (*dhānyābhra*).

[The Killing of Grains of Cloud (dhānyābhra): Grains of cloud, having been thoroughly rubbed with the juice of kāsamarda, are killed by being subjected to ten *puṭa* cycles; there is no doubt about this.
Likewise, it may be prepared with the juice of musta grass or with the juice of taṇḍulīya.
[Abhra:: Māraṇa] Abhra ground with yellow *āmalaka* and *saubhāgya*, formed into pills,
and subjected to sixty *puṭa* applications, becomes the color of vermilion.
It destroys all diseases, such as consumption and others, when used as a vehicle for medicines.
[The killing of mercury: By means of decoctions of the bark from the roots of the *vaṭa* tree, or from the essence of betel leaves;
or with *vāsā* and *matsyākṣikā*; or with *mīnākṣī* together with *kaṭhillaka*.
The thick [substance] of the *vaṭa* tree, rubbed with milk and processed in a closed crucible (*puṭa*) twenty times, will acquire a luster like that of vermilion (*sindūra*).
Combined with one-fourth part of ṭaṅkaṇa and rubbed with the juice of *musallī*,
it should be sealed in a crucible and strongly heated; thus the dense ore will assume the form of its essence (*sattva*).

[Regarding the extraction of essence from minerals: One should [process them] separately with the juices of *kāsamarda*, *ghanā*, *dhānyavāsā*, *punarnavā*, *matsyākṣī*, *kāṇḍavallī*, and *haṃsapādī*. (VRs 2.27)
Having ground [the ingredients] repeatedly with effort, one should dry them by means of heat;
[then add] one pala of wheat flour, small fish, and borax.
Having added one-eighth part [of mercury] at a time, one should rub it repeatedly;
with each rubbing, one should properly dry it in the rays of the sun.
Having cast in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five products of the goat (*pañcāja*), and likewise the five products of the buffalo (*pañcamāhiṣa*),
one should fashion cow-dung balls slightly larger than the size of a *tinduka* fruit.
The five products of the goat— milk, curd, ghee, urine, and dung— are said to be "goat" (aja).
Having blown [the crucible] in a downward-dropping furnace, one should cause the essence to fall.
Having collected the dross (kiṭṭa) from the crucible and pulverized it, one should extract the metallic globules (ravaka).

*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* The essence remaining within the crucible, which is adhered to the glassy dross, exists in the form of minute particles that are difficult to grasp; once the fire has subsided, one should collect and unify it, take it out, crush it, and powder it, thereby recovering the essential substance adhering to those particles.
One should extract it, having separated it from the dregs. Having ground those dregs with a small amount of lime and cow-dung, [one should proceed]. (VRṣṭī 2.32)
Having formed balls and dried them again in the heat as before,
one should once more collect the dross, crush it, and extract the essence.
Then, having boiled those grains of *sattva* with sour *kāñjika*, and having enclosed them within a crucible together with the group of purifying substances, one should seal it shut. (VRṢ 2.34)
Having properly melted it and collected it, one should heat the thick mass twice;
thus the sattva becomes pure and may be employed in mercury-based elixirs.
[For the softening of mica (*abhra*): It should be melted in honey, oil, fat, and clarified butter, and then repeatedly poured back and forth.
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* "Parivāpitam" means thrown in or infused.
// VRrsBo_2.36ab;1 Metals and other substances that are hard become soft after ten such infusions. // VRrs_2.36 //
Having prepared a powder of mica, one should then soak it thoroughly with cow's ghee and roast it seven times in a shallow pan placed upon a stove.
One should grind it again and again until it becomes the color of fire;
or one should perform the roasting until, when a blade of grass is thrown upon it, it burns.
Then, having ground it together with sulphur, one should roast it twenty times by means of the Vārāha-puṭa using a decoction of the root of the *vaṭa* tree.
Furthermore, twenty times [he should bathe] with a decoction made from the three myrobalans (triphalā),
along with muṇḍikā, bhṛṅgarāja leaves, pathyā, and the roots of akṣa.
Having prepared it, it should be administered in the proper dose for all diseases;
there is nothing else superior to *sattvābhra* in its freedom from adverse effects and abundance of qualities.
If prepared in this manner by means of a hundred-fold *puṭapāka* cooking,
it becomes exceedingly endowed with qualities, acting as a supreme digestive and appetizing agent.
[Abhra:: Māraṇa:
Niścandrika] Mercury processed with the juice of *gandharvapattrī* together with jaggery.
The leaves of the banyan tree are below and above; the sky-bird is without moon and possesses three folds.
By consuming it in a dose of half a *guñjā* seed, it produces excessive hunger;
yet, through formulations that alleviate specific diseases, it is the supreme remedy for all diseases.
The globule of *sattva* should be heated and quenched instantly in *kāñjika* mixed with grain; then, one should grind it with an iron pestle.
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):
Having heated it with an iron pestle (*lohapārayā*), one should then throw thick, dense lumps into sour gruel (*kāñjika*). *VRrsBo_2.45;1*
Having gathered it at that very moment and ground it, one should reduce it to powder.
And one should fry that powder three times as before with cow’s ghee,
or likewise with the juice of *dhātrī* fruits or with the juice of *dhātrī* leaves.
After each roasting, it should be ground with a stone slab;
then, it should be treated with the juice of *punarnavā* mixed with *kāñjika*.
One should roast it ten times and treat it ten times with fragrant substances.
Thus purified, the essence of *vyoma* (aerial mineral) is supreme in all its qualities;
it may be employed as desired in the processes of *jāraṇa* (digestion) and *rasāyana* (alchemy).
The liquefactions (drutis) have not been fully specified in the scriptures, even though they are clearly observed;
without the grace of Śambhu, they never succeed.
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):
A *valla* is two *guñjās*; three *guñjās* is a *līlāvatī*, while according to the *Rājanighaṇṭu*, it is one and a half *guñjās*. [Regarding *abhra*:: *mṛta*: VRrsBo 2.50;1.
Divine mica (divyābhra), combined with Vellahva and Vyōṣa, taken in a dose of one Valla along with ghee, cures consumption, anemia, dysentery, colic, skin diseases, and other ailments.

It conquers wasting disease, dyspnea, urinary disorders, loss of appetite, difficult-to-cure cough, weak digestion, and abdominal pain; through these formulations, it overcomes all diseases without exception.
Eight-sided, with eight facets, hexagonal, smooth, and heavy— [such is the high-quality vaikrānta].
And when it is endowed with pure and mixed colors, it is called vaikrānta.
White, red, yellow, blue, pigeon-colored, dark, black, and variegated— thus it is indeed eightfold. (VR 2.53)

Vaikrānta indeed bestows longevity, promotes strength and complexion, is highly aphrodisiac, grants wisdom, and removes all humors and diseases. It kindles the digestive fire, possesses qualities equal to those of iron, is full of vitality, and certainly produces physical strength and iron. (VRṢ 2.54)
In all elixirs (rasāyana), the powerful vaikrānta,
which is to be reckoned as the foremost and which destroys all defects, should be employed in place of diamond (vajra).
The lord of the Daityas, Māhiṣa, who had attained perfection through the grace of Sahadeva,
was crushed by the goddess Bhagavatī Durgā with her trident.
Wherever his blood fell upon the earth and remained there,
in those very places there appeared vaikrānta, a great mineral in the form of a diamond.
Vaikrānta exists to the south of the Vindhya mountains, or it exists to the north, or indeed everywhere.
[Etymology of vaikrānta]
Because it cuts through metals, it is known as vaikrāntaka.
White, yellow, red, blue, with the luster of a pigeon,
resembling a peacock's neck, and another with the brilliance of emerald.
Black vaikrānta brings about the perfection of the body; yellow when [the moon] is yellow, white when white;
red grants success in all aims, as does that with the luster of emerald;
the remaining two are fruitless and should be avoided—thus vaikrānta is of seven kinds.
In whatever field the vaikrānta stone is situated, one should worship Bhairava and Vināyaka there, and with a pure mind, take [the stone].
Vaikrānta, which resembles a diamond (vajra), is considered to bestow strength to the body and promote the formation of iron-like metal;
it destroys poison, is the king of mercury (rasarāja), and cures fever, leprosy, and consumption.
Vaikrānta stones become purified after three days when they have been steamed while being treated with alkaline salts,
or cooked in acidic liquids, animal urines, the water of horse gram (kulattha), plantain juice, or the water of kodrava grain.
Vaikrānta is thoroughly purified by being steamed in a decoction of *kulattha* beans.
[The killing of vaikrānta:]
It is calcined eight times, combined with the juice of *gandhanimbuka*.
When the vaikrānta stones have been heated, one should pour horse urine over them;
or one may repeat this process several times, applying a liquid and then placing them in a *puṭa* (a sealed crucible).
One should employ reduced-to-ashes vaikrānta in place of diamond (vajra).
Vaikrānta [for the extraction of its essence] should be processed with the alkalis of *mocā*, *morata*, and *pālāśa*, saturated with cow’s urine,
and combined with the paste of *vajrakanda* and *niśā*, along with the powder of their fruit.
That paste, combined with borax, lac powder, and that which is derived from vaikrānta,
together with navasāra and the juice of meṣaśṛṅgī;
When it is formed into a lump, placed inside a silent crucible, and heated by a fierce fire, the essence of vaikrānta falls back into that very [crucible]; of this there is no doubt.
Vaikrānta, having been ground by means of the process for precipitating the essence (*sattvapātana*) and formed into a pill,
should be placed in a crucible and heated for one *ghaṭikā*; thus, the vaikrānta will release its essence.

Vikrānta that has attained the state of ash, combined with a quarter-part of mercury (mṛta-hema) and taken in a dose of one guñjā along with *kaṇā*, clarified butter, and *vela*, conquers consumption, indigestion, jaundice,
hemorrhoids, asthma, cough, malignant dysentery, chest wounds, and other diseases, while restoring the body's vitality. (VR 2.70)
The ash of blue vaikrānta combined with half its weight of iron-pigment ash, along with an equal amount of the essence of dead mica, should be thoroughly rubbed together.
If one consumes a dose the size of a *guñjā* seed, combined with honey and clarified butter, in the morning,
it destroys all diseases that are difficult to overcome by other medicines;
for men, in twenty-one days, it is like the waters of the Gaṅgā destroying sin.
The golden fluid originating from the Golden Mountain was created by Viṣṇu among the Tāpyas, the Kirātas, the Cīnas, and the Yavanas.
Tāpya (copper pyrite) is seen in the month of Mādhava when it is heated by the rays of the sun.
Honey from the *mākṣika* bee is sweet, with a golden luster; that which is slightly sour resembles silver.
It is somewhat astringent and sweet, cooling, pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), and light.
By practicing that, one is not overcome by old age, disease, or poison.
Mākṣika is of two kinds: hemamākṣika and tāramākṣika;
[the former is] svarṇamākṣika.
Among those, the first is honey from Kānyakubja, which resembles gold in color.
That which is produced on the banks of the Tapatī, resembling five-colored gold,
yet abounding in stones, is called *tāra*; it is said to possess few qualities.
Mākṣika mineral destroys all diseases, is indeed the very life-force of mercury (rasendra), and is supremely aphrodisiac;
it facilitates the fusion of two metals that are difficult to meld, possesses superior qualities, and is the foremost among all elixirs (rasāyana).
Honey is purified when processed with castor oil, citron juice,
and water.
Alternatively, honey that has been boiled for two ghaṭikās with the juice of plantain roots and then cast into a decoction of *varā* attains purity.
Mākṣika mineral, ground with the juice of *mātuluṅga* and *gandhā*, placed inside a crucible,
and fired with five "boar-seal" (*kroḍapuṭa*) applications, indeed dies (is reduced to ash).
[The killing of honey: When cooked thoroughly in a crucible with castor oil, cow’s urine, or the juice of *mātuluṅga*,
it becomes as hard as a metal.
In this manner, mercury that has been killed should be employed even in the procedure for elixirs (rasāyana).
Combined with one-thirtieth part of lead (nāga) and processed with alkaline and acidic substances,
roasted in an open crucible, the *mākṣika* ore releases its essence (*sattva*).
Having melted it seven times and cast it into the juice of *nirguṇḍī*,
lead mixed with the essence of honey will certainly be destroyed.
Honey (mākṣika) has been repeatedly processed with honey-fragrance oil (gandharvataila), cow urine, clarified butter,
and the essence of the root of the plantain tree.
When heated in a crucible, it releases its essence, which is soft and resembles copper.
[The properties of the essence (sattva) of honey:
It has a luster equal to that of the seeds of the *guñjā* plant, it melts quickly when heated, and it is cooling.
That purified essence of iron is supreme for producing bodies and metals.
Having ground mercury with the essence of honey (mākṣīkasattva) and having placed the offering (bali) once it has melted,
one should mix and rub together the essence and the liquefied mica (abhraka-druti) within the mortar.
Having prepared a ball in an apparatus called *lavaṇayantra*, one should cook it for half a day over a gentle fire.
Once it has cooled naturally, one should thoroughly powder it and take a dose of one *valla* combined with *vyoṣa* and *viḍaṅga*.
Consumed with honey, it destroys old age along with its diseases and even untimely death;
it overcomes even incurable maladies within seven days, and there is no essence of nectar equal to this.
Castor oil, guñjā, honey, and ṭaṅkaṇa should be rubbed together; by sowing [the seed] of that mixture, the essence derived from *mākṣika* ore will liquefy.
Vimala is said to be of three types: that which begins with gold, that which begins with silver,
and the third is the brass-like vimala, which is characterized by its respective luster.
* COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:
* He states the variety of vimala: "vimala" [is as follows]. VRrsBo 2.89;1 * Vimala is a specific type of mākṣika (sulphur ore). VRrsBo 2.89;2

By their respective lusters—that is, by the radiance of gold and the other metals—the term *vimala* (pure) refers, in this sequence, to silver and *mākṣika* (pyrite). [Regarding the physical properties of *vimala*: it is pure.]
Round, with well-defined corners, smooth, and provided with a polished surface—
such *vimala* stone removes wind and bile, is aphrodisiac, and is an excellent rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
The first [type of Vimala] is prescribed for the preparation of gold; the second is considered suitable for making silver;
and the third is used in medicinal preparations. Among these, each preceding one possesses superior qualities.
[Vimala:: Purification] Vimala, when steamed in water from the *āṭarūṣa* plant, becomes pure; or it becomes pure when steamed in the fresh juice of *jambīra* or in the juice of *meṣaśṛṅgī*.
And it attains purity, just as other stainless elements do.
With ten *puṭas* of vimala, māraṇa, gandha, aśmalaka, and sour gruel (*amlaiḥ*), [the mercury] dies.
[The process of *sattvapātana* (precipitation of the essence):
Having ground together the juices of *saṭaṅka*, *lakucā*, and *meṣaśṛṅgī*, along with their ashes,
one should smear this inside the crucible (*mūṣā*), dry it thoroughly, and seal it shut.
Blown by six pairs of kokila-blowpipes, it becomes stainless and resembles lead;
when combined with that, the mercury releases its essence (sattva), and that mercury shall be an elixir (rasāyana).
[Vimala:: Sattvapātana] Vimala [mica] with the juice of *śigru*, along with potassium nitrate (*kāṅkṣī*), green vitriol (*kāsīsa*), and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*).
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* [This refers to the process of extracting the essence (*sattva-pātana*) of mica using the aforementioned reagents.]
*Kāṅkṣī* is the clay of Saurāṣṭra.
[It is] combined with *vajrakanda* and processed with the juices of the plantain tree.
When combined with the juice of *mokṣaka* and heated in a sealed crucible (*mūkamūṣā*), the essence falls down resembling the moon and the sun; of this there is no doubt.
Having ground that sattva well and combined it with mercury (sūta),
one should cast it into melted sulphur and digest it until three times its weight of metal has been assimilated.
One should indeed place stone possessing five qualities into a sand-press, along with a tenth part of silver ash,
and likewise dead vaikrāntaka.
Having ground everything together into a single mass and filtered it through a cloth,
one should place it inside a small jar and fill it carefully.
Licked with *vyoṣa* and *varā*, combined with *vimalaka* and taken with ghee, it destroys diseases caused by misfortune, fevers, swellings, anemia, urinary disorders, and loss of appetite;

it also cures pain in the bladder, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), incomparable colic, consumption, jaundice, all diseases of bile and wind, and—what need for other formulations?—it conquers all diseases without exception.

The mineral substance known as śilājatu is said to be of two kinds: that beginning with "cow's urine" (gomūtra), which is a rejuvenative (rasāyana), and another beginning with "camphor" (karpūra). Of these, the first type is further divided into two varieties.
Between these two, the one with a living being and the one without a living being, the former is superior in quality.
In the summer, from the feet of the snowy mountain, heated by the fierce sun,
the mineral substance *śilājatu* exudes from those foothills whose interiors contain gold, silver, and copper.
That which is born from the mountain containing gold, resembling the *japā* flower,
heavy, slightly bitter, and very sweet— that is the supreme elixir (*rasāyana*). (VR 2.104)
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):

First, regarding that [mercury] which smells like cow’s urine and is of three types according to its different origins from gold and other sources, he states its characteristics and so forth with the words "svarṇa... etc. (VRrsBo 2.104;1).
However, in another treatise, such as the Caraka-saṃhitā, a fourfold classification of that same substance is mentioned based on its different origins.
"Its origin arises from four elements that are neither too hot nor too cold:
from gold, silver, copper, and even iron.
Thus it is said.
However, iron [as a medicinal substance] has not been mentioned here; its characteristics should be seen in that very same [source], as follows:
"That which resembles bdellium (guggulu), is bitter and endowed with saltiness, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and cold—such iron is the best of all. (VRrsBo 2.104;4)
"The cow-urine-scented [guggulu] is suitable for all rituals among all [medicinal substances];
however, it is especially distinguished for the application of elixirs (*rasāyana*).
Thus [it is said].

In this context, since golden śilājatu has been described as the supreme rejuvenative (rasāyana), it should be understood that iron (āyasa) is not mentioned separately because it also possesses the primary qualities of a rejuvenative and thus performs the same function.
Śilājatu produced from a mountain containing silver is sweet, pale white, and heavy;
it destroys diseases of the bile (pitta) and specifically removes anemia (pāṇḍu-roga).
Śilājatu derived from copper is produced from mountains; it is blue in color, dense, and heavy.
Śilājatu destroys phlegm and wind, is bitter and hot in potency, and cures the disease of consumption (kṣaya).
That which, when thrown into fire, takes on the shape of a lingam and is smokeless,
and which dissolves in water— that indeed is pure śilājatu.

[The medicinal properties of *śilājatu*: It certainly pacifies fever, anemia, and swelling; it removes urinary disorders and weak digestion, cuts away excess fat, and alleviates consumption (*yakṣman*).

It uproots the disease of colic, destroys abdominal tumors and splenic enlargement, and cures pain in the stomach and heart. It removes undigested matter (*āma*) and destroys diseases of the entire skin; what more need be said? It is beneficial for both the body and for metal. (VR 2.108)

Whatever qualities reside in the minerals, secondary minerals, mercury, gems, and metals, those dwell in the mineral substance known as śilājatu for the sake of conquering old age and death. (VR 2.109)
Washed with alkaline substances, sour liquids, cow’s urine, and water, bitumen (śilājatu) is indeed purified.
Having placed the mineral substance (śilādhātu) in an iron vessel with milk, along with the juices of triphalā and mārkava, one should purify it with great care.
Śilājatu,
having been placed inside a sudation apparatus together with alkaline substances, acids, and guggulu,
becomes purified after being sweated for the duration of one ghaṭikā.
[The killing of *śilājatu*: ] Encased with realgar, sulphur, and yellow orpiment, along with the juice of *mātuluṅga*,
the mineral *śilādhātu* is indeed killed by eight applications of the *giriṇḍaka* fire.

One should consume an equal measure of powdered *śilājatu* (bitumen) originating from stone, along with *kānta* and *vaikrāntaka* iron, combined with *triphalā*, the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*), and ghee, in a dose equivalent to a *valla*.

This is effective for jaundice, consumption, loss of digestive fire, urinary disorders, diseases of the bladder, abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, various types of ascites, diverse kinds of colic, and vaginal diseases. (VR 2.114)
If one practices this for six months according to the procedure for elixirs (rasāyana),
one shall be freed from wrinkles and graying hair and live happily for a hundred years.
The mountain-born *śilājatu*, ground with the group of fluxing agents (*drāvaṇavarga*) along with sour liquids,
is placed inside a crucible, sealed, and strongly blown with *kokila* coals.
Let the stone element release its essence, which, through the winds, becomes like iron.
The *śilājatu* known as *karpūra-śilājatu* is pale white and has the appearance of sand.
[Karpūraśilājatu:
medicinal properties] It destroys dysuria, urinary calculi, urinary disorders, jaundice, and anemia. (VRṢ 2.117)
[Karpūraśilājatu: Purification] When thoroughly mixed with the water of cardamom (*elā*), that [karpūraśilājatu], once processed, attains purity.
[Karpūraśilājatu: Killing]
Regarding the "striking down of beings," the wise have not prescribed the killing of beings as the "striking down of beings."
Having drunk the *hālāhala* poison vomited up by Garuḍa after he had swallowed the nectar of immortality,
[the gods] produced emeralds on the mountain called Marakata by means of that poison mixed with amṛta.
For that which has been vomited up becomes solidified and indeed arises as sasyaka.
That which has the luster of a peacock's neck and is rich in weight is highly praised as being of excellent quality.
A substance that is mixed with poison will possess qualities superior to those of the substance itself;
likewise, halāhala poison mixed with nectar will possess qualities superior to those of nectar.
[Mayūratuttha:
medicinal properties] It is supreme in removing all defects, poisons, heart disease, colic, root-diseases, leprosy, acidity, bilious disorders, and constipation.
Herein, mayūratuttha has been described as an elixir (rasāyana), an emetic and purgative, a destroyer of poisons, and a remover of vitiligo.
Sasyaka attains purity when it has been processed with the red group of substances.
Sasyaka (green vitriol) that has been sprinkled seven times with a fatty substance,
not spoiled, and well-steamed in a dolāyantra for three praharas,
becomes pure as five kharparas when processed in the urine of cows, buffaloes, and goats.
[The killing of *tutthakharpara*:
When combined with the juice of *lakuca*, sulphur, and *ṭaṅkaṇa* salt,
and sealed inside a crucible, it dies by means of *kaukkuṭa* puṭapākas.
As for the powder of *sasyaka* (calamine), combined with one-quarter part of *saubhāgya*,
one should place it within *karañja* oil and let it remain there for one day.
One should heat three *kokila* [minerals] placed inside the mouth of a blind crucible;
the resulting essence (*sattva*) will be beautiful, having the appearance of an *indragopa* insect.
Having sealed the crucible with lime and the juice of *nimbū* fruit, copper and *rūpya* (silver) ore, when strongly heated, release their essence (*sattva*). (VR 2.128)
Pure iron ore, treated with mica and combined with the aforementioned medicinal substances,
certainly releases its essence through various methods of processing. (VR 2.129)
Having taken this essence, which feeds upon the creatures of the earth and the nagas,
the touch of its seal shall instantly become a destroyer of the trident-bearer's [enemies].
This mudrā, which produces immediate proof, should be performed to conquer the poison of all moving and stationary beings that has entered the sight of spirits and ḍākinīs. VRs 2.131.
Just as with Rāma, so too did the commander of the moon-army (Somasenānī) utter those same words.
On the northern side of the Himalayas stands the great tree Aśvakarṇa;
there a trident appeared, and in that very place it vanished.
"A lotus formed by a mudrā, drunk after being consecrated seven times with this mantra, is said to instantly remove colic; thus it was spoken by Bhālukī. (VRṣ 2.133)

Oil heated over fire with this *mudrā* and applied with certainty destroys colic wherever it may arise by its force; it immediately induces labor in a woman and instantly removes eye disease. (VR 2.134)
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* Capala is known in the world as yaśada and dasta.
[Capala:: subtypes]
It is of four types: fair, white, reddish, and black;
it is also flickering, golden-hued, and star-like, being especially bound by rasa.
The remaining two middle types [of capala] are like lac in that they dissolve quickly, yet they are fruitless.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya (Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā):
Now, following the order of enumeration, after the description of tuttha, he describes capala with the words "gaura" and so forth.* (VRrsṬī_2.136ab;1)
1. This substance is not well-known in common parlance by its conventional name in this region or in the world.
2. It is inferred that this particular kind of stone is found within the earth in proximity to a zinc mine. 3.
Some maintain that this very substance is what is known by the name "radium" in the English language.

The artificial [mercury], however, will be described in the chapter on technical rules (paribhāṣādhyāya). Regarding the etymology of *capala*: it flows (*dravate*) like tin (*vaṅga*) when placed in fire; therefore, it is celebrated as *capala*.
Capala is considered to be scraping (lekhana), unctuous (snigdha), and a builder of the body and the metals;
it is an assistant to mercury (rasarāja) and is regarded as bitter, hot, and sweet.
Capala is transparent like crystal, hexagonal, glossy, and heavy.
[Medical properties of Capala]
It destroys the three humors, is highly aphrodisiac, and brings about the binding of the vital essence (rasa).
Among the great rasas, capala is indeed proclaimed by some as one of them.
The purification of *capala* is achieved by repeated saturation with *jambīra*, *karkoṭaka*, and *śṛṅgavera*.
Having powdered a mountain stone with grains, fermented liquors, and poisons,
one should form a ball according to the prescribed rite and likewise cause the *capala* to fall.
Rasaka is said to be of two kinds: *durdura* and *kāravellaka*.
That which possesses scales is called *durdura*, while that which is scaleless is *kāravellaka*. (VRrs 2.142)
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):
[The author] states the two-fold nature and the definition of *rasaka* in the verse beginning with "rasaka.
*Rasaka* is a specific type of *kharparītutthaka*, as stated in the Bhāvaprakāśa: [...]
*Kharparī-tutthaka* is distinct from *tuttha*; that is known as *rasaka*.
Whatever qualities are proclaimed for *tutthaka*, those same qualities are recorded for *rasaka*.
Thus it is said.
"With its stalks and leaves" means it is like the green leaves of bamboo and yellow orpiment (*haritāla*); such is the sense.
(VRrsBo 2.142) *Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya*: Now he describes *rasaka*, which follows in the order of the enumeration, starting with "rasaka. (VRrsṬī 2.142)
*Rasa* is the mineral earth that serves as the material cause for the production of mercury (*jasa*). That mercury arises as something truly equal to gold.
When the *sattva* (essential quality) descends, the first [result] is auspicious, and the second occurs in medicinal herbs and the like.
Rasaka destroys all types of urinary disorders (meha), eliminates phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta),
cures eye diseases and consumption (kṣaya), and serves as a coloring agent for iron and mercury.
Both Rasa and Rasaka were taught by Nāgārjuna;
these two excellent perfected elixirs (siddharasa) are renowned as being supremely effective for the transformation of the body and for the production of metal.
He by whom both mercury and cinnabar are made fire-resistant has,
without a doubt, made the accomplishment of body and metal his servant.
Having stirred the *rasaka* with the exudation of bitter *alābu*, one should cook it;
it becomes purified, freed from defects, and turns yellow in color. (VRrs 2.146)
When heated and immersed seven times within the juice of the citron (bījapūra), *kharpara* attains complete purity. (VR 2.147)
Having been heated thoroughly and then immersed in human urine, horse urine, buttermilk, or sour gruel, the *rasaka* (calamine) becomes completely purified. (VR 2.148)
Rasaka kept in human urine for one month will certainly impart color [to other metals],
just as pure copper, mercury, or silver may take on the luster of purified gold.
Having ground together haridrā, triphalā, rālā, sindhu-dhūma, ṭaṅkaṇa, and āruṣkara—
each in a quarter-part— with acidic liquids, one should rub the crucible (kharpara).
Having smeared a bottle-gourd in a crucible and dried it, one should seal it;
then, placing a shallow dish over the mouth of the crucible, one should blow [into the fire] from below.
If, when struck upon the iron pan, the flame becomes blue or white,
then one should hold the crucible with tongs and turn it face downwards.
One should strike it gently against the ground so that the stalk does not break;
having taken up the substance that has fallen, which has the luster of tin, one should apply it.
In this manner, after three or four attempts, the entire substance will emerge.
Rasaka,
together with Abhayā, tin, bhūnāga, turmeric, soot, and ṭaṅkaṇa,
when heated inside a closed crucible (mūkamūṣā), releases its pure essence (sattva).
Having thoroughly powdered lac, jaggery, asurī, harītakī, turmeric, sarja resin, and ṭaṅkaṇa, that [powder] is cooked with cow’s milk and ghee. VRṢ 2.155.
Having enclosed the substance in the form of a pill between a gourd and a mouse-dung pellet,
and having repeatedly blown upon it and drawn it out, one should melt it on a stone slab; thus the essence,
beautiful as mercury, is obtained in the form of tin.
Alternatively, one should bury a vessel filled with water inside the belly of a crucible;
a perforated lid should be placed over its mouth, and another vessel turned upside down should be set upon that lid.
Having cast the fire-crested [metals] upon the crucible, one should blow strongly;
once the essence has fallen into the water in the vessel, one should take it and employ it.
Having indeed cast that *sattva* together with *tālaka* into an iron pan (*kharpara*), [one should proceed].

*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* [The commentary explains: "That *sattva*" refers to the *sattva* of mercury (*pāradasattva*). "Together with *tālaka*" means combined with yellow orpiment (*haritāla*). "Into an iron pan" means into a shallow vessel made of iron. One should place these ingredients therein. (Note: The term *kharpara* is interpreted here as an iron pan or shallow dish used for heating and processing metallic substances.)
"In a *kharpara*—meaning in an earthen pot—one should crush [it] with an iron rod;
it will certainly be reduced to ashes. (VRs 2.159)
One should combine that ash with an equal amount of dead kānta iron.
Eight guñjās of this powder, combined with a decoction of triphalā, [should be taken].
Sesame seeds soaked overnight in a beautiful vessel,
when consumed, certainly and swiftly destroy even diabetes mellitus (madhumeha).
It cures bile disorders, emaciation, jaundice, edema, abdominal tumors,
blood-tumors in women, menorrhagia, and somaroga.
It cures all diseases of the female reproductive organs without exception, as well as irregular fevers,
menstrual pain in women, cough, asthma, and hiccups.
Sulphur, realgar, orpiment, antimony, red arsenic, mica, collyrium,
and kaṅkuṣṭha— these are the eight minor minerals (uparasas) used in the processing of mercury.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, tell me that secret concerning the majesty of Gandhaka."
Īśvara said:
O Goddess, in former times, on Śvetadvīpa, which was adorned with all kinds of jewels, [there appeared sulfur].
On the delightful shore of the ocean of milk, which consists of every object of desire.
And by the foremost women of the Vidyādharas and others,
by the excellent wives of the Siddhas, and likewise by the hosts of Apsarases, [the yogins were honored].
He was entertained by the charming celestial maidens with captivating songs,
diverse dances, and various kinds of musical instruments.
As she was thus sporting, her flowing menses appeared;
that menses, O lady of beautiful hips, was exceedingly fragrant and most enchanting.
Due to the excessive abundance of dust, her garment turned red;
having left that garment there, she bathed well in the Ocean of Milk.
Surrounded by celestial nymphs, you have returned to Kailāsa;
meanwhile, that cloth of dust has been carried by the waves into the midst of the ocean.
Thus, O blessed lady, your blood entered the ocean of milk;
and during the churning of the milk-ocean, it emerged together with the nectar of immortality.
Gladdening all those Danavas with his own fragrance at all times, he was then addressed by the hosts of gods: "Let him be named Gandhaka."
"May this [process] serve for the binding and the digestion of mercury;
may all those qualities which have been proclaimed for pārada likewise exist here. (VRrs 3.11)
Thus it was spoken of old by the delighted hosts of gods, O Queen of the Suras;
therefore, this substance is renowned on the circle of the earth by the name Gandhaka.

[The varieties of Gandhaka: And that, O Goddess, is also of three kinds: the best is like the beak of a parrot; the middling is yellow in color; and the inferior is white in color, O Beloved. (VRrs 3.13)
[The Varieties of Gandhaka (2)] Gandhaka is indeed to be known as fourfold according to its colors, beginning with white.
Here, the white variety is called khaṭikā; it is used for plastering and for the killing of metals.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya*:
"Khaṭhikā" is well-known in the world by the names *khaḍu* and *cās*. Likewise, *āmalasāra* is that which is yellow in color. (VRṢṬī 3.14; 1)
That very [substance] which resembles a parrot’s feather is the best for the purpose of alchemy (*rasāyana*).
The red variety, known as *śukatuṇḍa*, is excellent for the practice of alchemy (*dhātuvāda*);
it is rare and black in color, and it destroys old age and death.

[The Qualities of Gandhaka: Gandhaka is an excellent rejuvenator (*rasāyana*), very sweet, and is considered pungent and hot in its post-digestive effect (*vīrya*). It destroys itching, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), erysipelas (*visarpa*), and ringworm (*dadru*); it kindles the digestive fire and acts as a digestive (*pācana*). It releases undigested matter (*āma*), is drying, and removes poison; it bestows potency upon mercury (*sūtendra*) and, being born from the flower of Gaurī, is truthful in nature and conquers mercury. (VR 3.17)
It was formerly used by Bali for the sake of attaining great strength.
As he was dragging Vāsuki, the fat, rich with the scent of sulfur, melted by the flame from his mouth and issued forth from every part of the body.
Having attained the state of being a mineral (gandhaka), it became known as poisonous mercury;
therefore, this exceedingly captivating mineral is called *balivasā*.
Sulfur that has been steamed in milk for one *ghaṭī* and washed with water,
when melted in cow’s clarified butter and strained through a cloth, attains purity. (VR 3.21)
Thus thoroughly purified, he would cast away stones from the sky,
poison from clarified butter, and husks as well as his own physical form.
Thus, for pure sulfur (gandhāśman) does not undergo transformation through unwholesome [substances];
otherwise, due to unwholesomeness, it would destroy [the practitioner], just like the Hālāhala poison when drunk.
Sulfur, when melted and cast into the juice of *bhṛṅga*, becomes purified;
sulfur is completely purified when divided seven times with that same juice. (VR 3.24)
[The Purification of Sulphur (2): Having poured milk into a pot and tied a cloth over its mouth,
one should place powdered sulphur, which has the consistency of sand, into it.
One should cover the sulphur with a wide and long earthen pan,
and then ignite it from above the pan using forest chaff as well as stones.
The odor fallen into milk flows away and becomes purified;
indeed, when this is done a hundred times, it certainly becomes odorless.
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* [This refers to the purification of mercury by means of milk.]

He states another opinion with the words "in a pot" (*sthālyām*). Regarding the word "should kindle," the word "fire" (*vahnim*) is to be supplied as the object. "With forest-chaff" (*vanacchāṇaiḥ*) means with forest-stones (*vanopalaiḥ*).
[With stones and dried cow-dung balls from the house:
Thus, when the pure formulation of Triphalā, clarified butter, Bhṛṅgarāja, and honey— measured at one śāṇa— is licked, it is indeed purified.
He makes his pair of eyes equal to those of a vulture and attains a long life free from disease.
Sulfur combined with a one-sixteenth part of the three pungents (vyoṣa), finely powdered,
should be scattered upon a cloth measuring one cubit (aratni) in length and wrapped around it. VR 3.29.
Then, having wrapped it with thread, one should immerse it for a watch (yāma) in oil;
holding it with tongs, one should ignite the center of the wick,
so that the melted fragrance falls drop by drop into a glass vessel.
One should place three drops of that liquefied sulfur onto a leaf of the betel vine (*nāgavallī*).
One should then grind the pure mercury, measured by means of a tube, with the medicinal paste.
Then, one should consume that mercury (druti) along with the leaf [of the plant] and the ore (sūta), using a finger;
it produces intense digestive stimulation and destroys consumption and jaundice.
It quickly destroys cough, dyspnea, pain, distress, and extremely difficult-to-subdue grahaṇī, and it brings about lightness of the body.
Pure sulfur, once melted in an iron vessel smeared with ghee, [is used for the preparation of] fragrant oil (gandhataila).
One should consume two niṣkas of this, cast from a ladle smeared with ghee;
it destroys diseases such as consumption and, in particular, leprosy.
One engaged in yoga should indeed avoid alkaline substances, acids, oils, fermented gruel, burning foods, and pulses while practicing purified sulfur.
Gandhaka mixed with an equal amount of marica and combined with six times its weight of triphalā,
when rubbed with the root of śamyāka and drunk, destroys all types of kuṣṭha.
One should grind its root in water and apply it to the body every day;
this proven and effective application is powerful in all respects,
as has been correctly proclaimed here by the illustrious Somadeva.
Having ground two niṣkas of fragrant substance and combined it with oil,
one should then indeed add water from the apāmārga plant along with oil and black pepper.
Having smeared his entire body [with ashes], he should thereafter remain in the heat;
indeed, during the third watch, he should eat curd-rice.
Likewise, he should worship the fire at night and likewise upon rising at dawn;
having smeared himself with buffalo dung, he should bathe in cold water.
Then, having anointed the body with ghee, one should bathe with desired warm water;
by this sequential application, even long-standing scabies and itching that are difficult to conquer will certainly be destroyed with great speed.
A hundred applications of incense have not been proclaimed here by King Somadeva, for fear of making the book too voluminous.
Alternatively, one should smear a cloth seven times with the milks of *arka* and *snuhī*. Then,
having ground sulfur with fresh butter (*navanīta*), one should coat the cloth thickly with it.
One should place that burning wick, held at the bite, with its tip facing downward;
the oil will fall into the vessel below and should be collected for use in medicinal formulations.
Pure sulfur removes diseases such as leprosy, death, old age, and the like.
The fire-maker is greatly heating and increases virility.
Gairika is of two types: one is stone-gairika, and the second is gold-gairika.
Stone-geru is said to be hard and copper-colored.
Gold ochre is extremely red, unctuous, and smooth.
Gold ochre is sweet, unctuous, cooling, beneficial for the eyes, astringent, and a subduer of blood-bile (raktapitta).
Gold-ochre (svarṇagairika) destroys hiccup, vomiting, and poison, and it is a blood-purifier;
[so too is] stone-ochre (pāṣāṇagairika).
And there is another variety, stone-ochre, which is inferior to the former in its qualities.
Red ochre, when processed with cow's milk, attains purity.
Gairika is indeed the form of *sattva*, as proclaimed by Nandin.
Some have said that the sattva falls from red ochre moistened with alkaline acids;
it attends upon the lord of mercury (sūtendra) and becomes one with it, possessing even greater qualities.
Kāsīsa is of two types: one beginning with *vālukā*, and another preceded by *puṣpa*.
Vālukāpuṣpa-kāsīsa has the appearance of the smoke of alkaline substances, acids, and agaru; it is hot in potency, destroys poison, cures vitiligo, and dyes the hair. (VR 3.53)
Flower-sulfate (puṣpākāsīsa) is highly praised; it is slightly warm, astringent-sour, and extremely beneficial for the eyes.
It destroys diseases caused by poison, wind, and phlegm, as well as wounds; it cures leucoderma and consumption, and it dyes the hair black.
Kāsīsa becomes free of impurities when moistened once with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
Just as one extracts the essence from *tuvarī*, one should likewise extract the essence from this [copper]. (VRṣ 3.56)
Kāsīsa attains purity through bile and by means of a woman’s menses.
Equal parts of *kāsīsa* killed by mercury and *kāsīsa* killed by mercury,
combined with equal parts of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and *vella*, [should be used].
Taken at dawn in a dose of one śāṇa, saturated with an unequal portion of ghee and honey,
it swiftly destroys vitiligo, anemia, and consumption.
When consumed for the duration of a year according to the procedure for elixirs (rasāyana), it cures abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, colic, and especially diseases of the bowels.
The consumption of *āmā* is excellent for kindling a weak digestive fire;
it certainly destroys gray hair along with wrinkles.
That which is produced from the *saurāṣṭra* stone is considered *tuvarī*;
it adheres to clothes and binds the dye of madder.
The second is proclaimed to be of two types: *phaṭakī* and *phullikā*.
Slightly yellow, heavy, and unctuous, *pītikā* destroys poison;
it cures wounds and leprosy, and especially destroys all types of *kuṣṭha*.
Nirbhārā is considered to be white in color and unctuous, while the other is sour;
that is called phullatuvarī, which, when applied as a paste, causes copper to turn into iron.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Regarding its varieties, he says: "the crystalline (*sphaṭikī*) and the yellow (*pītikā*)" (VRṢṬī 3.65).

Having smeared a copper leaf or an iron leaf with the crystalline [substance] one hundred times, it should subsequently be made to move—that is, it should be caused to be consumed—by means of mercury, by the agent who performs the action. This is the meaning.

* Because this [substance] is employed as a *viḍa*-reagent (*viḍadravya*) in the process of *jāraṇā* (digestion/digestive assimilation). // VRrsṬī_3.65;3 * Here, the verbal root *car-* has the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it. // VRrsṬī_3.65;4 $ * Commentary: Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:
Regarding the phrase "from smearing" (*lepāt*):

by means of a smear of *phullatuvarī*, copper abandons its iron portion; that is to say, whatever iron constituent exists in the copper departs. Alternatively, it means that the copper acquires hardness like iron.
*Kāṅkṣī* (vitriol) is astringent, pungent, sour, beneficial for the throat, good for the hair, a healer of wounds, and a destroyer of poison.
It removes vitiligo, is beneficial for the eyes, bestows the pacification of the three humors, and acts as a solvent for mercury.
Tamarind, having been cast into sour gruel (kāñjika), attains purification after three days.
When *tuvarī* is rubbed with alkaline substances and acids and then blown upon in a furnace, it certainly releases its essence (*sattva*).
Then, one should saturate saurāṣṭra a hundred times with cow bile;
having blown upon it, one should cause the essence to fall— this most secret *krāmaṇa* [transmuting agent].
Haritāla is said to be of two kinds: that which consists of leaves (pattrādi) and that known as a solid mass (piṇḍa).
Gold-colored, heavy, glossy, thin-leaved, and radiant—
that is called *pattratālaka*; it possesses many leaves and is an elixir (*rasāyana*).
Piṇḍatālaka is leafless, resembling a cluster (piṇḍa), possessing very little sap, and likewise heavy;
it removes the menses of women, but that piṇḍatālaka has few medicinal qualities.

Haritāla (yellow orpiment) is said to destroy phlegm, blood disorders, poisons, wind, and spirits; it specifically removes [the affliction of] women who have lost their menses. It is unctuous, hot, pungent, digestive, and a destroyer of skin diseases.
Haritāla is purified by means of the dolāyantra (swinging apparatus) in either the juice of a gourd (*kūṣmāṇḍa*), or in water mixed with sesame ash,
or in water combined with a powder. *Vīrasiṃhāvaloka* 3.74.
Impure haritāla (orpiment) destroys longevity and causes phlegm, wind, and urinary disorders.
It causes the limbs to crack and contract; therefore, one should purify it with that [remedy].
Having reduced realgar (tālaka) to small particles and adding one-tenth part of borax (ṭaṅkaṇa),
it should be washed with the juice of jambīra fruits and then washed with fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika).

Having tied it in a fourfold cloth, one should cook it for a day in a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*) with powdered *āranāla* (fermented gruel) or in the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa* (pumpkin gourd) for a day; or it should be sweated with the waters of *śālmalī*— thus *tālaka* attains purification.
Having ground the haritāla (orpiment), it should be infused three times with a decoction of brahmamūla that has become thickened like honey; then, it should be ground again in buffalo urine.
Having sealed the crucible with ten stones and then ground it, one should cook it in this manner twelve times; thus purified, one may employ it in medicinal formulations.
Having soaked yellow orpiment in a decoction of horse gram (kulittha), along with *saubhāgya*, buffalo ghee, and honey,
one should place it in a pot and subject it to distillation using an acidic liquid through a perforated vessel.
Having properly sealed [the opening], one should ignite the fire, increasing it gradually,
for the duration of one watch (prahara), covering the hole with cow dung.
At the end of the watch, having opened the aperture and seeing pale smoke,
one should remove the cold vessel, extract the essence, and take it away.
There are indeed tens of millions of varieties of all stone-beings;
however, fearing excessive prolixity in the text, I have certainly not written of them here.
One should grind *palālaka* with the milky sap of the sun (*arka*) for one day;
then, having cast it into *ṣoḍaśikā* oil and mixed it, one should cook it.
In an unobstructed place, one should certainly collect a white being that has been lying beneath for seven watches until its body has become cold to the touch.
Then, having thoroughly ground haritāla together with the hair of a goat and the bile of a cat for two days with great effort, [one should proceed with the extraction of the essence].
One should place it, combined with the group of fluxing agents, into a glass vessel;
having smeared it three times with clay and dried it thoroughly in the hot sun.
Then, having inserted that half-earthen vessel into the opening of the crucible, one should kindle the fire for a period of twelve hours;
once it has cooled, one should collect the pure essence (sattva) situated at the neck of the crucible.
Having tied haritāla weighing half a *pala* in a firm white cloth,
one should carefully smear it with *bali* and dry it thoroughly three times.
When the three myrobalans have been liquefied, one should throw a cloth-bag of talaka into the molten copper;
one should quickly cover it with ash, and once it has cooled and been encased in copper, one should obtain the soft essence (sattva), which is prescribed for alchemical elixirs (rasa-rasāyana).
Realgar (manaḥśilā) is said to be of three types: Śyāmāṅgī, Kaṇavīrakā, and that called Khaṇḍā; their characteristics are described hereafter in detail.
