*Manaḥśilā* (realgar) is considered *śyāmikā* when it is dark-bodied (*śyāmāṅgī*), dark (*śyāmā*), red (*raktā*), pale-white (*sagaurā*), and heavy with weight (*bhārāḍhyā*).
[Regarding *manaḥśilā* as *kaṇavīraka*:]*
The Kaṇavīrakā is radiant, not pale, and has a coppery luster.
The *manaḥśilā* known as *khaṇḍa* has limbs that are intensely red when powdered; it is accompanied by its mineral essence (*sabhārā*) and is preceded by fragments (*khaṇḍapūrvikā*).
It is proclaimed to be excellent due to the qualities mentioned subsequently and is said to abound in living beings (*bhūrisattvā*).
[The Qualities of Realgar (Manaḥśilā): Realgar is the foremost of all elixirs; it is bitter, pungent, and hot, and it destroys phlegm and wind.
Being of the nature of consciousness (*sattva*), it removes possession by spirits, poison, sluggish digestion, itching, and consumption. (VR 3.94)
Impure realgar causes urinary calculi and dysuria.
When purified, it removes all diseases, including weak digestion and the retention of waste matter.
[The Purification of Realgar: Realgar is purified by being infused seven times with the juice of *agastya* leaves or with the juices of fresh ginger.
[The purification of realgar:
One should cook realgar for one *yāma* each in the red juices of *jayantī*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, and *agastya*,
and for one *yāma* each in goat's urine, using a *dolāyantra*.
One should wash it with fermented rice water and employ it for all diseases.
[The extraction of the essence from realgar (1):
Having enclosed realgar in a crucible with one-eighth part of its own dross, along with jaggery, *guggulu*, and clarified butter,
and having strongly blown upon it, the realgar shall release its essence.
[The extraction of the essence of realgar] (2):

Having prepared a crucible with *kāravallī* leaves and water, one should place therein realgar that has been processed with *bhūnāga*, washed *saubhāgya*, and *madana*, and thoroughly rubbed together.
Immediately thereafter, one should blow [into the mouth] a stone ground with alkaline acids;
indeed, by blowing it in the measure of two *kokila* fruits, that [stone] relinquishes its essence.
Sauvīra collyrium is proclaimed first, and after that, rasāñjana;
then there is srotoñjana, and also puṣpāñjana.
Indeed, their true nature here is described as being like blue collyrium.
Sauvīrāñjana (antimony) is smoky-colored, cooling, and removes *rakta-pitta* (bleeding disorders).
It destroys poison, hiccup, and eye diseases, and it cleanses and heals wounds. (VR 3.102)
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya*:
*Sauvīra* is "black surmā" in the vernacular language. [Rasāñjana] (VRṢṬī 3.102;1)
Rasāñjana, which has a yellowish luster, removes poisons, [diseases of the] mouth, and ailments;
it cures asthma and hiccups, improves the complexion, and destroys wind, bile, and blood disorders.
(VR 3.103) *Commentary: Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā:*
Regarding "rasāñjana":
this is well known in the northern regions as "rasaud" in the Braj dialect.
Some also say that while this [rasaud] is produced from the dross of ore (*rīti-kiṭṭa*), *rasāñjana* is produced by cooking it with a decoction of *dāruharidrā* and goat's milk.
Srotoñjana is cooling, unctuous, astringent, sweet, and scraping;
it is beneficial for the eyes and cures hiccups, poisoning, vomiting, and diseases of kapha, pitta, and blood. (VR 3.104)
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Regarding "srotoñjana":
it is commonly known in the world as "white-colored surmā" (śvetavarṇasurmā).
*Puṣpāñjana* is white, unctuous, and cooling; it cures all eye diseases, overcomes even the most difficult-to-restrain hiccups, and removes poisons, fevers, and ailments. (VR 3.105)
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* "Flower-antimony" (puṣpāñjana) refers to that which is produced from the flowers of the rīti plant. (VRṣṬī 3.105;1–2)
*Jasṭaphūl* is well known in the Mahārāṣṭrī language.
Blue antimony (*nīlāñjana*) is heavy, unctuous, beneficial for the eyes, and removes the three humors (*doṣatraya*).
Rasāyana is that which destroys gold and makes iron malleable.
(VRs 3.106) *Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* "Nīlāñjana" refers to [the following]. (VRsṬī 3.106;1)
He is well known in the world as Nīlavarṇasurman.
Eye-salves are purified by the natural juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
Just as with the essence of realgar, one should extract the essence from the various types of collyrium.
Srotoñjana has the shape of an anthill peak; when broken, it possesses the luster of a blue lotus.
A wise person should recognize that *srotoja* (antimony) which has been rubbed reveals the luster of red chalk (*gairika*) and possesses a shape like the summit of an anthill—
characterized by many peaks rising and falling like an anthill.
Srotoñjana [is prepared] in the juices and urine of cow dung, and in ghee, honey, and fat.
And when that [element] has been cultivated extensively, it quickly binds the *sūtaka*.
Rasāñjana attains purification through a formulation with sūryāvarta and other ingredients.
From antimony as well, the essence should be extracted like that of rājāvartaka, for the purpose of causing the descent of the sattva.
Kaṅkuṣṭha is produced on the peaks at the foot of the Himavat mountains. [Subtypes of kaṅkuṣṭha:]
Among those, one is indeed called a *nālikā*, while the other is considered a *reṇuka*.
Kaṅkuṣṭha of the *nālika* variety, which has a yellow luster and is heavy and unctuous, is the foremost and best;
[so too is] *reṇuka*.
Dust that is dark-yellow, light, and devoid of essence is indeed undesirable.
Some say that *kaṅkuṣṭha* is the dark-yellowish excrement of a newborn elephant, and it is described as a purgative. (VR 3.115)
Some [authorities] maintain that *kaṅkuṣṭha* is not suitable for the transporters of vitality (*tejovāha*).

Now, he describes *kaṅkuṣṭha*, which follows in the sequence, beginning with "Himavat" (VRṢṬī 3.116;1). It is yellow in color (VRṢṬī 3.116;2).
It is a mineral consisting of small stones, distinguished by many smooth and shimmering surfaces, and it is also found in living beings (VRṢṬī 3.116;3).
Both of these are of two kinds, namely *nalikā* and *reṇuka*, which are varieties of mineral ores.
Among liquids, the best elixir (*rasāyana*) is that which is devoid of essence and possesses many transformations.
Kaṅkuṣṭha is bitter and pungent, hot in potency, and a powerful purgative;
it removes pain from wounds, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), colic, abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders, and ailments of the rectum.
[Sūryāvartaka, kadalī, vandhyā, kośātakī, and suradālī are used for the purification of mahārasas and uparasas and for the extraction of their essence (sattvapātana).]
And the śigru, the vajrakanda, the niraṅkaṇā, and the kākamācī.

When repeatedly treated with salt, alkali, and sour substances using a single essence of these [liquids], the primary and secondary minerals (rasoparasa) are purified; when smelted, they release their essential natures (sattva).
Kaṅkuṣṭha attains purification by being infused three times with water boiled with ginger.
The extraction of its essence has not been taught, because it is indeed composed of essence.
One should consume this with a dose the size of a barley grain along with binding substances for the purpose of purgation;
having purged in a mere moment, it destroys the accumulation of undigested matter (āma).
If eaten together with betel leaves, it causes purging and may destroy life.

A person should repeatedly drink an equal quantity of a decoction of *barburī* root, cumin, and *saubhāgya*, along with *kaṅkuṣṭha*, for the destruction of poison. *Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī Commentary:* Barburī is the name of a plant; its root is used here. *Jīra* is cumin (*cuminum cyminum*). *Saubhāgya* is another name for *śatapuṣpā* (Foeniculum vulgare). *Kaṅkuṣṭha* is a yellow mineral (orpiment). These should be taken together to eliminate the effects of poison. One should consume this preparation again and again.
Gaurīpāṣāṇa is white stone, known in common parlance as *phulkhaḍi*.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya*:

*Kampilla* is a specific type of small stone well-known in the world by the name *kapilā*; this particular stone, which is of the nature of a virulent poison (*dāruṇaviṣa*), is known as *somalā* in the Mahārāṣṭra language.

[Common Substances]: Kampilla, capala, gaurīpāṣāṇa, and navasāraka. *Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):* Kampilla is a substance resembling the color of a parrot's beak; it is found in the Vindhya mountains and is used for purifying mercury. Capala is a mineral resembling mica, which is red when heated and white when cooled; it is found in the Vindhya mountains and is used for the purification of mercury. Gaurīpāṣāṇa is a stone that resembles a conch shell; it is found in the Vindhya mountains and is used for the purification of mercury. Navasāraka is a substance produced from the ash of salt-pit earth; it is used for the purification of mercury. These four are common substances.
Vahnijāra is a specific medicinal substance well-known by its own name, originating from the western ocean.

Kaparda, vahnijāra, girisindūra, and hiṅgula.

When the wood of the *karīra* and *pīlu* trees is being burned,
an alkaline substance arises; this is *navasāra*, known by the name *cūlikālavaṇa*.
The light white salt produced by burning bricks is called *navasāra*;
it is also known as *cūlikā-lavaṇa*.
[Navasāra: Alchemical Properties] It effects the digestion of mercury, the liquefaction of metals, and stimulates the digestive fire.
[Navasāra: Medical Properties]

Cūlikā-lavaṇa is considered to destroy abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders, and dryness of the mouth; it digests meat and other foods immediately after eating, and it is known as viḍa-salt which alleviates the three doṣas.
The *varāṭikā* is yellowish in luster, knotted at the back, and long and round;
it is designated by physicians of mercury as *carācara*. VRrs_3.137 //
The best [vārāṭikā] is said to weigh one and a half niṣkas; the middling, one niṣka;
and the lowest, three-quarters of a niṣka.
[Varāṭikā: medicinal properties] It cures colic resulting from indigestion and other such conditions, destroys disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī) and consumption (kṣaya);
it is pungent and hot, stimulates digestion, is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and removes wind and phlegm.
The varāṭikā is said to be used for the digestion of mercury by the king of rasas (rasendra) and is recommended among the viḍa substances.
But other types of varāṭikas are heavy and increase phlegm and bile.
Cowrie shells, having been steamed in fermented rice-water (kāñjika) for one watch (yāma), attain purification.
The placenta of the fire-crocodile was cast out by the ocean;
having dried up through the heat of the sun, it is known as *agnijāra* (fire-born).
Agnijāra destroys the three doṣas, cures dhanurvāta and other wind disorders,
increases the potency of rasa, and acts as a digestive stimulant and a digestive catalyst. (VR 3.143)
That [agnijāra] is purified by sea salt; therefore, no further purification is required for it.
The mercury situated within small stones among the great mountains is dried and red;
it is designated by the name *girisindūra*.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):* Regarding the essential characteristics of *girisindūra*, [the author] says "mahā... (*VRrsBo_3.145;1*).

* Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:

This [substance] is generally not found in the world.

However, some say that this substance, well-known by the name *kāmiyā-sindūra*, is of an exceedingly red color. But in common worldly usage, it is indeed *nāgasaṃbhava* (red lead) that is most well-known.
And that very substance is what should be used here; this is the opinion of Rāvaṇa.
According to his statement, "sindūra is derived from the nāga," [it refers to] girisindūra.
Girisindūra is said to pacify the three doṣas, act as a purgative, be the foremost binder of mercury, strengthen the body and the metals, and benefit the eyes.
Hiṅgula is known as Śukatuṇḍa, and Haṃsapāka is another name for it.
The first type of hiṅgula is śukatuṇḍa; it possesses few qualities and is called carmāra.
That which has white streaks and the luster of coral is called *haṃsapāka* vermilion (*hiṅgula*).

Now, he describes *hiṅgula*, which has reached its turn according to the order of the headings, in the verse beginning with "hiṅgula.
This *rasa* is a specific kind of earth found in the mines of mercury (*pārada*).
For this very reason, it was stated in the first chapter:
"They cause that clay to fall into a distillation apparatus, and from it, the mercury [is extracted].
Thus [it is said].
Even artificial [mercury] is seen in the world, produced by the processing of mercury, sulfur, and fresh sea-salt.
This mineral is of two kinds. Regarding the characteristics of the superior kind, he says: "white and so forth.

Because it is distinguished by its white and red colors,
this is the best;
whereas the first is inferior, as it possesses fewer qualities than the others.
He, however, is called a coppersmith (*carma-ra*).
Vermilion (*hiṅgula*) destroys all defects, stimulates digestion, and is an excellent elixir (*rasāyana*).
It removes all diseases, is aphrodisiac, and is highly praised for the process of digestion (jāraṇā).
The mercury extracted from this [mercury] by means of cinnabar is equal in its qualities to mercury that has been processed with sulfur.
[The purification of *hiṅgulaka* by extraction:
Having been dried and then soaked seven times with the juice of fresh ginger or with the water of *lakuca*, it indeed becomes free from defects. (VRs 3.152)
What is there to marvel at here? Cinnabar, well-processed many times with milk, goat's urine, and groups of acidic substances,
likewise makes gold— when heated repeatedly by intense heat— possess the very luster of excellent saffron.
Cinnabar, when subjected to sublimation in a *pātanāyantra* over a reservoir of water, causes its essence—which resembles mercury—to fall;
of this there is no doubt. (VR 3.154)
The *mṛddāraśṛṅgaka* stone is accompanied by its stalk and is yellow in color;
it is found in the region of Gurjara, produced on the side of Mount Arbuda. (VR 3.155)
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):
[The author] states the characteristics and the place of origin of mṛddāraśṛṅga as "possessing petals" (*sadala*).
It is distinguished by its membranous layers, like bamboo leaves or green *haritāla*. 3.155;1–2.
The synonyms and other details of *mṛddāraśṛṅga* are not seen in the *Nighaṇṭu* or in any other treatise;

however, that which is well known in our country by the name *mudrāśaṅkha* is called *murdārśiṅ* by the people there in the western regions. Therefore, I believe that *mṛddāraśṛṅgaka* is indeed the *mudrāśaṅkha*.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* In the Gurjara region, that is, in the country of Gurjara (VRṢṬī 3.155), there is a substance produced—

that is, originated— on the side of Mount Arbuda, which is a site for the extraction of nāga-minerals; it is a specific material consisting of small stones, characterized by a yellow color with leaf-like markings, and it is known by the name mṛddāraśṛṅga.
It shall become renowned.
He states its qualities as "the essence of lead" (*sīsasattva*). The taking up of the essence of lead is the cause.
Lead ore is heavy, pacifies phlegm, and removes male diseases.
It is the most excellent binding of mercury and the supreme means for dyeing hair black.
All common medicinal substances (sādhāraṇarasa), having been infused for three nights with the juice of citron and fresh ginger and then dried, become free from defects.
Whatever beings there may be, they are all purified without exception;
blown by the wind of purification, they come together with one another.
Thus ends the section on Karavālabhairava.
Regarding Rājāvarta:
Rājāvarta has a luster mixed with slight redness and deep blue.
That which is heavy and smooth is the best; any other is considered middling.
Rājāvarta removes urinary disorders, consumption, hemorrhoids, anemia, phlegm, and wind;
it is digestive, carminative, aphrodisiac, and a rejuvenative elixir. (VR 3.160)
Minerals such as rājāvarta and others are indeed purified by being steamed two or three times with lime-water mixed with the juice of nimba and cow urine.
One should purify rājāvarta with the fresh juices of śirīṣa flowers.
Rājāvarta combined with the juice of *luṅga* and *gandhaka*, when finely powdered and subjected to *puṭapāka* seven times, becomes killed (*mṛta*). (VRs 3.163)
One should cook the powder of rājāvarta mixed with *kunaṭī* and clarified butter,
together with buffalo milk, in an iron vessel.
One should cause the [ore] to be swallowed by means of the "five products of the cow" (pañcagavya) mixed with auspicious substances;
when blown upon with charcoal from the khadira tree, it releases beautiful essence (sattva).
By this sequential application, red ochre becomes pure;
[this is the extraction of the essence from red ochre].
In succession, the yellow and red essence falls beautifully.
Furthermore, the jewels should be understood as those which effect the binding of the mercury.
Vaikrānta, sūryakānta, diamond, pearl, and ruby.
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā):
Rājāvarta is called "rāuṭī" in the Braj dialect.*
Likewise, moonstone (*candrakānta*) and rājāvarta are the seventh.

*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Vaiḍūrya is that which, when there is the sound of water-laden clouds in the sky, becomes distinguished by sprouts.
For this very reason, it has another synonym: "cloud-metal" (abhraloha).
This is well known in the world as *pirojā*.
Vaidūrya and likewise blue [gems]— these are considered to be the jewels that should be collected with effort for the sake of the fixation of mercury (*rasabandha*).
The five excellent jewels are known as the ruby (padmarāga), the sapphire (indranīla), the finest emerald (marakata),
the topaz (puṣparāga), and that which is called diamond (vajra).
Gems for the nine planets in order are: ruby, pearl, coral, emerald, topaz, diamond, sapphire, agate, and cat’s-eye.

For the sake of attaining desired success, one should wear as amulets, in their respective order, the planets' friendly gems: kuruvinda, coral, pearl, emerald, diamond, sapphire, hessonite, and cat's-eye.
For the sake of success, well-born gems are said to be easily protected when used for aesthetic enjoyment, elixirs, charity, wearing as ornaments, or the worship of deities.
The first is called *māṇikya*, known as ruby (*padmarāga*); the second is *nīlagandhi*.
A ruby that has the luster of a lotus petal, which is clear, glossy, large, and transparent,
with a body that is round, elongated, and symmetrical, is said to be the best.
The *nīlagandhi* ruby is dark blue, produced from the waters of the Gaṅgā, with a luster that is dark within and reddish on the outside;
it is the most excellent of rubies, like the ancient *māṇikya*.
A ruby is defective in eight ways when it is possessed of flaws, hardness, impurity, roughness, lack of clarity, flatness, lightness, and curvature. (VR 4.12)
Ruby (māṇikya) is digestive, aphrodisiac, and removes the afflictions of phlegm, wind, and consumption;
it destroys spirits, vampires, and sins, and eradicates diseases born of past actions.
Delightful, white, light, glossy, radiant, pure, large, renowned, water-like in luster, and round— pearl is auspicious in these nine ways. *Vṛttaratnākara* 4.14.

*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* "Having the luster of water" means having the appearance of water, such that it produces the illusion of water from afar wherever it is situated; or alternatively, it means possessing a shimmering radiance like water, that is to say, distinguished by its brilliance (*lāvaṇya*). [Regarding the medicinal properties of pearl: *VRrsBo_4.14;1*
Pearl is light, cooling, and sweet; it bestows luster, strength to the eyes, and nourishment to the digestive fire; it is an antidote to poison and is purgative.
It provides virility, and the pearl-oyster from which it originates, as well as its refined processing, will certainly and swiftly eliminate the pain of indigestion.

"Waterless" (*nirjala*) means "lacking moisture" (*nirjaḍa*), since *ḍa* and *la* are interchangeable; thus it means "not cool," that is, "hot. Alternatively, the term "water" (*jala*) is used metaphorically for "beauty" (*lāvaṇya*), as it is observed that the very shimmering luster of a pearl is what is signified by the word "beauty. As it has been said:
"Within pearls, there is a certain shimmering quality of luster..."
"That which shines forth upon the limbs is here called *lāvaṇya* (loveliness). In this context,
by the word "water" (*jala*), the shimmering luster residing in the pearl is to be understood.
A pearl that is rough-surfaced, waterless, dark-brown, copper-colored, or resembles salt is of inferior quality.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* "Vikaṭa" means having an irregular or deformed body.
One should reject pearls that are half-white, irregularly shaped, or knotted. (VRrs 4.16)
Pearl is considered to destroy phlegm, bile, and wasting; it cures cough, dyspnea, and weak digestion; it is nourishing, aphrodisiac, life-prolonging, and a destroyer of burning sensations. (VR 4.17)

That which is greenish-yellow in color, heavy, glossy, radiant with a mass of shimmering rays, and auspicious— [is the best].

Topaz is auspicious when it is heavy, clear, glossy, large, even, soft,

Lusterless, rough, dry, yellowish, dark, and unevenly raised and depressed.

Vajra is said to be of three types: male, female, and neuter.

Iron is known to be of three kinds: muṇḍa, tīkṣṇa, and kānta.

Hard iron (*khara*), core iron (*sāra*), heart-iron (*hṛnnāla*), star-iron (*tārāvaṭṭa*), horse-iron (*vājira*), and that called black iron (*kālaloha*): these six types are said to be *tīkṣṇa* (sharp/steel).
That which is rough, free from dross, possesses a luster like mercury when broken,
and is brittle when bent— that is declared to be *kharaloha* (cast iron).

That which is rough, hard, and free from *pogara*— meaning free from those curved lines like curls (*alaka*)—
is called *sāraloha*, having a blade that is flexible due to its speed and strength.
That which is produced from white soil and resembles a lotus bud is called *sāra*.
The heart-stalk,
which has a body that is blackish-pale and possesses large joints like seeds in its beak,
and which is exceedingly harsh when cut, is called the "heart-stalk."
Pogara,
aṅgakṣaya, and vaṅga are the three names for pogara;
cikura and bhaṅgura are considered to be the next [names] for that which is derived from iron (lohāt).
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):
Regarding the definition of *khara*, it was stated that it is "freed from *pogara*"; therefore, he states its synonyms and so forth with the words "aṅgakṣaya" etc. (*VRrsBo_5.78;1*).
Furthermore, the state of being threefold here should be understood in relation to *pogara*; thus, *aṅgakṣaya*, *vaṅga*, and *pogara* have the same meaning (*ekārtha*) (*VRrsBo_5.78;2*).
He states the essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) of *pogarā* as "curly hair" (*cikura*). [The commentary notes:
"From iron" (*lohāt*) means on an iron body.
Here, it should be understood that the ablative case is used in the sense of the locative. "Curly" (*cikura*) means possessing a particular kind of bend, like curled locks of hair.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:
* The word *pogara* occurs here [in verse 5.78];
and its meaning is not prohibited [or restricted].
Therefore, for the sake of understanding, he states its synonyms: "aṅgacchāyā," "vaṅga," and "cikura. Thus, there are three names, three designations, for the *pogaraka*.
And the meaning of these names is that they possess a specific form and luster.
It is called "vaṅga" because the lines [on the stone] have a white luster (chāyā) like that of tin (*vaṅga*).

Because it has the form of a lock of hair (*cikura*) among beauties—that is, because it has the appearance of hair—it is also named "the lock" (*cikura*). Regarding what was said concerning "hard iron": if that iron is brittle when struck by a heavy blow of iron—that is, if it breaks—yet it is seen to be *pogara*, distinguished by its *pogara* quality, then even that hard iron is considered supreme and most excellent.
It is held that [the horse] has hooves resembling thunderbolts, with fine lines and dense [joints].
And that which has a dark-colored body and is well-built is proclaimed as the Vājīra.
That which has a dark blue-black luster, is dense, smooth, heavy, and radiant,
and maintains its integrity even when struck by iron, is considered *kālaloha* (black iron).
Sharp iron; coarse;
medicinal properties.

Kharaloha is dry, sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and cold in potency (vīrya); it is bitter and hot, and it destroys phlegm (kapha), bile (pitta), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), abdominal disorders, spleen enlargement, and anemia (pāṇḍu).

It immediately removes colic, liver disease, wasting (kṣaya), old age, urinary disorders (meha), and rheumatism (āmavāta). It is highly stimulating, an excellent rejuvenative (rasāyana), strength-promoting, and it cures hemorrhoids (durnāma) and burning sensations.
Everything beyond iron is superior, each being a hundred times better than the one preceding it.
Magnetite is of four kinds: the attracting (bhrāmaka), the kissing (cumbaka), the drawing (karṣaka), and likewise the melting (drāvaka); the fifth is the Romakānta.
[The subtypes of the *mukha* type of *kānta*: It is indeed that which faces one, two, three, four, five, or all directions.
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā:*

And regarding that [mercury], it is said that this distinction—whether applied individually or collectively—is for the purpose of digesting all metals; mercury thus becomes "mukha" (the mouth). Thus he says: "one, two, three," etc. (VRṢṬī 5.84ab;1). Even by means of the digestion according to the prescribed method of the purely *bhrāmaka* (*sattva*) mercury, the "mouth" of the mercury is produced (VRṢṬī 5.84ab;2). Thereafter, the mercury swallows all [metals] such as iron and the rest (VRṢṬī 5.84ab;3).
Therefore, even a single variety may become "turned toward mercury" (*pāradamukha*). That which has that [mercury] as its sole face is called "single-faced.

If the two substances, the *bhrāmaka* and the *cumbaka*, having been unified, are made "turned toward mercury" through digestion according to the prescribed method, then that [substance], characterized by the union of the two varieties, is called "desirable" (*kānta*) and "two-faced" (*dvimukha*).
In this very way, the meaning should be understood regarding the *trimukha* and other [types].

Even if this [mercury] is accompanied by the swallowing of heterogeneous substances at intervals, if it is first liquefied (*jārita*), it becomes "mouthed" (*mukha*); therefore, it is called *sarvatomukha*.
The meaning is that this becomes "mouthed" when distinguished by various types—whether homogeneous or heterogeneous, individual or combined.
Yellow, black, and likewise red— these three colors exist individually;
their respective deities, in order, are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):
"Touch-penetrating" (*sparśavedhi*) means that which effects penetration merely by touch, or that which accomplishes the refinement known as "penetration" (*vedha*) for mercury.
Regarding the verse: "The yellow [mercury] becomes touch-penetrating; the black is best for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*)."
Likewise, the red color is also praised for the binding of mercury.
The *bhrāmaka* is the lowest, the *cumbaka* is likewise the middling,
the *karṣaka* is the superior, and the *drāvaka* is the most excellent of all.
That which causes the various kinds of iron to revolve is considered "magnet" (kānta), specifically that which possesses the power of attraction (bhrāmaka).
She should kiss the lover who kisses her, and likewise draw toward herself the lover who draws her.
That which directly causes iron to melt is *kānta*; it is the fluxing agent (*drāvaka*).
[Romakānta]:
That is the *romakānta* gem, from which, when it is cracked, the growth of hair occurs.
The *kaniṣṭha* [type of *mukha*] has one face; the *madhya* has two or three faces;
the *śreṣṭha* has four or five faces; and the *uttama* has faces on all sides.
Bhrāmaka and cumbaka are both praised for the destruction of diseases.
In the matter of alchemy and elixirs, the *karṣaka* and *drāvaka* [processes] are beneficial.
O charioteer, a goad is said to be the beloved of an elephant intoxicated with rut.
Having identified the field, it should be gathered with diligence by the wise;
one should avoid that which is scattered by wind and sun— of this there is no doubt.
When a drop of oil spreads upon its water without adhering, when asafoetida loses its pungent odor and neem paste its bitterness,
and when milk, upon boiling, forms a peak-like crest and does not sink to the bottom— that iron is called *kāntaloha*; it possesses these stated characteristics and no other.

Kāntaloha is the most excellent among supreme rejuvenatives; it bestows long life upon the healthy, is unctuous, cures urinary disorders, pacifies the three *doṣas*, and removes colic and indigestion.

It alleviates diseases of the abdominal tumors, spleen, liver, and wasting, destroys jaundice and abdominal enlargements, and is bitter and hot in taste yet cold in its potency (*vīrya*). What more need be said? Through its application, it dispels all ailments. (VR 5.96)
Among the various pharmaceutical preparations of medicinal herbs, the preparation involving iron is highly praised;
therefore, with every effort, one should purify and process pure iron.
One should not cook iron [vessels] weighing less than five palas, nor more than thirteen.
First the mantra, and then the ritual action should be performed; thus the mantra is described.
"Oṃ, svāhā to the one arisen from nectar. By means of this mantra, iron is killed (liquefied).
All iron becomes endowed with a hundred thousandfold quality, each subsequent type being superior to the last.
In that regard, *kāntaloha* possesses ten millionfold quality, and even that is likewise of superior quality.
Iron, including all varieties such as muṇḍa and the rest, when smeared with rabbit blood and heated three times, is freed from all defects.
One should boil sixteen *palas* of *triphalā* in eight times that amount of water;
when the decoction is reduced to one-fourth, five *palas* of iron are added to it. (VR 5.102)
Having heated the leaves, one should sprinkle them seven times;
in this way, the impurity arising from the mountain [ore] or from iron is dissolved.
Iron heated and then quenched in a decoction of triphalā mixed with sea salt will surely cast off its mountain-born impurities. (VR 5.104)
A decoction of the juice of tamarind fruits and other such substances removes the impurity of iron known as *giridoṣa*.
Alternatively, iron that has been boiled for a moment in cow’s urine together with the three fruits (*phalatraya*)— [this is the *vāritara* method for killing].

*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):* Alternatively, iron that has been boiled for a moment in cow’s urine together with the three fruits (*phalatraya*)— [this is the *vāritara* method for killing].
That which has been stirred and drained is called *recitam*. Having cast *recitam* mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into an iron pan, one should cook it.
One should stir it with an iron rod until even a thrown blade of grass is consumed by the heat;
having ground it again and again, one should cook it in this manner five times more than that.
Alternatively, by subjecting the iron to four cycles of *puṭapāka* using either the juice of *dhātrī* fruit or water decocted with *triphalā*, it will indeed become soluble in water.

Iron powder smeared with oil should be roasted seven times separately— once in cow’s urine and seven times in the juice of *dhātrī* fruits over the course of a night; this may then be employed for all diseases.
[The killing of sharp iron:
Having heated the thin, leaf-like sheets of sharp iron in a strong fire, one should immediately cast them into water inside a stone mortar. (VR 5.110)
One should pound it vigorously with a thick iron pestle;
then, having placed large chunks from its midst between two mallets, [one should strike them].
Having blown [the fire] and properly cast it into water, one should indeed grind it as before;
that powder should then be subjected to twenty cycles of heating with mercury and sulphur.
In each successive layer, the grinding should be performed most firmly;
thus reduced to ash, the metal may be applied for various diseases.
Kāntaloha (magnetite) produces beauty and loveliness, uproots the disease of jaundice,
destroys the malady of consumption, removes poison, and eradicates the three *doṣas*.
It destroys various types of leprosy, bestows strength, acts as an aphrodisiac, and stabilizes youth;
it removes all diseases and is the supreme elixir—there is no other "earthly nectar" like it.
One should grind five *pala*s of cinnabar with breast milk;
with that, one should smear five *pala*s of iron leaves.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* vessel, one should cook it again with the decoctions of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
or with *jambīra* fruits or fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), using vermilion (*hiṅgula*) in a twentieth part [of the total weight].
Having ground and sealed the metal, one should cook it; then one should cook it again with those juices.
By forty such *puṭa* applications, *kānta*, *tīkṣṇa*, and *muṇḍaka* iron are killed; there is no doubt in this, provided that *hiṅgula* is applied at each stage.
[Sharp Iron:
Killing] Now, the aforementioned sharp iron should be carefully processed thirty times by being enclosed in a crucible (*puṭita*) with the juices of *vasu*, *bhallātaka*, and *vāsā*.
Blood arises, appearing like the shimmering of vermilion applied to ashes.
Alternatively, having ground the powder produced from sharp iron leaves with the juice of the three myrobalans (triphalā),
and having given it some cooked rice and formed it into a small cake (cakrikā): VRs 5.119.
Having dried it with great effort, one should cook it with five *puṭas*;
that ash is indeed red in color and should be applied according to the specific requirements.

Having smeared the entire iron with *matsyākṣī*, *gandhabāhlīka*, and *lakuc* juice ground together, and having coated it with the paste of *matsyākṣī*, [one performs] the *niruttha* [process] for the purpose of killing (*māraṇa*).
Having blown [the crucible] very firmly with two bellows until the emergence of the *triśūlī* (a three-pronged spike-like formation).
*Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī* commentary:
*Triśūlī* means a three-pronged formation resembling a trident (*triśūla*), consisting of three *caṭikās* (small spikes). 5.122ab;1
Then, having extracted [the oil], one should cast it into a decoction consisting of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and cow’s urine.
Therefore, having taken [the crucible], struck it, and taken up the dead [metal],
one should blow [the furnace] again as before and kill all the iron.
Having crushed it, one should then cook it thirty times with fragrant jaggery and triphalā; thus, ash that leaves no residue (niruttha) is produced.
Iron powder mixed with *samagandha* and saturated with the water of a virgin girl,
when enclosed in a sealed vessel for some time, will certainly cause iron to die.
When molten iron is repeatedly cast into mercury combined with the juice of *jambīra*, it dies; of this there is no doubt. (VR 5.126)

Cow’s urine and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) should be boiled; with that decoction, one should saturate [the iron] with diligence for twenty-one days, and then grind it again for one day. *VR* 5.127.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* vessel, one should cook it for a day and then grind it with a decoction;
grinding by day and sealing by night, one should continue this for twenty-one days.
By means of these twenty-one sealings, the three types of iron are indeed killed.
That which, when placed in a vessel filled with water, does not allow a drop of oil to spread,
and which, when thinned out, swirls around with mercury— that is kāntaloha.
One should pour molten iron into excellent molten mercury;
in this way, the metals, having been ground with some kind of acid, become purified.
One should cook [the substances] smeared with a quarter-part of dead mercury (mṛtasūta) in a closed crucible fire,
or with an equal amount of haritāla, gandhaka, and hāritejas.
Kāntaloha, when heated, smeared with alkaline and acidic substances, and placed in rabbit's blood,
becomes ash that is free from all defects.
Take pure mercury and sulphur in two parts, forming a kajjala paste with a mortar; then grind an equal amount of iron powder with both of these using the juice of *kanyākā*. VRrs_5.133 //
Having extracted that *gola* from [the vessel] for two *yāmas* and covered it with castor leaves in a copper bowl, it will become intensely hot within half a *yāma*.
One should place it in a heap of grain and later extract it at the end of three days;
having ground it, one should filter it through cloth, and it will truly become water-pervading.
It becomes lovely, sharp, refined, and "niruttha," and thus it is considered dead [as a base metal].
One should thus kill gold and other metals by turning them into powder, just as with base metals;
for this is known as the perfected yoga, received from the mouths of the Siddhas.
I have experienced this truth: it removes all diseases and old age.
One should employ Triphalā combined with honey for all diseases.

Indeed, this ash of iron, which prevents rebirth, is a divine nectar and a perfectly perfected elixir; when combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), *vella*, clarified butter, and honey, a single *niṣka* of it destroys old age, death, and the diseases born of time, while bestowing virtuous sons—just as it was formerly ordained by the illustrious Giriśa for the sake of Kālayavana’s father.

Iron cures disorders caused by parasites, anemia, depletion from wind (vāta), diseases of bile (pitta), obesity, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, fever, and phlegm (kapha); it also destroys edema and urinary disorders.

It removes abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, and poisons; it bestows strength and cures skin diseases and weak digestion; it is a rejuvenative tonic that brings comfort and averts death, just like *kāntaloha* and other such minerals.
Dead metals become liquefied and, when properly applied, they destroy even great diseases;
through the yoga of practice, they bring about the perfection of a firm body and the destruction of illness, birth, and old age.
That *kāntaloha* which has the luster of a ripe jambu fruit is the most excellent.
[Sharp::
Melting] Having impregnated it twenty-one times with cow urine and the ashes of *jālinī*, one should dry it;
by sowing that [into mercury], the sharp [metal] placed in a crucible will melt.
The ash of *suradālī*, having been dissolved twenty-one times in cow’s urine and dried,
makes even sharp iron (*tīkṣṇa*) as fluid as water when placed in a crucible by means of sowing.
The ash derived from *suradālī*, filtered with human urine twenty-one times,
results in the liquefaction of *kānta* iron through the addition of that alkaline solution.
Having powdered sulfur and magnetite in equal parts,
this should be added as a post-casting infusion (*pratīvāpa*) to molten iron; thus, the eight types of iron will melt.
Sulfur should be processed with the juices of *devadālī* for seven days;
by merely adding a small amount of that, iron remains like mercury.
Impure iron is not beneficial; from its consumption, it certainly destroys longevity, strength, and luster.
It indeed causes intense pain in the heart, produces numbness and affliction, and having purified [the humors], it brings about death.
O Shaven-headed One, muṇḍa is ten times superior to kiṭṭa; tīkṣṇa is a hundredfold superior to muṇḍa;
and kānta is a hundred-thousandfold superior to tīkṣṇa. Through its consumption, it produces excellent qualities;
therefore, kānta should always be utilized by men, as it removes old age and death.
It bestows long life, produces strength and vigor, destroys disease, and increases passion; indeed, for a living being, there is nothing else equal to iron as a supreme elixir.
One should blow upon the dross produced from iron using charcoal from *akṣa* wood; then one should repeatedly sprinkle it with cow's urine inside an *akṣa* vessel seven times over and over again.
This is declared to be maṇḍūra; one should employ it as a fine powder.
[Preparation of Maṇḍūra]:
Triphalā should be boiled with cow’s urine;
into that decoction, one should gradually sprinkle well-heated iron dross until it dissolves by itself.
That powder becomes a paste when ground; one should employ this as maṇḍūra.
Whatever qualities are present in purified *muṇḍa* are also present in *muṇḍakiṭṭaka*.
Therefore, one should employ rust (maṇḍūra) everywhere for the pacification of disease.
Vanga (antimony) is said to be of two types: *khuraka* and *miśraka*.
Among these, *khuraka* is superior in its qualities, while *miśraka* is considered not beneficial.

"Niḥśabda" means even when it has become like a leaf (pattrībhūta), it is devoid of sound; that is to say, it is not like another type of leaf which becomes noisy.
Niḥśabda is the khuravaṅga stone, while Miśraka is dark and white. (VRs 5.154)
Tin (vaṅga) is bitter and hot, dry, and slightly aggravates the wind (vāta);
it destroys urinary disorders (meha), diseases of phlegm (śleṣman), and fat (medas), and it is a destroyer of worms.
Having melted it and cast it into the juice of *nirguṇḍī* mixed with turmeric, the tin (*khuravaṅga*) is purified in three cycles; of this there is no doubt. (VR 5.156)
Tin (vaṅga) is purified for the second time by being cast into sour buttermilk mixed with *varṣābhū*, poison, and *viṣatindu*, and then placed in water containing *kaṭphala*.
Lead, tin,
and bell-metal are purified by seven applications of the juice of *nirguṇḍī* and by the addition of the powder of its roots, even when exposed to the sun’s heat.
Having smeared the leaves of tin and the leaves of *vaṅga* with *satāla* and the milky sap of the *arka* plant,
one should apply the ashes of the bark of the *bodhi* and *ciñcā* trees and provide small *puṭa* sealings.
Having ground it, one should employ the ash; it is recommended for use with juices and other substances.

Having given very small pieces from the wood of the forest-cotton tree (*vanakārpāsī*) belonging to Bhāradvāja,
and having ground them, one should employ the ash; it is recommended for use in elixirs and similar preparations.
[The killing of tin: One should smear a leaf of tin with the juice of *palāśa*;
then, enclosed within *tāla*, it dies—of this there is no doubt.
Tin smeared with oil of *bhallātaka* and wrapped in cloth undergoes death when placed in a fire of wood from the *ciñcā*, *pippala*, and *pālāśa* trees.
Take an amount of iron filings equal to the mercury-ash, and an equal amount of iron-ore ash;
one should grind these with the juice of *kanaka* flowers and also with the juice of *nimba* leaves.
Then, having separately added the juice of pomegranate and peacock,
along with an equal portion of the ashes of *bhūpālāvarta*, one should mix them together.
One should thoroughly rub it with cow’s urine, *kaśilādhātu*, and water;
then, having rubbed it with *guggulu* juice for eight days.
Having dried it and then powdered it,
one should combine it in equal parts with the juice of *bandhūka* and the powder of *nākulī* seeds, rubbing them together.

Either the seed of *nākulī*, the seed of *rāsnā*, or the seed of *śālmalī* should then be placed inside a basket, filtered through a cloth, ground with the essence of turmeric and cow’s buttermilk, and administered for drinking.
The mercury elixir (*vaṅgarasāyana*) is delightful and equal to four *vallakas*;
by it, the twenty types of urinary disorders (*meha*) are certainly destroyed. (VR 5.168)
Śāli rice, mung bean soup, fresh butter derived from sesame,
patola, bitter tuṇḍīra, and buttermilk are recommended for one's well-being.
Lead that melts quickly, has great weight, is black when cut, and is brilliantly bright;
which has a foul odor and is black on the outside— such lead is pure, and otherwise it is not.
Lead is extremely hot, unctuous, and bitter; it subdues wind and phlegm, destroys the urinary disorder of *prameha* and defects of the bodily fluids, stimulates digestion, and removes *āmavāta*.
One should add the powder of *sinduvāra* root, *kauntī*, and *haridrā* to molten lead;
then, one should immerse it three times in the juice of *nirguṇḍī*.
In this way, the Naga becomes pure; one should not perform acts such as fainting or striking.
In the case of the *māraṇa* rite,
one should place a jar with its opening facing downward upon a hearth shaped like an animal; and except for that opening, one should carefully cover everything else with clay.
One should place twenty palas of purified lead into that vessel called the *bhṛṣṭayantra*, and apply a fierce fire beneath it.
When the mercury has been liquefied, one should add one *karṣa* of pure, auspicious lead;
having rubbed it together, one should then add one *pala* of alkali at a time.
Of Arjuna, Akṣavṛkṣa, and Mahārājagiri as well—*COMM.
Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* Mahārājagiri is a specific type of vegetable, namely *rājaśāka*; it is of two kinds, small and large, and here the large variety is to be taken. (VRrsBo 5.176ab)
Having separately added the alkali of pomegranate and peacock [bone] to each.
In this manner, one should cook it for twenty nights over a fierce fire,
diligently stirring it with both arms using an iron ladle.

In this regard, the following procedure should be performed: having constructed a curved furnace and placed upon it a single jar with a curved mouth, one should cover all parts of the jar except for the mouth itself with a coating of clay. Into this machine, known as the *bhṛṣṭayantra*, one should place twenty *palas* of pure lead and liquefy it with intense heat; then, into that—
Having added one *karṣa* of purified mercury, one should stir it with a ladle; once it has become a homogeneous mixture,
having added one *pala* each of the ashes of *arjuna* and the other [specified plants] separately, one should cook it over a fierce fire for twenty nights, stirring vigorously with an iron ladle.

*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* A horizontal, oblique, and long hearth (cullī), known in the Mahārāṣṭra language as *āhāḷa*, is that upon which one should place—that is, set over—a jar with its mouth turned horizontally.
One should then cover and plaster that jar, excluding the mouth, evenly on the outside with clay to a thickness of one finger-breadth. (VRṣṬī 5.178;2)
Into that [substance] called *bhṛṣṭayantra*, one should cast twenty *palas* of lead.

When that has melted, having thrown one *karṣa* of pure mercury into it and stirred it about here and there with a ladle, once they have become a single mass, one should add one *pala* each of the alkalis of *arjuna* and the others.
Then, rubbing and stirring it with two iron ladles, one should cook it over a fierce fire for a period of twenty nights.

By that method, the ash of the *nāga* (lead) will become red-colored, or pigeon-grey, or a mixture of black and red. When the *nāga* has been reduced to ash, free from defects such as causing eruptions or other physical ailments, it becomes an elixir (*rasāyana*).
Lead that has been killed and then raised up is perfected in ten cycles;
that dead lead, freed from all defects, is an elixir (*rasāyana*).
[Lead:: Killing::
Niruttha] One should take the ash of the bark of the *aśvattha* and *ciñcā* trees in four parts of the snake [substance];
one should cook the snake in a vessel and stir it with an iron ladle.
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* With an iron ladle (*lohacāṭu*), [stirring] with an iron spoon (*lohadarvī*).
After one watch (*yāma*) [of heating], having removed that ash, [one should add] realgar (*manaḥśilā*) equal in quantity to the ash.
Having ground [the ingredients] with jambīra fruits or sour gruel (āranāla), one should seal it and cook it in a closed crucible (puṭa).
Having ground it again when cooled to the temperature of one's own body, combined with realgar (śilā) in a twentieth part,
one should cook it for one *yāma* in an acidic liquid within a *puṭa* as before;
thus, cooked by sixty *puṭas*, the lead (*nāga*) becomes well-reduced.
One should smear the lead leaves with the milk of the sun (milk) and stone;
by means of the *puṭapāka* method, one should kill it, and thus it becomes *niruttha*. VRrs_5.183 //
Thus, one should add lead-ash (nāgodbhava-bhasma) together with half a part of calamine ash (tāpya-bhasma),
and then add a quarter part each of copper ash and pure silver ash.
Furthermore, having separately powdered kāntaloha, abhraka, sattva, and crystal,
one should mix them all together and roast them with a decoction of triphalā.
Having pulverized that [substance] thirty times with thirty parts each of bamboo manna and mountain reed,
one should mix it together with equal portions of the powders of the three pungents (vyoṣa) and vella.
When licked in a dose of one *valla* along with honey and clarified butter,
it destroys eighty diseases born of wind (*vāta*), and especially *dhanurvāta*.
It cures all diseases of phlegm (kapha) and all urinary disorders without exception,
as well as asthma, cough, consumption, jaundice, swelling, and fever with chills.
It cures disorders of the *grahaṇī*, abdominal distension due to *āmadoṣa*, impaired digestive fire, and extreme indigestion,
as well as all water-related disorders, when taken with appropriate after-drinks (*anupāna*).
Brass (pittala) is of two kinds: rītikā and kākatuṇḍī. *— Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā*
That brass (*pittala*) is of two kinds: it is divided into the categories of *rītikā* and *kākatuṇḍī*. Among these, *rītikā* has two varieties.
Slightly copper-colored and gold-hued.
[Regarding the examination of *rītikā*:
when heated and cast into sour gruel (*kāñjika*), that which remains copper-colored is considered *rītikā*. (VRṢṬī 5.190; 4) (VRṢ 5.191)
Thus, that which is born black is considered to be *kākatuṇḍī*.
Bell-metal (rītikā) is bitter in taste, parching, destructive of worms, and a remover of blood-bile (asrapitta).
It cures anemia and skin diseases when used in combination; it is hot in potency yet cooling in its effect. (VR 5.193)
Kākatuṇḍī, when its oil has been removed, is bitter and hot; it subdues phlegm and bile,
cures liver and spleen disorders, and is proclaimed to be cold in its potency.
Brass (rīti) is heavy, soft, yellowish in luster, substantial in its constituent parts, and capable of withstanding hammering.
Such a style, which is very smooth and has polished limbs, is auspicious.
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):
"Barbarā" means inferior.*
Pale-yellow, harsh, rough, barbaric, and incapable of withstanding a blow— such is the inferior *rīti*.
Likewise, a foul odor and lightness are not desired in liquids and other such substances.

When combined with the dust of *śyāmā* and mixed with powdered turmeric, the metal attains purification through five cycles; this is certain.
Tin foil, when wrapped with lime juice, realgar, and sulphur, and subjected to eightfold *puṭapāka* firing,
is reduced to ashes; thereafter, it may be employed as required.
Having performed its calcination (māraṇa) like that of copper, one should employ it everywhere.

Melted brass, magnetite, and the essence of *vyoma* (mica), each of these three having been processed to death, are taken in equal parts; to this is added an equal amount of *vyoṣa* (the three pungents) combined with *jantughna*.
Combined with *brahmabīja*, *ajamodā*, *agni*, *bhallātaka*, and sesame seeds.
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* *Ajamodā* is *yamānī*, because it performs internal cleansing (*antaḥparimārjana*). 5.201ab;1
Indeed, even a mere niṣka weight of this, when consumed, destroys worms and cures leprosy;
it is especially effective against white leprosy, and is beneficial as a digestive stimulant and carminative.
The powder of gold and brass, when swallowed and then encased by the dung of a young, intoxicated black goat, [is liquefied]. (VR 5.202)
When smeared with this and burnt in a crucible, it releases a beautiful liquefaction;
possessing a luster like gold of fourteen brilliant colors,
it is said to transform the body into iron and is employed in mercurial alchemy (*rasāyana*).
By melting together copper in eight parts and tin in two parts, bell-metal (kāṃsya) is produced; that which originates from Saurāṣṭra is auspicious.
[Excellent quality bronze: It has a sharp sound, is soft and lustrous, and is slightly dark yet bright.
Spotless, glowing red when heated, and of six kinds—such bell-metal (kāṃsya) is praised.
That copper which is yellow when heated, hard, rough, and unable to withstand being beaten is of poor quality.
One should discard bell-metal that has lost its luster after it has been polished seven times.
Bronze is light, bitter, and hot; it is scarifying and clarifies the vision.
It destroys worms and skin diseases, subdues wind and bile, stimulates digestion, and is beneficial.
Except for ghee alone, everything else served by humans in bronze vessels bestows health and happiness, and is likewise beneficial and wholesome to one's constitution.
Bronze that has been heated and immersed in cow urine becomes completely purified.
[Regarding bronze: *māraṇa* :: *niruktha*] It dies by means of fragrance and *tālīśa*; it becomes *niruktha* after five *puṭas*.
[For the killing of bronze: One should saturate the three alkalis and five salts seven times with sour gruel.
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:*
*Ārakūṭa* is brass.
One should smear sheets of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and brass with that paste, seal them, and cook them in a *gajapuṭa*; thus they will attain the state of pure ash.
Bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), brass (*ārkarīti*), iron (*loha*), and that which is produced from copper (*ahi*); these constitute *vartaloha*.
This very same alloy is designated as "five-metals" (*pañcaloha*) by those who know metals. (VR 5.212)

Vartaloha is cold, sour, pungent, and dry; it destroys phlegm and bile, stimulates the appetite, is beneficial for the skin, destroys worms, is good for the eyes, and purifies the bodily excretions. (VR 5.213)
Everything— rice, side dishes, and soups— prepared in that vessel,
when devoid of sourness, is highly digestive, appetizing, beneficial, and wholesome.
Vartaloha, when cast into the urine of a horse, becomes purified.
Vartaloha is killed when encased with sulphur and haritāla;
it should be employed according to the prescribed rule in various formulations here.

The mercury is perfected by means of the *mahārasas* and other substances—those which are of noble origin, purified, and prepared according to the prescribed method; it is not accomplished otherwise. (VRrs 5.217)
Gems, metals, and substances produced from cowries, oyster shells, and stones— such as hooves, horns, and thorns—
along with the solid bodies found among the great essences (mahārasa) and others, shall indeed be reduced to ashes and thus become fit for the mercury (sūta).
For the purpose of liquefying the *vajras*, I shall describe the *sattva* born of *bhūnāga*;
that alone is the supreme brilliance of both the king of elixirs (*sūtarāja*) and the *vajra*.
One should grind [the substance] produced from purified *bhujaṅga* with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*,
with the juice of *nimbū*, and with the fresh sap of *nirguṇḍī*, separately for three days each.
Having crushed that [substance] together with the fluxing agents (drāvaṇagaṇa) and formed it into pills,
one should seal it firmly in a crucible and heat it strongly for two daṇḍas.
Having collected that which is naturally cool and placed it upon a slab,
he [prepared] pellets equal in size to mustard seeds, filled with an excessive amount of dust.
Having heated the gold pieces together with twelve parts of copper,
one should quickly wash the resulting grains and collect them with great care.
By means of that, one should perform the liquefaction of diamonds and other minerals as desired.
This is declared to be the "donkey-essence" (*kharasattva*), the unsurpassed elixir (*rasāyana*).
It is certain that the essence is produced within two, three, or even a single crucible.
Having taken four *prastha* measures of *bhujaṅgama* earth from the birthplaces of gold, silver, copper, iron, and magnetite, which are inhabited by *sattva* *bhūnāgas*, [one should proceed].
Having washed either a peacock, a hero, or a cock with water infused with turmeric and also with cool water, one who has observed a fast [should proceed].
Then, having caused it to circulate gradually, one should collect its excrement;
having ground it together with alkaline and acidic substances, one should dry it in the intense heat of the sun.
Then, having placed it in a crucible and roasted it, one should prepare ink;
this ink, combined with the group of fluxing agents, should be thoroughly ground.
Having placed it inside the crucible, one should heat it for two *ghaṭikās*.

*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):* *Khoṭa* refers to a specific substance used for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) and fixation (*bandhana*) of mercury. Since the essence of *bhūnāga* acts as a digestant for mercury, here by the word *khoṭa*, the essence of *bhūnāga* in the form of *ravaka* or *reṇu* is to be understood. (VRrsBo_5.229ab;1)
Having taken the *khoṭa* from the crucible once it has become cool, one should grind it.
Having washed the fine particles and carefully collected them,
one should blow upon them like gold, and having produced the sound, one should employ it.
This supreme *sattva* arising from *bhūnāga*, proclaimed by the illustrious Somadeva, is given as a ring (*mudrikā*) measured at one-quarter of a *pāda* and weighing two *śāṇas* of gold.
When smeared with water washed from it, it destroys the poison produced by mobile and immobile beings, eye disease, colic, chronic ailments, earaches, and the afflictions of childbirth.
Having crushed the roots of uttaravāruṇī in sour gruel (*kāñjika*),
one should add the crushed pulp of *aṅkolla* seeds.
That oil, thickened like clarified butter (ghṛta), should be collected according to the prescribed rule.
(*Peṭakārī* is *jyotiṣmatī*).
Having crushed the leaves of the *uttaravāruṇī* plant known as *peṭakārī*,
one should then rub [the oil] with that paste using sour gruel (*kāñjika*).

Having tied the seeds of *aṅkolla* in a thin cloth, one should suspend them in the intense heat of the sun; below that, one should place a cup. The oil that falls into it should be collected, as it destroys leucoderma (*śvitra*).
Having ground the powder produced from *aṅkolla* seeds with *kāñjika* vinegar and allowed it to steep for one night, one should thereafter form it into a ball.
Then one should heat it in a *kaṇḍuka* machine for two *ghaṭikās*;
thereafter, having bound that mass in a strong cloth and squeezed it with a wooden pestle, [one should extract the juice].

Having collected the oil situated at the bottom of the vessel, one should employ it; in this manner, all oils may be extracted by means of the ball-press (*kandukayantra*). *Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):* [The oil] located at the bottom of the vessel should be gathered and utilized; thus, by means of the ball-press, all oils are to be procured.
*Kākatuṇḍī* is white *guñjā*.
Oil may also be prepared from *aṅkola*, together with the roots of *kākatuṇḍī*.
*vākucī* is *somarājī*.
*devadālī* is *hastighoṣaka*.
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:*
*Karkoṭī* is called *karkoṭaka* or *kāṅkola* in the vernacular. [Regarding the extraction of oil:
It may be obtained from *vākucī*, *devadālī*, and the root of *karkoṭī*.
Oil produced from *viṣamuṣṭi* should be prepared with a decoction of *apāmārga*.
One should remove the oil derived from *jaipāla* by means of the decoctions of radish and *kumārī*.
One should extract *vākucī* oil using the decoction of red *apāmārga*.
One should prepare the powdered seeds of *kākatuṇḍī* (black *kākatuṇḍī*) and *kṛṣṇā*,
and having combined them with the powder of *kāntapāṣāṇa*, one should seal the mixture.
Afterwards, having extracted it from the heap of grain, one should take the oil.
Having examined all the treatises on the science of alchemy in their proper order,
this [work] is now being revealed for the benefit of practitioners.
Without the sequence there is no scripture, and without the scripture there is no sequence;
he who, having understood the scripture as endowed with the sequence, performs [the rite], is a possessor of accomplishment.
The preceptor is possessed of knowledge, skillful, and an expert in the science of alchemy;
he is accomplished in mantra, a great hero, and as steadfastly devoted to Śiva as Śiva himself.
One who is devoted to the Goddess, ever steadfast, intent upon the sacrifice to the deity,
a knower of the distinctions of all the Āgamas, and skilled in the work of alchemy—
one endowed with such characteristics shall be a teacher of the science of mercury (rasavidyā).
Devoted to their gurus, of virtuous conduct, truthful, firm in their vows, free from indolence, knowing their own duty, and always upholding the commands [of their teachers].
Free from deceit and envy, initiated into the traditional practices of their lineage,
supremely accomplished, tranquil, and devoted to the propitiation of the mantra— disciples endowed with such characteristics shall be suitable for the attainment of the *sūta*.
In that process of alchemical work (*rasakarma*), assistants should be appointed who are industrious, superior to the disciples, of noble birth, and devoted to their master.
Those who are nihilists, of evil conduct, and kissers of their teacher’s wife— those who desire to acquire knowledge through theft, fraud, and the revelry of the wicked.
For them, nothing whatsoever—be it jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, or the like—is successful;
if they act out of delusion, they merely destroy their own wealth.
There is no happiness for them in this world, nor likewise in the next.
Therefore, when the Guru is satisfied solely by the power of devotion,
then that [instruction] should be received by the disciple for the sake of attaining the realization of the science of rasa;
having obtained the boon through the joining of hands and heads, he should practice it well.
In a region free from affliction, a delightful kingdom of Dharma,
in a prosperous and auspicious city inhabited by Umā and Maheśvara.
In that place, which is an exceedingly beautiful grove adorned with four gates, the wise one should perform the practice of the king of essences (rasarāja).
There, a hall should be constructed— very spacious and beautiful,
provided with well-placed windows, and adorned with divine paintings.
Near that, on level and well-lit ground, one should construct a rasa-maṇḍapa—
extremely well-concealed, very spacious, and adorned with doors and bolts.
It was enriched with banners, parasols, and canopies, hung with garlands of flowers,
and resounded with the sounds of kettledrums, cymbals, bells, and horns.
The ground there should be made level, very firm, and like a mirror;
in its center, a beautiful altar endowed with the proper characteristics should be constructed.
One should grind three niṣkas of gold leaf and nine niṣkas of mercury with an acidic liquid for one watch (yāma); with that, one should fashion a liṅga.
One should cook it for a day in a swing-oven (*dolāyantra*) within a decoction of *sāra* wood, using a citron (*jambīra*).
There, one should worship that *liṅga* with most auspicious ritual offerings.
Whatever fruit results from the perfect worship of a thousand million lingas,
that fruit shall be multiplied ten million times by the worship of a mercury-linga (rasaliṅga).
Indeed, thousands of killings of Brahmins and tens of thousands of killings of cows perish in that very instant from the sight of the Rasaliṅga.
"Liberation is attained through touch; this is the truth spoken by Śiva.
One should worship in the southeast with the King of Mantras, the venerable Ghorarāja."
One should contemplate [the deity] as having eighteen arms, white in color, five faces, and three eyes; mounted upon a corpse, with a blue throat, and possessing a linga of the nature of the flavors.
Upon his lap, one should visualize the Great Goddess, who has one face and four arms;
she holds a rosary and a goad in her right hands, and a noose and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands,
possessing the luster of molten gold and wearing yellow garments.
The syllable of the power of Kāmarāja is the glory consisting of speech; "rasāṅkuśāyai namaḥ" is this twelve-syllabled vidyā known as Rasāṅkuśā.

With this [mantra], one should worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth; one should worship Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, and Kulīra in the order starting from the eastern direction,
using their name-mantras preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
In this manner, daily worship should be performed there for the sake of attaining mastery over the elixir.
The science of alchemy (rasavidyā), as taught by Śiva, should indeed be imparted to the practitioner by a joyful-souled Guru according to the prescribed injunctions.
At an auspicious moment, under a favorable constellation, and endowed with the strength of the moon and stars,
he [placed] a jar completely filled with water and joined with gold, gems, and fruits.
One should place [the vessel] before the mercury-liṅga wrapped in a divine cloth,
and worship it well with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, incense, and food offerings.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should perform a fire sacrifice in a well-characterized yoni-shaped sacrificial pit,
using sesame seeds, clarified butter, milk-rice, and flowers such as the *śatapuṣpā*, each separately.
At the conclusion of the oblation with the Aghora mantra and the Rasāṅkuśī mantra, he should summon the disciple,
who is united with the Kālinī-śakti and devoted to the attainment of the perfection of mercury (rasasiddhi).
She whose hair is curled, who is dark-complexioned with lotus-like eyes,
well-formed, youthful, broad-hipped, and auspicious— she is distinguished.
Her heart was agitated; she was bent low by the weight of her full breasts;
she was tender in her kisses, embraces, and touch; and she spoke with soft words.
A woman whose vulva is beautifully adorned like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree and who bears flowers during the dark fortnight is known as a *kālinī*.
She is supreme for the binding of mercury (*rasabandha*), its application, and for alchemy (*rasāyana*).
In the absence of such a person, any beautiful young woman may be given one *karṣa* of sulphur mixed with ghee every morning for three weeks;
she shall become equal to Kālinī.
Thus, the supreme guru, endowed with such power, should initiate him;
having had him well bathed, he should consecrate him with water from the ritual jar while reciting the mantra.
The true Guru should bestow the Aghorā-aṅkuśī-vidyā upon the disciple;
a suitable gift for the Guru should be given by the good disciple according to his capacity.
Then, by the command of the Guru, one should recite the mantra separately one hundred thousand times for each:

*oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ aghoryāratara prasphuṭa 2 prakaṭa 2 kaha 2 śamaya 2 jāta 2 daha 2 pātaya 2 oṃ hrīṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hrūṃ aghorāya phaṭ*. This is the Aghora mantra; [one should recite] *oṃ* [and] the Kāmarāja-Śakti-bīja-Rasāṅkuśā.
By command, [one should learn] the Vidyā Rasāṅkuśā;
with this Aṅkuśa-vidyā, one should worship the Goddess Śakti.
One should perform ten thousand oblations in a triangular fire-pit measuring one cubit;
using jasmine flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), and at the conclusion of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), there should be worship of a young girl.
Then, having prepared a clean hall smeared [with cow dung] and provided with an altar,
one should draw there a two-cubit hexagonal mandala using vermilion.
One should correctly draw [the mandala] upon the altar; outside of that, an eight-petalled lotus and a square adorned with four gates.
Upon the pericarp, one should place a crucible made of iron and inscribed with gold;
in its center, one should worship the king of mercury (rasarāja) in a quantity of exactly one hundred palas,
or fifty, or twenty-five, as if it were a liṅga of mercury.
One should worship in sequence within the hexagon these six: diamond, vaikrānta, vajra, abhraka, kāntapāṣāṇa, and ṭaṅkaṇa; as well as bhūnāga and the śaktis.
Gandhatālaka, kāsīsa, śilā, kaṅkuṣṭha, bhūṣaṇa,
rājāvarta, and gairika— these are known as the minor minerals (uparasa).
These are to be worshipped in the eight petals, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise to the northeast.
Rasaka, vimalā, tāpya, capalā, tuttha, añjana, hiṅgula, and sasyaka— these are known as the mahārasas (great minerals).
One should worship [the deities] at the tips of the petals, starting from the east and extending to the northeast.
At the eastern gate are gold and silver; at the southern, copper and lead; at the western, tin and magnetite; and at the northern, muṇḍaloha and tīkṣṇaloha.
One should worship all of these, together with the goad, using the Aghora mantra.
Vid salt, sour gruel-machines, alkaline earths, and salts;
crucibles, retorts, blow-pipes, husks, charcoal, and sandstone.
A bellows, various staffs, a stone, a mortar, and a pestle;
the tools of a goldsmith and all types of scales.
Various vessels made of clay, wood, copper, and iron,
as well as groups of divine medicinal herbs, dyes, and oils—
one should worship these outside the door with the root mantra.
The five-syllable mantra is *vāṅmāyā* (vāṃ), *hrīṃ*, followed by *kṣeṃ* and *kṣma*.
With this mantra, one should worship Bhairava there;
at that time, one should proclaim the names of all those who have attained mastery over the elixir (*rasasiddha*).
Vyālācārya, Candrasena, Subuddhi, Naravāhana, Nāgārjuna, Ratnaghoṣa, Surānanda, and Yaśodhana.
Indra, Māṇḍavya, Carpaṭī, Śūrasenaka, Āgama, Nāgabuddhi, Khaṇḍa, and Kāpālika are considered [the eight].
The enemy of Kāma, the Tantric practitioner, Śambhu, Laṅkā, Lampaṭa, and Śārada; the demon Bāṇa, the best of sages, Govinda, Kapila, and Bali.
All these lords of sūtas, accomplished in mercury and possessed of great power,
wander through all the worlds, eternally devoted to worldly enjoyments.
The twenty-seven physicians who bestow the accomplishment of mercury (rasasiddhi) should be honored with effort; thereafter, one should perform the worship of mercury.
Gladdening the twice-born and the gods, he should satisfy his chosen deities;
he should satisfy and worship with devotion, according to his capacity, the maidens, the yoginīs, the lords of yogins, and the practitioners of the melaka.
Thus, one should perform the festival of the elixir (rasotsava) endowed with all these requisites,
for the purpose of pacifying all obstacles and bestowing the fruit of all desired objects.
Otherwise, that deluded soul who, devoid of a guru, desires to perform the practice of mercury (sūta) without the sequence of mantra-initiation, [will fail].
He does not attain success even through hundreds of millions of efforts;
therefore, with every possible exertion, one should perform the rites prescribed in the scriptures.

Those who possess correct means of accomplishment, who exert effort, who are joined with a guru, adorned by the king’s command, averse to various worldly activities, devoted to the essence (*rasa*), wealthy, sought after by people, skilled in the work of measuring, apparatus, and proper cooking, and proficient in all medicinal herbs—for them alone, through the power of the prescribed ritual, does the glorious mercury (*pārada*) succeed; not otherwise.
The science of alchemy (rasaśāstra) should be imparted for the sake of righteousness to Brahmins;
to a king or a Vaiśya for the sake of prosperity; and to others for the sake of servitude.
When the Guru is pleased, Śiva is pleased; when Śiva is pleased, Rasa is likewise pleased.
When Rasa is pleased, all ritual actions (kriyās) are accomplished without a doubt.
The science of alchemy must be strictly concealed, certainly like a mother’s secret;
it remains potent when kept hidden, but becomes powerless through disclosure.
A task known only to the patient should not be performed by many people; likewise, medicine known by many patients becomes devoid of its potency.
One should construct an alchemical laboratory (rasaśālā) in a delightful place free from all disturbances, abounding in all medicinal herbs, and provided with a well. (VRs 7.1)
In the beautiful quarters of the directions guarded by Yakṣas, Tryakṣa, and Sahasrākṣa,
it was provided with various implements and adorned with a magnificent wall.
One should install Rasabhairava in the eastern part of the hall;
fire-related rites in the southeast, and stone-related work in the south.
One should perform surgical operations in the southwest, cleansing and so forth in the west,
drying in the northwest, and likewise the rite of piercing in the north;
one should carry out the installation of accomplished objects in the northeast.
One should prepare a collection of substances for the purpose of accomplishing the *rasa*,
as well as a very beautiful *sattvapātana* crucible and a *jharat* crucible.

An earthen crucible, a movable crucible, and many types of water-vessels; likewise, a pair of bellows, as well as tubes made of bamboo and iron. *Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā):* The "earthen crucible" (bhūmikoṣṭhī) is a crucible made of clay. The "movable crucible" (calatkoṣṭhī) is a crucible that can be moved about. "Water-vessels" (jaladroṇyaḥ) are various types of containers for liquids. A "pair of bellows" (bhastrikāyugalam) consists of two bellows used for blowing air. Similarly, there are "tubes" (nalikāḥ) made of bamboo and iron. These are the instruments required for alchemical work.
* *Kuṇḍyas* are round vessels made of gold and other materials.
One should likewise collect various tools and materials for leather-workers, such as gold, iron, bronze, copper, stone, and *kuṇḍyas*.
There were small mortars and pestles, round wooden troughs,

A winnowing fan, mats, skewers, and earrings; 7.9.
The sieve (*cālanī*) is said to be of three kinds, and its nature is now described:
it is constructed from bamboo strips and bound together with cords.
It is described as always beneficial for the draining of coarse substances;
this [instrument] is four-cornered and long, like a winnowing fan.
In that regard, long bamboo sticks and crosswise bamboo strips should be made with their tips protruding from the holes in the four-cornered wooden frame and bound with thread. Furthermore,
another bamboo shaker should also be made for the purpose of moving the powder.
It was fashioned from the wood of the *karṇikāra*, the *śālmali*, and the *harijāta* tree,
using a handle four finger-breadths in width, and it was auspicious.
The *kuṇḍalī* sieve has an expanse of precious jewels and is wrapped in goat skin;
another type of sieve has its base covered with horsehair cloth.
With that [sieve], one should perform the shaking in order to remove the most subtle dust.
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā):
One should prepare a third sieve, circular in shape and coiled like a ring.*

[The materials for crucibles are] clay from a furnace, chaff, cotton, sand, and ground stone.

*Śikhitra*, *śarkarā*, *śikhitra*, cow-dung (*govara*), and white sugar (*sitopalā*). (VRs 7.14)

Now he states their commonality and internal distinction with the words "śikhitrāḥ" (those with crests). Those which are embers (*aṅgāra*) left over and discarded by fire (*pāvaka*, *vahni*) after it has consumed [fuel] are considered both *śikhitrāḥ* and *kokilāḥ*. The distinction is as follows: those which are *śikhitrāḥ* are those discarded by fire itself after it has consumed [fuel]; whereas *aṅgāraḥ* are those separated from the fire through effort, such as by forcibly throwing dust or earth against the contrary wind, or by other means of suppression.
If it is argued that they are considered *kokilās* (cuckoos), [the author replies:

The *pālikā*, the *karṇikā*, and the various tools for cutting vegetables.
Indeed, all work beginning with the sweeping of the halls and ending with the cooking of the broth,

Having consulted with Śrīrasāṅkuśā regarding everything, one should perform the worship;

Physicians who contemplate the tastes, those who know the medicinal lexicons (nighaṇṭu), commentators,

For one should always cause the recitation of the Aghora mantra until the completion of the digestion of the elixir (rasapāka).
The attendants were industrious, pure, brave, and very strong.
One who is most righteous, truthful in speech, learned, a worshiper of Śiva and Keśava,
compassionate, and lotus-handed should be employed in the science of alchemy (rasavaidyaka).
One who has on his palms the marks of a banner, a water-pot, a lotus, a fish, and a bow,
and whose ring finger is marked by a line below it, shall possess hands that hold the nectar of immortality.
A physician who lacks instruction, is devoid of compassion, greedy, abandoned by his teachers,
and draws black lines [on the patient's body] is said to have "burnt hands."
Those who know the mantras for subjugation should be employed in the accomplishment of the treasure.
Those who are powerful, truthful, red-eyed, and dark-bodied,
and who possess the knowledge for terrifying spirits— these should be employed in the accomplishment of the *bali* offering.
Those who are free from greed, speakers of truth, worshippers of the gods and Brahmins,
self-controlled, and eaters of wholesome food, should be employed in the practice of *rasāyana*.
They will be wealthy and generous, provided with all necessary utensils;
they will always delight in the words of their teachers and be auspiciously engaged in the alchemy of extracting metals.
Those who know the names of various medicines, who are pure, free from deceit,

The essence of those who are pure, speakers of truth, believers, high-minded,
and whose minds are free from doubt, is always accomplished.

In the eighth chapter of the Rasaratnasamuccaya,
Somadeva speaks for the awakening of ignorant physicians;
this technical terminology of mercury has been proclaimed by those perfected in the scriptures.
Half of the perfected mercury (*siddharasa*), one-eighth part of oil and ghee, and likewise one-seventh part of all prepared iron powders, pills, and the like—
whatever is offered to the best of physicians after invoking Dhanvantari for the attainment of total health and happiness— that is declared to be the portion belonging to Dhanvantari. (VR 8.2)
Even that eleventh share consisting of goods purchased for medicinal purposes which is taken from the merchants by physicians is called the *rudrabhāga*. (VRs 8.3)

In this context, the substance called *navanīta* is the "eaten" (*bhakṣya*), and mercury (*pārada*) is the "eater" (*bhakṣaka*).

When the sixty-fold rubbing with mercury mixed with a fourth part of gold is completed,
that becomes *pātanapiṣṭī*; it bestows the supreme accomplishment upon the mercury.
