[Grastayantra]

The wise have described the *grastayantra* (swallowed apparatus) as having a crucible inserted into the belly of another crucible, being perfectly round at the top and bottom and flattened at the base;
it has indeed been proclaimed by those who know the art of mercury for the purpose of cooking the lord of elixirs (*sūtendra*). (VR 9.65)
* Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:
* He describes the *grasta* apparatus with the words "the crucible" (*mūṣām*).
It is for the purpose of cooking the Lord of Mercury—that is, for the sake of the maturation of the mercury.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Now he describes the *grastayantra*: "A crucible (*mūṣā*)... (VRṢṬī 9.65).
One should fashion a small crucible that is capable of entering the interior of a large crucible and is of equal circularity at its beginning, end, and middle sections. (VRṢṬī 9.65).
This yantra is known as the *grastayantra* (the "swallowed" yantra).
For by means of this, mercury—its movement obstructed within its own belly—is swallowed, crushed, or killed by a lethal medicinal agent (*mārakabhaiṣajya*).
Having gathered the mercury—which has been turned into a black collyrium (*kajjalī*) or rubbed with another medicinal substance—inside the base of a thick crucible (*sthūlamūṣā*),...
To prevent its escape, physicians place a small, shallow crucible upside down over it, ensuring the joint is firmly sealed,
and thus reduce the mercury to ash using the *gajapuṭa* method.
(The term *randhraṇa* here refers to the act of binding or sealing.)
[The *sthālīyantra*]:
Having placed copper or other metals in a pot and having sealed its opening with a lid (*malla*), it is heated from beneath the pot; this is known as the *sthālīyantra*. (VR 9.66)
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya*:
Now he describes the *sthālīyantra* (pot apparatus) with the words "in a pot" (*sthālyām*).

Having placed copper, iron, or other metals into an earthen vessel (*sthālī*), one seals its mouth with a lid (*malla*) so that the medicine is cooked by a fire situated beneath the pot; this is the *sthālīyantra*.
This is well known.
Having prepared an iron vessel for the incense-mechanism (*dhūpayantra*), eight finger-breadths in width and eight finger-breadths in height, one should proceed.
Indeed, at a distance of one finger-breadth below the throat, it is located there at the base of the neck.
One should insert thin iron needles horizontally,
and place thin gold leaves upon them.
One should indeed place that which is about to be described right here beneath the vessel;
one should then cover that vessel with another vessel turned upside down.
Having smeared the joints with clay, one should ignite a fire beneath;
by that, all the leaves are struck [into powder] according to the prescribed method.
The mercury moves with speed, and it melts rapidly within the womb [of the crucible],
especially when combined with sulphur, realgar, and mica, or with collyrium, or with dead snake.
The fumigation of gold leaves is proclaimed as the first;
for the sake of silver, one should fumigate silver leaves with dead mercury (mṛtavaṅga).
One should also fumigate [the substance] with other appropriate secondary minerals (uparasa).
This is declared to be the fumigation apparatus for the preparation of substances used in the process of digestion (jāraṇā).
Regarding the phrase "having prepared the incense-burner" (*vidhāya*):
it means a specific type of support (*ādhāra*) resembling a small bowl placed on the neck, intended for inserting a probe into the base of the throat.
Here, the first [clause], "a horizontal iron probe," is connected with the second, "and one should insert."
The grammatical construction is as follows: "one should insert thin, fine iron rods that are oblique and curved in an oblique, curved manner.
Regarding the passage beginning with "by that" (*tena*):

according to the stated procedure, all the beaten leaves quickly melt within the crucible; consequently, the mercury—that liquid gold leaf—flows with force and accomplishes its own purpose. This is the meaning.
"One should place the smoke beneath the leaf"—having been asked what that smoke is, he says: "fragrance," etc.
First, the best [method]:
having had one iron vessel made measuring eight finger-breadths in length and width, at a location two finger-breadths below its neck...
Having placed fine horizontal iron rods across the neck-support in a transverse manner, one should set gold leaves that are to be pierced by thorns upon them.
Having placed inside the vessel beneath those leaves a kajjali made from sulphur,
yellow orpiment, and realgar, or dead lead (mṛtanāga), and having covered that vessel with another vessel turned face down, one should seal the joint with clay or similar materials.
And one should ignite a fire beneath the vessel; by means of that, smoke emerging from the heated kajjalī and other substances will adhere to the gold leaf.
Those leaves turn to ash and melt within the core.
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā:*
Now, regarding the incense burner (*dhūpayantra*), he says "having prepared" (*vidhāya*).
Here, having prepared an iron vessel of the dimensions as previously stated, one should place a water-receptacle—a specific small vessel—two finger-breadths below its neck.
The vessel that serves as the support for holding the solid substance is designated by the term "water-receptacle."
There, having placed iron rods horizontally, one should set down and arrange gold leaves upon them. Below those, one should place the fumigating substances to be described later.
Then, one should cover the vessel of the apparatus with another vessel turned upside down.

Having applied a seal of clay, one should apply fire beneath the apparatus. By the prescribed method, the beaten leaves turn black. Then, by rubbing them according to the rules in a moistened heated mortar, the mercury consumes them.
And once consumed, they quickly liquefy within the belly of mercury.
Here, he describes the incense substances:
[they consist of] a collyrium made from either one or all of sulphur, yellow arsenic, and realgar, together with mercury.

Incense-making with that collyrium, or with the ash of a burnt snake, is declared to be the primary substance for the incense preparation intended for the purification of gold leaves. The remainder of the sentence is: "incense for the sake of mercury (tāra) is now being described."
Regarding this, he says: one should fumigate the leaf-sheets with the aforementioned collyrium (kajjalī) and with killed (mṛta) tin.

One should also fumigate them with suitable secondary minerals (uparasa) fit for the process of killing (māraṇa), such as cinnabar (hiṅgula), mercury (rasaka), honey (mākṣika), and so forth. The "preparation of the liquid for digestion" (jāraṇā-drava-sādhana) means the preparation of a liquid containing mercury that is useful for the digestion (jāraṇā) of the leaf-sheets.
[Ball-mechanism (1):
Having poured water into a large pot and tied a cloth tightly over its mouth,
one should place the substance to be steamed therein and seal its opening.
One should ignite a fire beneath this apparatus, which is called the *kanduka* (ball) machine;
other wise men call this the *svedanī* (sweating) machine.
This is clear.

Although this was previously mentioned as a "sweating apparatus" (*svedanīyantra*), it is stated again here for the purpose of showing another designation; alternatively, since no specific type of vessel was mentioned there, any vessel whatsoever may be taken, whereas here a large vessel (*sthūlasthālī*) is required.
Therefore, it should be understood that the excellence of this [apparatus] lies in its being distinct from the previously mentioned *svedanīyantra*.
*Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā*:
He refers to the very *svedanīyantra* mentioned earlier by the name *kandukayantra*, stating "in a large vessel" (*sthūlasthālyām*).

Other wise and learned men say, as will be described below, "or else" (yad vā) that it is a "ball-machine" (*kandukayantra*). Thus, according to their view, the meaning is that the *svedanīyantra* is indeed distinct from this.
The application of this apparatus should be understood for the purpose of steaming very soft substances such as flowers or medicinal pastes (*kalka*).
Alternatively, having poured water into a pot and placed grass over its opening— this is the *kandukayantra* (ball-press).
Having placed the substance to be sweated inside and having provided a lid, one should kindle a fire beneath it; that apparatus is known as the *kanduka* (ball) yantra.
A grinding stone suitable for a mortar should be blue, dark, smooth, firm, heavy,
sixteen finger-breadths in height, and nine finger-breadths in width.

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of yoga for the sake of the body and iron": this means for the sake of those yogic practices intended to achieve the strength of iron (*lauha*) in the body, that is, for the purpose of accomplishing those specific actions. *Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā*: [Commentary] 10.18;3–4. Regarding the phrase "arisen from the clay of those respective [substances]," in the variant reading "arisen from the clay of those respective *viḍa*s," the meaning is that they are produced or fashioned by the aforementioned *viḍa* and the aforementioned clay. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of yoga for the sake of the body and iron": this means for the sake of those yogic practices intended to achieve the strength of iron (*lauha*) in the body, that is, for the purpose of accomplishing those specific actions.

Now, he speaks of *viḍamūṣā*: "arising from those various *viḍas* and clays" (VRṢṬī 10.18). This refers to the powders consisting of *viḍa* that are useful for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*) and for the digestion of gold, which have been impregnated (*bhāvita*) with the juices and other substances as specified; likewise, it refers to the powder in the form of *viḍa* useful for the digestion of all metals and so forth, mentioned on the occasion of the description of *viḍa* in the chapter on technical definitions (*paribhāṣādhyāya*).
As previously stated:

likewise, the crucible (*mūṣā*) that has been smeared inside with various kinds of white earth and other such materials mentioned before— which have been processed and prepared therefrom— and with specific powders used as means for the digestion of the *viḍa* bolus,
is called a *viḍamūṣā*.

This crucible is for the purpose of the body, meaning it is useful for the body, insofar as it serves as the instrument for the alchemical process (*rasāyana*) that makes the body firm. Likewise, it is useful for the killing of metals;
for this very reason, it is for the purpose of the metals.
Likewise, "wealth" (*artha*) refers to riches such as gold and the like, serving as the means for the practice of alchemy (*dhātuvāda*) which produces gold and other precious metals.

Similarly, it serves as the means for the preparation of various medicinal elixirs (*rasa*) that cure diseases— such as those that destroy coughs, the "jewel-casket" (*ratnakaraṇḍaka*), those that eliminate hemorrhoids, and the "elixir of refuge for all the world"— and thus it is employed for these four kinds of purposes.
[The Vajradrāvaṇika Crucible (2): Equal parts of refined gāra, nāga-iron, husked *tuṣa*, and *mṛṣṭa* hemp,
combined with an equal amount of crucible-clay, should be kneaded with buffalo milk.
For the *krauñcikā* is proclaimed to be of many kinds merely by its mechanical construction;
a crucible fashioned from it should be smeared with the blood of bedbugs (*matkuṇa*).

And with the roots of *bālā*, *abdadhvani*, and *vajradrāvaṇa*, the *krauñcikā* plant, when afflicted by disease, endures fire for four watches (*yāma*) by means of its juice. *Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):* *Bālā* is *Sida cordifolia* Linn. (Fam. Malvaceae). *Abdadhvani* is *Cymbopogon citratus* DC. (Fam. Gramineae). *Vajradrāvaṇa* is *Euphorbia tirucalli* Linn. (Fam. Euphorbiaceae). *Krauñcikā* is *Hedychium spicatum* Buch.-Ham. (Fam. Zingiberaceae). "Afflicted by disease" (*vyādhitā*) refers to being processed with medicinal substances. "Endures fire" (*sahate 'gnim*) means it can be heated in a crucible. "For four watches" (*caturyāmam*) means for a period of six hours. "By means of its juice" (*draveṇa*) means by means of its decoction or extract. "When afflicted by disease" (*satī*) indicates that the plant must be prepared through specific pharmaceutical processing. This verse describes the method for preparing a medicinal preparation from these plants that can withstand intense heat during alchemical processes.

This crucible, though distressed by the liquid within, endures the fire even while being continuously oppressed by the contact with the fiery substance situated inside and by the contact with the external fire. [The replenishing of the crucible.]
When the crucible has become liquid at its opening due to the application of heating, the lifting [of the contents] for a moment is called "satiating the crucible" (mūṣāpyāyana).

*Commentary: Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* When the crucible has attained a state of liquefaction at its mouth through the process of blowing [the fire], the brief extraction [of the material] is termed the "satiating of the crucible."
Regarding the replenishment of the crucible, he says "in the liquid" (*drave*).

"Dhmāna" is that by which one blows, namely fire; through its application—that is, through contact with fire—when a substance suitable for liquefaction has begun to become liquid, the momentary removal of the crucible from the fire, which is its lifting up, is what is meant.
The meaning is "causing to descend"; that is nourishment (*āpyāyana*), satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*), and the accomplishment of stability—this is the meaning.
[Regarding the *vṛntākamūṣā*:
In a crucible shaped like a *vṛntāka* (eggplant), the tube is twelve finger-breadths long.
Like the flower of the thorn-apple, it is turned upward and as firmly attached as a well-fastened blossom.

Eight finger-breadths long and provided with a hole, that is the "vṛntāka-mūṣikā" (eggplant-shaped crucible). By means of this, one should extract the essence (*sattva*) from soft substances such as earthenware shards (*kharpara*). *Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):* The *vṛntāka-mūṣikā* is a crucible shaped like an eggplant (*vṛntāka*), measuring eight finger-breadths in length and having a small aperture at its base. It is used for the extraction of the essence from soft materials such as broken pottery and the like. One should first coat the interior of the crucible with a paste of clay and cow-dung, dry it, and then place the material to be processed inside. After sealing the joint with a mixture of clay and cow-dung, the crucible is heated over a fire until the desired essence is obtained. This method is particularly effective for soft substances that would otherwise be difficult to process.
Regarding the *vṛntākamūṣā*, he says "vṛntāka" and so forth.
Having fashioned a crucible (*mūṣā*) shaped like the fruit of the eggplant (*vārttāku*), one should attach to it a tube (*nāla*) twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long;
the portion at the tip of the tube should be eight finger-breadths in length, positioned in pairs above and below like a datura flower.
And one should make it perforated.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya*:
Regarding the "eggplant-shaped crucible" (*vṛntākākārā*), he says: [it is] shaped like an eggplant.
Twelve finger-breadths [in width].

Twelve finger-breadths long, the upper portion of the mouth of the upright, upturned crucible (*ūṣā*) is broadened gradually like a dhattūra flower; likewise, it is provided with three or four corners when joined together at the time of blowing [the fire], even though it is covered.

When the opening exists, by means of the construction of the corners precisely for the purpose of allowing the smoke situated within to exit through the path of those corners, that opening becomes perforated.
And that opening is eight finger-breadths wide; the meaning is that it is measured at eight finger-breadths by the winding of a circular thread.
The crucible shaped like a cow’s udder, which has a lid provided with a spout—
such a crucible is known as the *gostanī* (cow-udder) crucible, used for the liquefaction and purification of substances. (VR 10.25)

A medicinal crucible (*bheṣajamayamūṣā*) is like a cloth pouch (*vastramayapoṭalī*) filled with medicinal ingredients; it is a vessel used to hold cowrie shells, conch shells, and so forth, which are to be cooked on the ground by means of the "elephant-pouch" (*gajapuṭa*) or other methods. One should grind the leaves of *pāṣāṇabheda* and black earth in equal parts with the juices of *vajravallī* for one day, or grind them firmly;
with that [mixture], one should construct crucibles, blowpipes, and diamond-receptacles (*vajramūṣā*).
The name "furnace" (koṣṭhī) is well known for a vessel made of clay.
And that is of two kinds:
the ground-furnace (bhūmikoṣṭhī) and the movable furnace (calatkoṣṭhī).
That which was previously described as the *koṣṭhīyantra* is called the *calatkoṣṭhī*. Now, all those *bhūmikoṣṭhyas* that are being discussed are of two kinds.
There are two types, distinguished as the open furnace (*prakāśakoṣṭhī*) and the closed furnace (*sapidhānakoṣṭhī*).
The charcoal furnace (*aṅgārakoṣṭhī*) is one *rājahasta* in height, with its length and width being half of that.
And it was square, enclosed by a wall made of clay.
One should make a door on a single wall, provided with a width of one span;
the door itself should be measured at one and a half spans, very firm and auspicious.
Below the threshold, a wall measuring one span (prādeśa) should be constructed as appropriate for blowing [the bellows], and above the lintel (uttaraṅga).
A door should indeed be made at the top, measuring one span;
then, having closed the joint of the door with bricks and smeared it [with plaster].
Having filled it with fire, one should blow upon it with two bellows;
one should cast the fire and the material for blowing through the upper opening.
One should repeatedly prepare five *golās* (boluses) for the extraction of the essence (*sattva*) [of each metal];
this shall be an iron charcoal furnace suitable for the extraction of the essence of hard metals.
*Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī*: This refers to a furnace made of iron charcoal that is effective for precipitating the metallic essences of hard substances.
He states the characteristics of the charcoal pit (*aṅgārakoṣṭhikā*) as follows: "With the measure of a *rājahasta*," etc.
(VRrsBo 10.38). It is one *rājahasta* in height and two *hastas* in elevation.
The detailed explanation of the *rājahasta* should be consulted in the explanation of the *gajapuṭa*.
* Quadrangular means having four corners.
* "Endowed with a span in its extent" means twelve finger-breadths wide. * "And with a door of one and a half spans"—this is connected with the phrase "below the threshold" (*dehalyadhaḥ*).
The *dehalī* is the pedestal at the base of the door.

A *prādeśa* is defined as being one span in measure; its characteristic is stated to be the width of the thumb together with the forefinger (*tarjanī*), thus having the measurement of the thumb extended along with the forefinger.
The *uttaraṅga* is the wooden beam situated above the door.

Having fashioned a single earthen apparatus in the shape of a hearth, measuring two cubits in height and one cubit in length and width, square on all sides and enclosed by clay walls, one should make a door one span wide in one of its walls,
and beneath the threshold of that door, an inner opening measuring eighteen finger-breadths.

Having established a wall at the upper part of the door, as wide as the space between the thumb and the forefinger, one should construct another door above it of the same width. Then, having closed the joint of the door with a brick and smeared it,
one should fill the crucible with charcoal and blow upon it with two bellows.

When the charcoal has been reduced to ash, one should again take five portions each of charcoal, the *sattva*-falling ball (*golaka*), and so forth, and repeatedly insert them through the upper opening. This charcoal furnace is to be known as excellent for the precipitation of the *sattva* of hard substances. *Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā:* [Commentary] When the charcoal has been consumed by fire and turned to ash, one should again take five portions each of charcoal, the *sattva*-falling ball, and other materials, and repeatedly insert them through the upper opening. First, he describes the covered box (*sapidhānakoṣṭhī*) with the words "rājahasta" and so forth.
Its height (*utsedha*), meaning its elevation, is measured at one and a quarter cubits (*sapādahasta*), which consists of thirty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). It is described as such.
Its length and width are each half of that measure; it is described as such.
Likewise, for the sake of complete stability, it should be surrounded on the outside by a wall made of clay, forming a square with four corners.
By that means, four walls come into existence in the four directions.
Although it was stated generally as "on one wall," it results in the specific meaning of either the eastern wall or the western wall according to the requirements of the situation.

On that wall situated in that direction, a door measuring one span (*vitasti*) should be made. Having placed a cord measuring one span in length and forming a circle, the meaning is that a circular space four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) in measure should be prepared, corresponding to whatever internal space is possible.
One should perform this for the purpose of examination, so as to perceive the time when a sentient being emerges from the flame situated within.
For that purpose, illumination is necessary.
Since it is obtained more abundantly in the east or the west, the specific direction characterized by its suitability for light is what is intended here.
The lower part of that door is the threshold (*dehalī*), which protects the body of the door; it should be made measuring two or three finger-breadths [in height].

On the lower portion of such a threshold, the floor should be joined as before and demarcated by a cord measuring one and a half *vitastis*; that is, a circular opening of six *aṅgulas* should be made for the purpose of joining the bellows.
Here, a wall merely one *vitasti* long would not be sufficient for the two doorways, even if it were one and a half *vitastis* long.
Therefore, it is stated that the thread [used] is one *vitasti* long and circular.
However, some maintain that even the portion of the horizontal trench dug into the ground with a gradual slope should be included for the purpose of measuring one and a half *vitastis*;
thus, there is no requirement for the length of the thread mentioned in the Sūtra, and such is the current tradition among smiths regarding the procedure for smelting.
They say, "It is seen.
But that is not appropriate,
because such a portion of a pit will be described later as being within the chamber of Pātāla.

The wall to be constructed above the upper part of the chamber, including both the northern and the upper sections, should be of four kinds and measured at one *prādeśa*— that is, ten finger-breadths— and should be made to taper like the shape of a flame. At the location of the flame, the door above should be made with a length and width of exactly one *prādeśa*.

Then, having blocked that door with brick, and having filled the previously mentioned door measuring one *vitasti* with cuckoos (*kokila*), one should blow [upon it]. (VRsṬī 10.38) Having done what, and having blocked what, should one blow? To this he says: first, one should gradually insert through the upper door the fire-birds (*śikhitra*, i.e., *kokila*) and the liquid of mica (*abhraka*) and so forth suitable for blowing. (VRsṬī 10.38) In response to the inquiry as to what that substance for blowing is—whether it should be inserted as a solid mass, part by part, or all at once—he says: "the balls for precipitating the essence (*sattvapātana-gola*). (VRsṬī 10.38)

Having blown continuously at every interval for repeated insertions, when the charcoal reaches a state of emaciation and becomes covered with white ash, then one should again add *kokilā* and perform blowing once more. (VRṢṬī 10.38;24) In this way, by blowing continuously with two bellows for the duration of a *prahara*, the time for the extraction of the essence (*sattva*) from hard substances generally arises. (VRṢṬī 10.38;25)
However, this is not a time that independently indicates the departure of the vital breath (*sattva*); rather, it is only when the white flame of fire itself is perceived [that it does].
For it is said in the *Paribhāṣādhyāya*:
"When the fire has blazing rays and is accompanied by the rising of a white [flame]..."
"Then that time should be known as the Pure Rotation (*śuddhāvarta*) when the essence (*sattva*) has emerged. Thus [it is said].

(VRṢṬī 10.38;27) At that time, having drawn out the globules of the *sphuṭi* externally and having separated the dross (*kiṭṭa*), the pure essence alone (*sattvamātra*) is to be taken by way of the Guru’s path. (VRṢṬī 10.38;28)

* Now, it should be understood that the second time for throwing in the lumps of metal (sattva) has arrived. // VRṢṬī 10.38;29 * Furthermore, for the purpose of dropping the soft substances, a slight blowing is required. // VRṢṬī 10.38;30 [The Dropping Furnace]
On firm ground, one should dig an auspicious circular pit measuring one span;
then, in the middle of that, one should fashion another pit.
It should be provided with a depth and width of four finger-breadths,
extending from the pit to the edge of the ground, and equipped with a horizontal tube.
One should place a clay wheel-pan, slightly elevated at the rim and sloping downward toward the outer trench,
provided with five holes, into the interior of the central pit.
Having filled the crucible with cuckoos (kokilas), one should blow it with a single bellows;
for this is the Pātālakoṣṭhikā, which precipitates the essence (sattva) of soft substances,
as proclaimed by Nandin for those materials that cannot be accomplished by mere blowing.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):
[The author] describes the subterranean crucible (*pātālakoṣṭhikā*) with the words "on firm ground" (*dṛḍhabhūmau*).
Having made a single circular pit one span (*vitasti*) deep in hard clay soil, one should [prepare] a space in its center four fingers wide.
One should make another pit four finger-breadths deep, joined with a curved-shaped tube extending from the pit to the surface of the ground, and slightly elevated. Then,
having placed a clay crucible provided with five holes in the middle of the inner pit and having filled the furnace with charcoal, one should blow it with a single bellows.
The essential point is that this should be known as the "Pātāla crucible" for the purpose of precipitating the essence (*sattva*) of soft substances.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya*:
Therefore, he describes the specific crucible suitable for that [purpose] with the words "on firm ground."

There, having prepared a pit twelve finger-breadths deep, and having made another circular pit in the center of its base with a depth and width of four finger-breadths, one should construct a door starting from the bottom of the inner pit and extending to the rear portion, facing toward the outer pit, joined to it, slightly elevated, and provided with a horizontal tube; then, upon the inner pit...

One should insert a clay wheel provided with five apertures for the purpose of making the air rise upward. Having placed charcoal upon that and, on top of that, the balls for the precipitation of the *sattva*, one should fill the entire furnace with *kokila* [fuel] and blow it with a single bellows.
This is called the "Pātāla furnace."
The crucible should be twelve finger-breadths deep and one span in width;
it should be four finger-breadths high and provided with a rim.
One should place a crucible containing many holes upon a ring;
having placed firebrands therein, one should heat it with a blowpipe.
This is called the *gārakoṣṭhī* furnace, which destroys refined metals.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Regarding the furnace characterized by downward blowing and the furnace characterized by upward blowing, he says "twelve" [in verse 10.44].
(VRṣṬī_10.44;1) A furnace one span in length and width should be constructed upon the surface of the ground. (VRṣṬī_10.44;2)

Starting from the base portion and leaving a space of four finger-breadths above it, one should fashion that [pipe] so as to be provided with a ring or collar at its upper part; then, having inserted a wheel (*cakrī*) above the ring which is furnished with many holes, and having placed *kokilā* [blowing tubes] therein, one should blow through a curved tube (*vaṅkanāla*).
This crucible, which consists of a soft raw material mixed with a greater proportion of charcoal compared to clay, is called a *gārakoṣṭhī*.

The meaning is that among the various cast metals such as bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and brass (*rīti*), this [crucible] acts as a separator between two substances in contact, leaving one behind while destroying the second.
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):* [The commentary provides further technical details regarding the composition and application of the crucible.]
Regarding the crucible, he says "twelve":

one crucible should be made twelve finger-breadths deep and distinguished by a width of one span (*prādeśa*). Above that, having provided a basin (*ālavāla*) in the shape of a ring four finger-breadths high, one should place upon it a wheel (*cakrī*) with many holes.
"Having placed charcoal [into the crucible], one should blow [upon it] with a blowpipe (*vaṅkanāla*).
[The term] *mṛṣṭalohavināśinī* means that which destroys purified metal—that is, it ruins refined iron.
[Vaṅkanāla]
A firm crucible, measuring one cubit (aratni) in size, should be constructed from clay mixed with powdered ore;

its mouth should face downward, and a tube five finger-breadths long should indeed be attached to its opening. This is called the "bent-tube" (vaṅkanāla), and it is prescribed for providing a strong blast.

*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* Regarding the inquiry as to what is meant by "vaṅkanāla" (the heating tube) mentioned in connection with the iron-furnace (*gārakoṣṭhikā*), he says: "with crucible-clays.
(VRrsBo 10.45;1) Having fashioned a firm tube measuring one *aratni* in length using any of the clays suitable for crucibles—such as gravel and so forth—at its opening...

One should join a single tube five fingers in length with its opening facing downward for the purpose of firm blowing; that is to be known as the curved tube (*vaṅkanāla*). [This refers to the crucible-furnace (*mūṣākoṣṭhī*) and the horizontal-blowing furnace (*tiryakpradhamanakoṣṭhī*).]
A crucible is prescribed for the preparation of perfected elixirs and the like;
it is twelve finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths at its base.
It has a mouth for blowing from the side and is used for purifying soft substances.

*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Now, he describes the crucible (*koṣṭhī*) which serves as the means for purifying perfected mercury (*siddharasa*)—such as that bound in pills (*khoṭabaddha*) and the like—as well as the essences (*sattva*) of mica (*abhraka*) and other minerals, by means of glass (*kāca*), borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), natron (*sauvīra*), and so forth. [He says: "Twelve finger-breadths... (VRṣṬī 10.46). 1. Having placed the perfected mercury and other substances into the interior of a crucible situated within this crucible (*koṣṭhī*), one should blow [upon it] continuously while intermittently adding powdered glass and other materials from time to time. (VRṣṬī 10.46). 2. At the occasion of continuous blowing, one should repeatedly add glass powder and the like at intervals and then blow. (VRṣṬī 10.46).
* Soft substance refers to *sattva* and so forth.

// VRrsṬī_10.46;3 It should be understood, even though not explicitly stated, that this crucible (*koṣṭhī*) is to be made gradually wider from the base portion up to the mouth portion, with a circular opening measuring one span (*prādeśa*).
// VRrsṬī_10.46;4 This is because the measurement and the mouth of the preceding [crucible] have already been described. // VRrsṬī_10.46;5
A *puṭa* is that which makes known the correct measure for the cooking of substances such as mercury and others.
A cooking process that is either deficient or excessive is not desired; a well-cooked medicinal drug is beneficial. (VR 10.47)
The non-recurrence of defects such as impurities in iron, the increase of its qualities, and its superiority [over other metals] result from this;
likewise, the absence of sinking in water and the filling of the lines [of the crucible] occur from the crucible (*puṭa*).
From the crucible and the stone, there arises lightness, rapid pervasion, and digestive stimulation;
even more than from the processed mercury-king, the quality of the metals is superior.

Just as fire may enter a stone through the application of an external crucible, so too is the attainment of qualities in metals certain, owing to their reduction to a state of powder. *Commentary: Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā:* Just as fire enters a stone by means of an external crucible, so indeed is the acquisition of qualities in metals determined through the process of pulverization.

Now, in order to describe the *puṭas* that generate even more fire than those dependent on the crucible (*mūṣākoṣṭhī*), he states their purpose beginning with the word "rasa": The complete digestion (*samyakpāka*) of hard substances such as mercury and metals is required for medicinal purposes.
Furthermore, that digestion—which is of the nature of an action—cannot be determined by weight or by measure.

* Only a specific type of vessel (*puṭa*) that indicates the correct measure for perfect cooking (*supāka*) is possible when it is a pit or similar receptacle completely filled with fire, embers, stones, husks, and cow-dung.
(VRṢṬī 10.50;4) * "One perfect cooking occurred by means of the fire and stones filling this pit"—thus, the application of that specific type of vessel must be performed.
(VRṢṬī 10.50;5) * The sense is: "until the attainment of the qualities as described. (VRṢṬī 10.50;6)
* By insufficient heating, the fragrance, color, taste, and touch do not arise properly.
* But by excessive heating, the substance becomes essence-less and burnt, like boiled rice.
* Now, he describes the qualities residing in the metals resulting from the application of the *puṭa* (herbivore) process, beginning with "of iron and so forth."

Non-return [to worldly existence] does not consist in the restoration of one's ordinary nature, even through the refinement by the five friends (*pañcamitra*). When that [elixir] has been consumed while it is in its state of "fullness" (*āmāvasthā*), the qualities that ward off disease—such as nourishment (*puṣṭi*) and so forth, as well as suppleness (*mārdava*) and so forth—which were previously unmanifest, appear to increase through their manifestation.
By means of that, there arises preeminence (*agratā*), excellence (*śreṣṭhatā*), and high value (*adhikamūlyatā*).
Likewise, when it is thrown into water, there is neither sinking nor floating;
and when pressed between two fingers, it enters into the fine lines of the fingers.
Furthermore, in specific types of stones such as mica, diamond, and yellow orpiment, qualities such as lightness become manifest through heating in a crucible (*puṭa*).
What is the use of much description of its qualities?

Since all qualities, gathered together and intensified, reside therein, therefore the qualities of the well-refined metals in the body of a man who uses them according to the prescribed rules are indeed superior to those of mercury, the minor minerals (uparasas), gems, and base metals, even when these have been processed to their full maturity.

For even when possessed of abundant fruit, the elixir of accomplishment (*siddharasa*) requires for its penetration (*krāmaṇa*) a passionate woman whose youth has slightly blossomed, for the purpose of speaking, kissing, and embracing, and for the purpose of massaging the body with her breasts. In her absence, there is no penetration throughout the entire body, and thus no passion (*manmatha*).
But if sexual intercourse occurs through negligence while [the teacher] is present,
then death is the penalty.
Furthermore, for one who indulges in [forbidden] tastes, there is a specific period of exclusion lasting for one year.

* First, the process of "field-making" (*kṣetrīkaraṇa*) is necessary. (VRṢṬī 10.50; 23) In the case of the perfection of mercury (*pārada*), the accomplishment of all ritual actions requires an abundance of materials and other resources. (VRṢṬī 10.50;
24) For this very reason, the excellence of the qualities of iron—which is not entirely free from defects—is merely figuratively attributed [to it]. (VRṢṬī 10.50; 25)

An objection might be raised: "Since even harder varieties of metal than stone do not undergo the disintegration of their parts, how can the aforementioned attainment be possible? Anticipating this, he further confirms the qualities of the metal by means of an illustration with the words, "Just as in a stone...
The underlying sense is that everything becomes possible through the entry of the internal fire (*antaragni*).
[This refers to the *mahāpuṭa*].
In a square pit two cubits deep and wide,
filled with a thousand wild blue lotuses, one should place the medicinal herbs for the process of sublimation (*puṭana*).
One should carefully place the obstructed [substance] upon the *piṣṭikā* (a paste or layer);
one should arrange half a thousand *vanotpala* flowers upon the *krauñcikā*.
One should ignite the fire there; this is known as the *mahāpuṭa*. 10.52.

*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Now he describes the specific type of pit known as the *mahāpuṭa*: in the middle of the ground, within a wall constructed of bricks and the like, there is a pit made of masonry;
it is two cubits in both depth and width, and likewise four-cornered. In such a pit, one should fill it with a thousand measures of wild *chagaṇa*.
When [the vessel] is filled, one should place the medicine contained within a pair of earthen bowls upon the ground-covering (piṣṭikā) that has been spread over the dried cow-dung cakes (chagaṇa).
One should fill such a crucible (mūṣikā) with five hundred dried cow-dung cakes.
Then, one should ignite it.
[The *gajapuṭa*]:
one should prepare a square pit with a depth equal to the length of a king’s forearm,
fill it with river pebbles, and then place [the substance] therein up to the neck.

One should place a *kumudī* vessel filled with the substances for the *puṭa* process there; one should then insert half-full *giriṇḍa* cakes made from *chagaṇa*. This is called the "elephant-heap" (*gajapuṭa*), which bestows great medicinal qualities.

* Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā: * Now he describes the gajapuṭa [furnace] with the words "rājahasta" etc. // VRrsṬī_10.54;1 * A rājahasta measures thirty finger-breadths (aṅgulas). // VRrsṬī_10.54;2

One should understand that the pit should be of that same measure, deep and profound, and of that same width. In this context, the word "width" (*vistāra*) is indicated by ellipsis after the word "deep" (*nimna*).
One should fill it up to the neck with pebbles and gravel.

*Upalās* are hard and large; *vanya-chagaṇas* are smaller in body than those. *Śāṭhyas* are even smaller. Therein, having placed a crucible (*mūṣā*) containing medicinal ingredients, one should insert mountain-born *giṇḍas* or wild *chagaṇas* measuring half the size of the previously mentioned *chagaṇas*. This is known as the *gajapuṭa* (or *vārāhapuṭa*).
In this manner, the *puṭa* performed in an earthen vessel (*āratrika-kuṇḍa*) is called the Vārāha.
A *puṭa* on the surface of the earth that is two spans (*vitasti*) in height and as wide at its base is known as a *kukkuṭaka-puṭa*.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Now he describes the *kukkuṭapuṭa* (cock-pot):
"On the surface of the ground, a pit is constructed with a wall twenty-four finger-breadths in height, and of the same measurement at its base."
When a wide-mouthed pit of this kind is filled with stones and other materials to cook the medicinal substance, it is known as the *kukkuṭapuṭa* (cock-pit) method.
*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* [This refers to the commentary on the aforementioned verse.]
He calls the "hen's nest" a *puṭa*.
It is two spans (*vitasti*) in height, one cubit (*hasta*) in elevation,
and likewise one cubit in width at its base.
This, however, is to be performed only upon the ground and not by digging a pit.
As for the "pigeon-cup" (*kapotapuṭa*):
it is a cup placed on the ground made of eight pieces of forest stone.
Having bound [the mercury], for the purpose of producing the ash of mercury and copper (*sūtārkabhasma*), the "pigeon-cavity" (*kapotapuṭa*) is described.

*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā):* That pit which is made on the surface of the ground with clay and other materials, and into which eight numbers of forest-stones (*vanopala*) are placed and ignited with a flame for the purpose of turning bound mercury into ash— that is called the *kapotapuṭa*.
* COMMENTARY (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):

"Having bound" means having sealed it within the crucible (*mūṣā*). // VRrsBo_10.57;1 For the sake of the ash of mercury and copper—that is, for the sake of the ash of mercury (*rasa*) and the ash of copper (*tāmra*). // VRrsBo_10.57;2
Cow-dung that has been trampled by oxen within a cow-pen and dried until it is powdered is designated as *govara*;
it is the most excellent for the preparation of mercury.
[Govarapuṭa]:
That in which a *puṭa* (sealed vessel) is provided with cow-dung or even with husks is called a *govarapuṭa*, for the purpose of preparing the ash of mercury (*rasabhasma*). (VRrs 10.59)
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya*:

Where a medicinal substance is placed in a pit for the *gajapuṭa* and the heating is performed using cow-dung or husks, that is called a *gorvarapuṭa*. [This is also known as *bhāṇḍapuṭa*. *VRrsṬī* 10.59;1.
When a thick-walled vessel filled with husks and provided with a crucible in its center is subjected to heating by fire, that is called a *bhāṇḍapuṭa*.
Indeed, that sand-pit is covered above and below by *krauñcikā* grass,
where there is burning sand.
One should properly bury [the vessel] two finger-breadths below the surface of the earth within a "mountain-shaped" (bhūdhara) crucible;
that crucible in which there is a lid on top is called the *bhūdhara*.
* COMMENTARY on the Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:
* The crucibles are called "friends of fire" (*vahnimitra*) because they remain with the fire for a long duration; thus, their status as "friends of fire" should be understood.

*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Now he describes the *bhūdharapuṭa*: "vahnimitrā" refers to the crucible (*mūṣā*), that is to say, the shallow bowl (*śarāva*). (VRṢṬī 10.62;1) *VRṢṬī 10.62;2*
The application of this [method] in the preparation of *jayasundara* and other such rasas should be understood.
[Regarding the *lāvakapuṭa*:
a *puṭa* [is made] above with sixteen-fold urine, or with husks, or with cow-dung.]
Where that which is called the *lāvaka* [puṭa] occurs, it is for the preparation of very soft substances.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Now he describes the *lāvaka-puṭa*: "Above," etc. (VRṢṬī 10.63).

Having placed a crucible in the shape of a shallow bowl joined together on the ground, the "lāvaka" [method] is that in which a sealed heating (*puṭa*) is applied above it using sixteen *vanya-upala* (wild stones) measured in weight, or with chaff or cow-dung, whereby the cooking is performed;
"sixteen" itself is "ṣoḍaśikā.
In this context, that number should be understood as referring specifically to the wild stones.
The meaning is that they should be weighed against the same amount of ash as the ingredients themselves.
However, when the measure of the *puṭa* has not been specified, it should be determined according to the strength or weakness of the substance to be processed.
Having identified the *puṭa* (the vessel or covering), it should be administered by those skilled in reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*).
For, since *puṭas* are generally prepared with wild cow-dung (*vanya-chagaṇa*), there is a need for its availability.
Now I shall describe the *kumbhapuṭa* as stated in another treatise: having made forty finger-breadths' worth of many holes in an earthen pot, one should then place cold charcoal powder within it.
Having filled it half-full, one should place the bowl in the mouth [of the crucible];
having smeared it with clay and a cloth, one should let it dry in the shade. Then, having cast charcoal into it—either in a furnace or upon bricks—[one should proceed].
Having placed [the medicine] for three days in a cool place, one should take it and extract the medicinal herb.
This is to be known as *kumbhapuṭa*, as described by those who have seen the scriptures.
*Piṣṭaka*, *chagaṇa*, *chāṇa*, *utpala*, and *copala*,
as well as *giriṇḍa*, *upalasāṭhī*, and *varāṭī*, are synonyms for *chagaṇa*.
The six non-artificial metals are gold,
silver, copper, tin, lead, and iron;
these six metals, along with brass and bell-metal, are artificial alloys.
Regarding salts, six are enumerated: sea salt, rock salt,
biḍa salt, sauvarcala salt, romaka salt, and likewise cūlikā salt.
The three alkalis are declared to be barley-alkali, sarjikā-alkali, and ṭaṅkaṇa-alkali.
The five alkalis are the alkali of *palāśa*, the alkali of *muṣkaka*, barley ash, *suvarcikā*,
and the alkali derived from sesame stalks; these combined constitute the "five alkalis."
Ghee, jaggery, and honey are to be known as the "triple sweet" (*madhuratraya*).
*Tumbinī* is the bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*) or the resin of *sarala* wood.
[For medicinal processing: *Kaṅguṇī*, *tumbinī*, *ghoṣā*, and that which is produced from *karīra* and *śrīphala*.
[One should avoid] that which is produced from bitter vegetables, white mustard, *soma-rājī*, and *vibhītaka*.
Likewise, [the oil] from linseed, from *mahākālī*, from neem, and from sesame,
as well as from *apāmārga*, *devadālī*, *dantī*, and *tumburu*.
Likewise, having taken oil from aṅkola, unmatta, bhallātaka, and palāśa, one should employ it in the process of extracting the essence.
[The Section on Fats]: Fat derived from the jackal, the frog, and the tortoise;
fat from the crab, the porpoise, the cow, the pig, and human beings.
Likewise, the fat of goats, camels, donkeys, rams, and buffaloes [is forbidden].
[The Group of Urines] One should employ the urines of elephants, young camels, buffaloes, donkeys, and horses;
and for cows, goats, and ewes, one should apply the female's menstrual flow and the male's seed. *Vṛddhatrayī Rasāyana*, 10.75.
The five products of the buffalo: buffalo water, curd, milk, clarified butter, and the essence of dung;
[the five products of the goat].
That is to be known as the "five-buffalo" [penance], and likewise the "five-goat" [penance].

Ambaṣṭhā, tintiḍīka, nāgara, and rasapattrikā—

It is beneficial for the liquefaction and digestion of mercury and other substances in order to purify them.

Brick, red ochre, salt, ashes, and anthill earth—
these are proclaimed as the five earths by those skilled in the application of elixirs.
[The Chapter on Poisons] Śṛṅgīka, kālakūṭa, vatsanābha, along with artificial poison and bile— this is proclaimed as the excellent category of poisons. VR 10.82.

the vulture, and also the cock.
Indeed, the purification of all metals is achieved through smearing and heating in a closed crucible (*puṭana*).
[The Section on Red Substances:
Safflower, khadira, lac, mañjiṣṭhā, red sandalwood,
akṣī, bandhujīva, and likewise karpūragandhinī.

(VR 10.94) *Commentary: Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā:* [The term] "bound" (*baddha*) refers to mercury that has been rendered stable through various processes such as sublimation (*ūrdhvapātana*). "Metals" (*lohānām*) refers to the eight types of base metals (*aṣṭaloha*), beginning with iron (*loha*). "Impurities" (*mala*) refers to the defects inherent in those metals. "Kāpālī" refers to a specific defect in mercury characterized by its black color and astringent taste; "kaṅkuṇa" refers to a defect in mercury characterized by its yellow color and bitter taste. It is said that this [substance] destroys both these defects. *Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* He states the definition of the "reflected" (*ābhāsa*) [mercury]: that mercury which has been processed (*bhāvita*) together with minerals such as realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and sulphur (*gandhaka*), as well as with roots and the like such as *sarpākṣī*, and with leaves, flowers, and so forth; having been given liquid and then rubbed (*mardita*).

When processed by the *puṭa* method in a *bhūdharayantra*, it is reduced to ashes and, by its very nature, abandons its inherent qualities such as volatility and difficulty of grasping; it then enters into union with various minerals and acquires the medicinal properties of the specific formulations that destroy particular diseases, thereby becoming a provider of therapeutic virtues. Furthermore, if after a short period of time, even for a person who has been following a wholesome regimen (*pathya*), there occurs a corruption of its qualities—that is, a transformation of its virtues—then that bound mercury is designated as "merely apparent" (*ābhāsa*).
Because it produces the appearance of qualities (*guṇa*).
*Vaikṛta* is simply a modification (*vikṛti*). [It is devoid of action.]

That best of mercurial preparations which is processed with unrefined metals and the like should be known as deficient in its ritual application; it undergoes adverse transformation due to unwholesome treatment.
[The Binding of the Paste]:
Through intense heating and thorough kneading, it becomes a paste in the form of butter;
that essence is the binding of the paste, which is highly stimulating and digestive.
That mercury which is prepared with conch shells, oyster shells, cowrie shells, and the like, is known as *kṣārabandha*;
it produces supreme luster and nourishment, and destroys colic. (VR 11.70)
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Regarding the phrase "conch and oyster shell":

having prepared a crucible (*mūṣā*) from conch shells, oyster shells, and the like, as well as tree-alkalis and the like, once they have been reduced to ash, one places mercury (*pārada*) within the sealed casket (*saṃpuṭa*) of that crucible.

Mercury, having been cast [into the crucible] and sealed, becomes reduced to ash by the application of a light *puṭa* (roasting); this is *kṣārabandha*, which serves to produce the brilliance of fire and other such effects. *Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī* Commentary: Mercury, having been cast [into the crucible] and sealed, becomes reduced to ash by the application of a light *puṭa* (roasting); this is *kṣārabandha*, which serves to produce the brilliance of fire and other such effects.
Regarding the "alkaline bond" (*kṣārabandha*), he says "conch-shell" (*śaṅkhā*) and so forth.
"Fully prepared" (*saṃsādhitaḥ*) means well-processed by means of grinding, encapsulation (*puṭana*), and other such methods.
The rest is clear.
That which becomes a *khoṭa* when bound, and which goes to destruction as it is repeatedly smelted—
that is to be known as *khoṭabandha*; it quickly removes all diseases.

*COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* He speaks of *khoṭabandha* [the sealing of the pill] as "bandha" (binding). Regarding what was stated: "The state of being a *khoṭa* [a solidified mass], which is the nature of not flying up even while situated in fire."

"When one stands in the midst of fire, that is the characteristic of [the substance] bound in a pill. Thus [it is said]. "Blown upon, blown upon"—that is to say, repeatedly inflated by means of a bellows—it would go to destruction; the meaning is that it would reach a state of invisibility due to becoming one with another substance.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:
Now, regarding the "bandha" (fixation), he speaks of the *khoṭabandha*. As for the method of producing the *khoṭa*, the *Rasasāra* stated: [VRrsṬī_11.71;1]
Furthermore, with those eight famous great medicinal herbs (*mahauṣadhi*) used in binding,
one should saturate the Lord of Mercury (*raseśvara*) together with *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
When blown [into a furnace] within a crucible smeared with them, it attains the state of a solid bolus (*khoṭatā*).
Thus.
Due to excessive inflation, that very [substance] goes to destruction.
And that should be understood as the "bond of the pellet" (khoṭabandha).

* Here, mercury (pārada) that has digested six times its weight of sulphur (gandha) should be taken. // VRrsṬī_11.71;6 * Or it should be taken as a paste (piṣṭī) prepared by the addition of mica (abhraka).
// VRrsṬī_11.71;7 * Having ground it in the juice of the Somavallī plant, one should administer it in three puṭas (closed crucible roastings).
One should saturate it seven times with the juice of the *somavallī* creeper.
That mercury (abhraka) should be placed in an earthen vessel together with the juice.
Furthermore, one should rub the root of the *śarapuṅkhā* plant with cow’s milk.
One should mix mercury with *kalka* (paste) and place the *gagana* (mica) above and below it.
One should set it in the heat of the sun; facing away [from the heat], it swallows [the paste] in an instant.
A paste (*piṣṭikā*) is quickly produced; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus [ends the section].

Regarding the statement "the binding of the paste (piṣṭībandha) is called a khoṭaka," it is here said that the form of the paste (piṣṭikārūpa) is intended. However, the definition of a khoṭaka is found in another text as follows:
When blown [in the furnace], the *khoṭa* becomes liquefied; when struck, it turns to powder.
When blown again, it liquefies as *khoṭa*: such is the characteristic of *khoṭa*.

If it is digested by one-quarter of *ghanasattva*, or digested by one-quarter of *kānta*, or digested by equal parts of both *tīkṣṇa* [iron] and [the others], it is also highly recommended for the purpose of transforming the field (*kṣetrīkaraṇa*).
[Poṭabandha:
Quick-soot (drutakajjalikā) flattened upon a plantain leaf (*mocāpattra*) constitutes that *poṭa*;
it is indeed *parpaṭī*, which cures all diseases of children and others.

*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* [The author] defines *pāṭabandha* with the word "druta" (melted). (VRṣṬī 11.72;1) That collyrium (*kajjalī*) which has become liquid— having been melted by the heat of the fire below in a cauldron— is immediately cast onto a plantain leaf.

Covered with its own leaf and flattened by pressing, it is known as *pāṭabandha* and *parpaṭikābandha*; when administered as a post-drink (*anupāna*) according to specific variations for children, the elderly, and others, it destroys all diseases.
[Kalkabandha]

Mercury (sūta), when processed by means of sweating (*sveda*) and other methods and has attained the state of a paste (*paṅka*), should be known as "bound by a paste" (*kalkabaddha*); it bestows the fruits mentioned in the [relevant] applications (*yoga*). *Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī Commentary:* [The commentary explains that mercury, having been purified through processes such as *sveda*, becomes a thick paste-like consistency; this stage is termed *kalkabaddha*, and such mercury yields the specific results prescribed in the medicinal formulations.]
It means that it bestows the excellence of the fruit of whichever yoga it is employed in— that is, it grants the superior result of the specific yoga being practiced.
Alternatively, it means it bestows the fruit resulting from the application of medicinal pastes (*kalka*) taken for the purpose of fomentation (*svedana*) and massage (*mardana*).
[Kajjalībandha:
Kajjalī is produced from mercury and sulfur; it is very fine and resembles collyrium.
When combined with various specific formulations, it is called kajjalībandha. (VR 11.74)
* COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:
* Regarding the preparation of *kajjalī*, he says: "As for *kajjalī*... // VRrsBo_11.74;1 * It is very smooth and glossy. // VRrsBo_11.74;2
The meaning is that they are purified by being joined with their respective [counteragents] through the combination of substances that purify mercury and sulfur.
(VRrsBo 11.74) *Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya*:
It defines the "kajjalī-bandha" (the kajjali-bond). (VRrsṬī 11.74)
When [the mercury] is joined with the process of mixing and grinding medicinal herbs specifically selected to ward off diseases through their respective applications, it is called *kajjalībandha*.
Here, the phrase "joined with their respective applications" is not an essential part of the definition,
because *kajjalī* is established even without that.

However, that statement was made to demonstrate that this [mercury], by virtue of its capacity for union (*yogavāhitva*), is the destroyer of all diseases. When mercury, together with the living being (*sajīva*), is reduced to ashes through contact with fire, it is indeed designated as "living" (*sajīva*).
When properly cultivated, this [mercury] does not act as a reducing agent (bhasma), but swiftly effects the destruction of diseases.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya (Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā):
Regarding "reduced to ash" (bhasmīkṛta), he speaks of that which is bound with life (sajīvabaddha).*

After being rubbed with the juice of betel leaves, it is placed inside the bulb of the *vandhyākarkoṭakī* plant and enclosed; then, wrapped externally with two soft cloths and subjected to the "elephant-pot" (*gajapuṭa*) method in the ground, it is reduced to ashes.
Mercury thus reduced to ashes by this alternative method, when held in a vessel over fire, flies into the sky, because its wings have not been clipped.
But it does not perform the work of the fire, which consists in the absence of old age and death;
nor does it effect the destruction of disease.
[It is] devoid of life.

Whether it be old abhraka (mica) whose odor has completely vanished, or the foremost of all metals reduced to ashes—that mercury-ash known as "lifeless" (nirjīva) instantly destroys all diseases without exception. *Commentary: Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī:* This refers to mica that has been thoroughly processed until its characteristic smell is gone, or the best of all metals (iron) reduced to ash; this "lifeless" medicinal ash indeed destroys every ailment immediately.
Regarding the bond of the lifeless (*nirjīvabandha*), he says "digested mica" (*jīrṇābhraka*).
(1) "Digested mica" means that the mica has been swallowed.
(2) "Completely digested sulfur" (*parijīrṇagandha*) means that the sulfur has been properly swallowed.

*Akhi*la* etc.: "Of all" (*akhilānām*) means of all metals, such as gold and so forth. "Crown" (*mauliḥ*) means having the nature of a head-ornament; the meaning is that it bestows qualities even superior to those qualities which arise from the employment of all other metals.
Its "lifelessness" (*nirjīvatvam*) is to be understood because it lacks the capacity to flow out even when subjected to fire.

The seedless (*nirbīja*) mercury, however, is that which has been digested by a quarter-part of gold, turned into a paste through the application of sulfur, and then successively roasted with equal parts of sulfur; it is named "seedless" and destroys all diseases. (VR 11.77)

*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* It defines seedless fixation (*nirbījabandha*) with the words "the mercury... (VRrsṬī_11.77;1). Here, gold is not to be taken as having been made into a seed (*bījīkṛta*), but rather as pure gold, processed in a digestion vessel (*jāraṇāyantra*), and in the form of a leaf (*pattrarūpa*). (VRrsṬī_11.77;2)

The mercury, ground into a paste, is mixed with one-twelfth part sulphur; having added it little by little repeatedly while rubbing it with acid, it is then successively roasted with equal parts of sulphur.

First, having added a fourth part of sulphur, it is roasted in a *bhūdhara* apparatus; then, having added half a part of sulphur, it is roasted likewise; then, having added three-quarters of a part of sulphur, it is roasted; and after that, [it is roasted] with an equal portion.
Having given, it is "folded"—this is the meaning of the word *krama*. (VRṢṬī 11.77;3) Regarding the plural number in *gandhaiḥ* ("with perfumes"), it is not restrictive.
(VRṢṬī 11.77;4) [This refers to the state of being bound by seeds.]
That [mercury] which has been thoroughly roasted with powdered essences of mica, gold, copper, silver, and sun-stone,
and then killed with six times its weight of sulphur, becomes bound with seed (sabījabaddha) and possesses immense power.
[The Chain-Binding Method]:
Mercury struck by diamond and other substances is "slain"; such slain mercury is of another kind.
However, mercury bound by chains is that which effects the transmutation of the body and the production of iron.
Śaṅkara knows with speed the pervasion of that which possesses variegated power.
[Commentary: Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā:
When mercury has been killed—that is, reduced to ashes or pulverized—one may also place another killed mercury within it.
That mercury, when bound in the form of a *khoṭa*, is said to be "bound by a chain" (*śṛṅkhalābaddha*).

This method of killing [the mercury] is stated in the *Rasārṇava*. *Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):* [The commentary provides a detailed explanation of the process of binding mercury through various chemical operations.]

Regarding the "chain-binding" (*śṛṅkhalābandha*), he says "vajra etc. (VRrsBo_11.79;1). Mercury (*sūta*) killed by diamond and so forth—that is, killed through association with diamonds and the like—is equal to that, meaning it is measured in equal proportions. Furthermore, another [mercury] is killed, killed in another manner. This is "mercury bound by a chain," because of the grinding of both; this is the implied sense. (VRrsBo_11.79;2)

The remainder of the sense is: "in the body of the mercury (sūta) bound by chains, there is a pervasion with speed, possessing variegated radiance and extraordinary power (*alaukikasāmarthya*). Even if the mercury is joined with external fluxes (*bāhyadruti*) and has attained a state of binding, it may take the form of ashes.
That [mercury], when bound by liquefaction (drutibaddha), destroys even difficult-to-cure diseases when applied in a dose of one-quarter of a rājikā seed.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya (Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā):
Now he speaks of "bound by liquefaction" (drutibaddha) with the words "even when combined," etc.* (VRrsṬī_11.80;1)

If mercury becomes of great power through the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of seeds, that is not surprising. Even when combined with the liquefactions (*druti*) of the metals (*rasa*), the secondary metals (*uparasa*), and the minerals (*dhātu*), and even when digested by them, mercury—whether merely bound (*baddha*), subsequently fixed (*bandhottara*), or reduced to ash—is called "bound by liquefaction" (*drutibaddha*). If it is consumed in a dose measuring only a fourth part of a mustard seed, it [cures] diseases difficult to cure.
It destroys [the defects].

Regarding the binding of the liquefied metal (*drutibandha*), he says: "When joined," etc. (VRṢṬĪ 11.80). *COMM. Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī*: [He states this] regarding the binding of the liquefied metal. (VRṢṬIBO 11.80).

Even when endowed with external fluxes (*bāhyadruti*), which are specific operations that produce fluidity in mercury, if it has reached a state of binding (*bandha*)— that is, attained a state of fixation— or alternatively, if it has become ash in nature (*bhasitasvarūpa*), such mercury is to be known by the name "bound by flux" (*drutibaddha*).
That mercury bound with flux is known as *rājikā* (black mustard), a specific type of red-colored mustard seed; one-fourth part—that is, a quarter-measure—of it is used.
When combined with yoga, the "child" (*bāla*) born of Śiva, once aged and tempered like a cloud, becomes swift when employed.
It is an elixir (rasāyana) that wards off future diseases and destroys even fatal illnesses (ariṣṭa) accompanied by their complications.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya (Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā):
This verse defines the [preparation] known as Bālābaddha.*
*Abhra* is the essence of the black vajra-cloud.
*Śivaja* is mercury (*pārada*).
It is digested with *abhra* according to the sequence of sixty-four, thirty-two, sixteen, and so forth [parts].
Its application should also be understood in the context of leaf-smearing (*pattralepa*).
[Regarding *kumārabandha*:
that which is produced from Śiva (*harodbhava*) and has been processed with double the amount of *abhra* (mica) is *kumāra*; it contains a limited quantity of rice.]
Indeed, after three times seven nights, it destroys the multitude of evil diseases and serves as an elixir of rejuvenation.
This elixir named *Tarūṇa*, which consists of four parts of *vyoma* (mercury) and is the foremost of elixirs,
destroys all diseases within seven nights and bestows vigor and strength. (VR 11.83)
That mercury for which sixfold abhraka has been digested and which has attained friendship with fire is indeed named "Vṛddha" (the aged);
it should be employed in both the body and in metal—who, other than Śiva, can describe its qualities? (VR 11.84)
That mercury which has been rendered resistant to fire by means of divine roots is called *mūrtibandha*;
even without the process of *abhrajāraṇā*, that great mercury (*mahārasa*) constitutes *mūrtibandha*.
For this mercury, even when being processed by fire, is not diminished;

when employed in all medicinal formulations, it bestows incomparable fruits. *Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayaṭīkā):* This mercury, though subjected to heating, does not suffer depletion. When applied in all types of pharmaceutical preparations (*yoga*), it yields results that are beyond compare.
He defines "bound in form" (*mūrtibaddha*) as follows:

The sixty-four medicinal roots previously mentioned are the "divine roots. By means of them, through processes such as rubbing and sweating with their juices, [the mercury] undergoes "wing-clipping" (*pakṣaccheda*).

Even without the digestion (*jāraṇā*) of mica (*abhra*), when it is rendered capable of withstanding intense fire and is bound solely by the body itself—without being permeated by other substances—it is called "bound in form."
Likewise, from contact with *vaikrānta* diamond (*vajra*), [the mercury becomes bound].
By rubbing it together with that which has been reduced to powder, the mercury also becomes bound; this too is called "bound in form" (*mūrtibaddha*).
Thus, there are two possible types of binding in form.
Bound by waters issuing from the mouths of stone conduits, this is known as *jalabandha*;
it destroys old age, disease, and death, and bestows the fruits described in the Kalpas.
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* He defines *jalabandha* (water-bound mercury):
Mercury that has been bound through processes such as rubbing with waters such as *śilātōya* (rock-water), *candrātōya* (moon-water), and others, is known as *jalabaddha*. (VRṢṬī 11.87)
"Stated in the *Kalpa*":
this means having the result stated in the *Pāradakalpa*.
The details of this water have been clarified in the *Rasārṇava*.
Wood thrown into water may appear as if it has become stone;
O Goddess of the Gods, that which pierces both the exterior and the interior is proclaimed as the "piercing" (*vedhaka*).
Cinnabar, yellow orpiment, sulfur, and realgar—

That which effects the removal of their odor is called *vedhaka*. When it is heated alone or in combination with other substances, it may take the form of a pill (*guṭikā*). [This is the binding by fire.]
This [mercury], when bound by fire, is undecayed and indeed effects such states as the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva).
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):
He describes the "binding by fire" (agnibandha) with the words "kevala" and so forth.*
* "Pure" means not joined with any other substance.
* "Joined by yoga" means joined with another substance. * "Heated" means made hot in fire.
* "Undiminished" means that even when heated by fire, it remains in its original measure and does not diminish in the slightest.
(VRrsBo 11.88;5) * "Producing the power of moving through the sky and so forth" means that when held in the mouth, it bestows the capacity for traveling through the air.

(VRrsBo 11.88;6) * In the summary text (*uddeśagrantha*), following the mention of "fire-binding" (*agnibandha*) in the phrase "water-binding and fire-binding are well-prepared," [it follows] after the fire-binding.

Since there is mention of another binding called *susaṃskṛtakṛta* prior to the *mahābandha*, yet no mention of it is seen in the *Vivaraṇa* commentary, I believe that binding has become invisible due to either the scribe’s negligence or some other oversight.
Furthermore, it is also not appropriate for the term *susaṃskṛtakṛtābhidha* to function as an adjective qualifying this *agnibandha*; for if that were the case,
since the *bandhas* would number twenty-four, it would result in the failure of the initial proposition (*pratijñāhāni*) that "we shall explain twenty-five *rasabandhas*."
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Now he describes mercury bound by fire (*agnibaddha-pārada*) with the words "pure" (*kevala*).

First, by means of sixfold digestion of mica (*abhraka*), the mercury becomes fire-resistant; having been digested by the *maṇi* [mineral], it is raised up by the *pātana* apparatus and thus becomes liquefied.
And when that [mercury], being alone or combined with sharp iron, is heated, it takes the form of a pill and becomes indestructible in fire.
For this very reason, it is called "fire-bound" (agnibaddha).

If this is held in the mouth, it brings about for a person liberation characterized by the power of traveling through the sky, invulnerability to weapons and fire, and the states of sāyujya and sārūpya.
[For the purpose of inducing fainting:
with *viṣṇukrāntā*, *śaśilatā*, the roots of *kumbhī* and *kanaka*,
*viśālā*, the tuber of *nāginī*, *vyāghrapādī*, and *kuruṇṭaka*.
One should grind *haṃsapādā* together with *vṛścikālī*, *bhaśuṇḍī*,
and the urine of cows that have not yet calved, or cook it in a clay pot (*kulaka*) along with those same substances.
In this manner, one should cook the mercury after it has been rubbed with the aforementioned calcined metals;
this is, in brief, the procedure for the "mūrchā" (solidification) of mercurial preparations in various apparatuses.
*Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī Commentary:* [The commentary explains that the metals should first be purified and then calcined; the mercury is then processed with these to achieve its solidification.]
*Dense* (*nibiḍaḥ*) means not unevenly raised or depressed, but having all its parts equal.
[This refers to the *mahābandha*.
Accompanied by gold or silver and smelted, it attains oneness; undiminished, dense, heavy, and in the form of a pill, it is exceedingly long and radiant.
*Commentary (Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī):
If the binding process has not been properly accomplished according to the rules (*nirbandha*), it melts in the fire in an instant; this is the implied meaning.

When struck and rubbed like cloth, it attains the state of powder; it does not release its impurity, becomes odorless, and melts in an instant—this indeed is the mercury known as *mahābandha*. (VRrs 11.92)
*Commentary on the Rasaratnasamuccaya:* Regarding the "great binding" (*mahābandha*), he says: "or with gold.
Here, gold should be taken as either a fourth part or a half part [of the mercury].
Silver is likewise treated in the same manner. When mercury—

which possesses the characteristics to be described— is heated within a crucible made of diamond smeared with the medicinal paste for binding, combined with either of those two [silver or gold], it becomes "fire-bound" (*agnibaddha*) and, being well-refined, receives the name "well-prepared" (*susamskṛta*) as well as the name "great binder" (*mahābandha*).

He states those very characteristics with the words "blown [into a flame], it goes to oneness," and so forth. Like a cloth, it becomes like salt-dust. It attains the state of being pulverized, equal to rock salt.

When half a *kanaka* of mercury is combined with an embryo (*garbha*)—either one-quarter of a *nāga* or five parts of *aṅguṣṭhaka*, *śālmalī* resin, honey, and seeds of *śleṣmātaka*—and likewise with the powders derived from the fruits of *tejinī* and *kolaka*, one should place sesame and leaf-ash upon a heated mortar-surface and grind them; thus produced, the *jalūkā* (leech) is excellent.
This very substance, having been soaked in the juice of *kapikacchū*, the hair of a *candrāvatī* plant, oil, the moon (*candra*), *ṭaṅkaṇa*, *kāma*, and *pippalī*, becomes *tejinī*.

When it has been thoroughly rubbed on a heated stone slab according to the prescribed method and fashioned into a pill, it is known as the excellent *jalūkā*, which destroys the intoxication and pride of women.
In childhood, it should be eight finger-breadths [in length]; in youth, ten finger-breadths;
and for those who are mature, twelve. Thus, the leech is considered to be of three types.
Having placed the vessel at the mouth of a goat-skin bag, one should cause the ewe’s milk to be poured in;
then one should set it in the intense heat of the sun for twenty-one days.
The second [mudrā] described here by me is beneficial for the liquefaction of the leech;
situated upon the head of men, it wondrously causes the seed to flow.
[The application of leeches: One should also use the juice of *munipattra*, the water from the stalks of *śālmalī*,
the water of the root of *jātī* combined with the water of *śiṃśapā*.
The wise one should grind together the fruit of the *śleṣmātaka*, the powder of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the powder of *kokilākṣa*, and mercury.
A divine leech is produced that captivates the minds of women;
at the time of passion, it should be applied so that the woman herself may desire him.

When lead has been infused seven times with a mixture of *triphalā*, *bhṛṅga*, *mahauṣadha*, honey, clarified butter, goat’s milk, and cow urine, and has been smelted while in a state of equilibrium, it becomes *jalūkā*. VRrs_11.101 //
One should take lead (sūta) equal in measure to the number of days in the solar year (365), having acquired it for dīnāras;
then one should perform its purification with the juices of *aṅkola*, *rājavṛkṣaka*, and *kanyā*. VRrs_11.102 //
One should thoroughly macerate [the powder] for twenty-one days together with the powders of *śaśirekhā*, *varavarṇinī*, *sakokilākṣā*, *apāmārga*, and *kanaka*.
Having administered sour gruel (*kāñjika*) or broth at night, one should introduce it into the vagina;
this should be applied according to the sequence of young, middle-aged, and old women after identifying their respective stages.
Even for men who are devoid of passion, a woman may become eager for union.
Take four parts of mercury, five parts of tin, an equal amount of *surasā* juice, and combine them with *ṭaṅkaṇa*. VRrs_11.105 //
Having rubbed that ball produced from mercury for three days and placed it at the tip of the linga within the yoni, it brings one under control for as long as one lives.
Having sprinkled a serpent with camphor, *sūraṇa*, *subhṛṅga*, and *sumeghanāda*, one should bind it with the juice in a mutual coil.
By means of this coil placed upon the penis, he becomes the master of broad-hipped women and their daily source of life.
By applying a paste made of *ṭaṅkaṇa*, long pepper (*pippalī*), *sūraṇa*, camphor,
and the juice of *mātuluṅga* to one's own penis, one may cause the vulva of women to dilate.
Having placed the seed-syllable of Hara upon a serpent coiled by fire within the circle of Madana, one should then double it;
subsequently, one should sprinkle the center of that with the sages, gold, serpents, and snakes, along with Dantī.
Having ground the *madanavalaya* with buttermilk and the *gaṇa*, one should prepare it;
at the time of sexual union, this destroys the pride of passion in women.
The juice of madanaphala, vyāghrī, and bṛhatī fruits, along with sūraṇa tubers, the sour leaves of chickpeas, and the powder of kapikacchu, vajravallī, pippalī, and tamarind; VR 11.111.
One should grind the naga-plant (nāga) processed with fire nine times with cooling substances;
having fashioned this into a bracelet, it causes the melting [of passion] in women.
[Mercury:: Killing] Mercury (sūtaka) together with the seed of *palāśa* and the juice of sour *jambīra*,
when ground while still "alive" and heated in a vessel (*yantra*), certainly dies.
Having made a paste with finely powdered *kharamañjarī* seeds combined with *puṣkara* seeds,
one should strongly heat the mercury in a sealed crucible (*dṛḍhamūṣā*); it will become ash.
Hiṅgu well-impregnated with the milk of *kākodumbarikā*,
through the procedure of rubbing and heating in a crucible (*puṭapāka*), certainly reduces mercury to ashes. (VR 11.115)
One should grind *devadālī* and *harikrāntā* with the juice of *āranāla*;
with those juices, one should subject mercury (*sūta*) to seven cycles of grinding and incineration (*mardita-mūrchita*).
One should place that extract in an iron pan and, having repeatedly added its liquid,
cook it over a stove during the day until it becomes an ash resembling salt.
[Mercury:: Māraṇa] One should grind the seeds of Apāmārga as well as those of Eraṇḍa;
that powder should be placed within the mercury, positioned both below and above in the crucible.
Having sealed it with small crucibles, one should cook it for four [periods] and reduce it to the state of ash.
Mercury,
having been steamed seven times with the bulbous root produced from a bitter gourd that has been soaked in a woman’s milk, dies by means of a fire of cow dung.
[Mercury:: Māraṇa] One should grind mercury combined with sulfur in a mortar with water from the roots of the *aṅkola* plant;
at the end of the day, one should seal it.
One should seal it in the Bhūdhara yantra; at the end of the day, it becomes dead.
One should grind mercury and iron with the milky sap of the *vaṭa* tree for three *praharas*;
by means of that wood, one should cook it, and that mercury will be reduced to ashes.
Now, the patient [should approach] the master of mercury (rasācārya), who is Maheśvara himself in visible form,
and the prepared mercury held within a horn, a tooth, a bamboo tube, or similar vessel.
Having worshipped the gods, cows, and Brahmins according to one's ability,
one should eat the meat held upon a leaf-fragment, followed by water as a drink.
[The soup] prepared with ghee, rock salt, coriander, cumin, and fresh ginger;
and [the vegetables] such as *taṇḍulīyaka*, coriander, *paṭola*, and *alambuṣā*.
Well-digested śāli rice, cow’s milk, ghee, curd, "swan-water," and mung bean soup— in brief, these constitute the category of wholesome foods.
Bṛhatī, bilva, kūṣmāṇḍa, the tips of vetra,
kāravellaka, māṣa, masūra, niṣpāva, kulattha, mustard, and sesame.
