One should strictly avoid jumping, rubbing the body with medicinal pastes, bathing, copper vessels, wine, fermented liquors, the meat of marshy animals, sour grain-ferments, eating from plantain leaves, bronze vessels, heavy foods, constipating substances, and anything that is sharp or excessively hot. (VR 11.127)
[The group beginning with *ka*: *Kaṇṭārī* fruit, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), tortoise oil, as well as black mustard (*rājikā*),
lime, *kataka* nut, *kaliṅgaka* fruit, pumpkin (*kūṣmāṇḍaka*), and cucumber (*karkaṭī*).

Kārī, the fruit of the *kukkuṭa* and *kāravella*, the fruit of the *karkoṭikā*, the eggplant (*vṛntāka*), and the wood-apple (*kapittha*)— this indeed is declared to be the group beginning with the letter *ka*.
This group beginning with the letter *ka* is considered as taught in the *Devīśāstra*; now,
the group designated in other scriptures is described according to another method.
Kaṅgu, kanduka, kola, kukkuṭa, kala-kroḍa, kulattha, kaṇṭārī, kaṭutaila, kṛṣṇagala, kūrma,
kalāya, kaṇā, karkāru, kaṭhillaka, kataka, karkoṭaka, karkaṭī, kālī, kāñjika, eṣaka, and so forth— this group has been proclaimed by the venerable Lord Kṛṣṇa.
In whichever rasa the letter *ka* and so forth are explicitly prohibited by direct statement, there they must be avoided; their propriety [is determined] from other [sources].
When there is belching, one should eat rice with curd, black fish, and cumin;
when there is agitation of the wind (vāta), one should perform an oil massage with *nārāyaṇa* and other such oils.
In cases of aversion to food, one should sprinkle cool water over the head;
in cases of thirst, coconut water with green gram and sugar [is recommended].
One should consume the fruits of the grape, pomegranate, date, and plantain for the sake of increasing the essence and potency [of the body]. Furthermore, curd, milk, sugarcane,
and sugar should be used as other cooling treatments during the procedure for the elimination of the essence.
One should eat bṛhatī and bilva; this is the general rule.
[This is indicated] in cases of fever, hemorrhaging, cough, dyspnea, asthma, hoarseness, consumption, as well as loss of appetite and excessive salivation. (VRs 12.1)
And also for vomiting and heart disease, for thirst, alcohol-induced disorders, and hemorrhoids;
for upward-moving wind (udāvarta), diarrhea, abdominal disorders of the small intestine, and dysentery.
[It is the remedy] for cholera, sluggish digestion, dysuria, urinary stones,
urinary disorders, somaroga, pustules, and abscesses.
[It is the remedy] for diseases such as enlargement of the spleen and abdominal tumors, for colics and abdominal enlargements,
for jaundice, edema, erysipelas, leprosy, vitiligo, and gout.
[It is indicated] for those with obstructed wind-blood (vātāsra), the barren, those suffering from disorders of pregnancy,
diseases of the puerperium and childhood, as well as for insanity and epilepsy.
In diseases of the eyes, diseases of the ears, diseases of the nose and mouth, in diseases arising in the head, in wounds, fractures, and fistulas; 12.6.
For tumors and the like, minor diseases, secret ailments, and poisons;
for old age and for those without offspring, it serves as a means for nourishing the seed.
Indeed, by this sequence, the entire medical treatment of diseases shall be explained here according to tradition, through formulations involving juices, metals, and poisons.
Horripilation, trembling, sweetness in the mouth, yawning, aching in the head, and a burning sensation—
these indeed are said to be the symptoms of wind-fever (vātajvara), provided they persist constantly after eating.
Purgation, dryness of the mouth, a pungent taste, intense burning heat, delirium, vertigo, and fainting—
these are the symptoms of fever caused by pitta, as are vomiting, thirst, and a burning sensation in the limbs.
Cough, labored breathing, numbness of the mouth, sweetness in the mouth,
excessive sleepiness, perspiration, and slight burning sensation are the characteristics of fever born of phlegm (śleṣmajvara).
That characteristic which is mixed belongs to two or three [of the aforementioned types].
One should form a ball from mercury and sulfur that have been thoroughly rubbed together with water;
then, having placed it inside a new vessel, one should subsequently place a copper plate over that ball.
Having suppressed it for half a moment, the wise one should kindle it with his blazing fire;
then, from below, this medicinal paste (parpaṭī) is perfected, acting as a cloud to extinguish the forest fire of acute fever.
Having first smeared the tongue and the region of the palate with Sindhu-born salt and moist cumin,
one should apply this [mixture] in the measure of a berry (valla), mixed with fresh ginger juice, and cover it with a cloth.
From this point forward, until the breaking of the sweat, buttermilk and rice are to be used as wholesome food;
if one proceeds thus for three days, what need would there even be for any suspicion of fever?
Equal parts of mercury, copper, sulphur, mercury-cinnabar, *jayapāla*, *tikta*, *pathyā*, *trivṛt*, and *viṣatinduka* should be processed with the milk of a *vajrī* cow.
This "elixir of the three worlds," taken with honey in three *valla* doses, destroys even recent fever.
One-fourth part of *sāra-ravi*, an equal portion of *gandha*, and *vipakva* ground with its own decoction— this liquid,
measured by the sequence of one *māṣa* for fevers caused by wind (*anila*) and the other humors, is indeed known by the name Meghanāda.

One should give two *valla* of well-ground pure mercury (*sūta*) and sulfur (*gandha*) along with *darada* and *jaladā*; this medicine, known as "The Lion for the Elephant of Fever" (*jvaragajahari*), should be taken with ginger water, and one who suffers from the burning sensation produced at the onset of fever should eat with milk-rice (*kṣīrabhakta*).
One should also mix mercury with heated lead, along with sulphur and long pepper,
each in equal parts, there according to the prescribed method.
One should grind everything for three days in the juice of jambīra,
and likewise for three days in the juice of meghanāda and kumārī.
One should soak [the ingredients] for two days in goat's urine and for three days in cow's urine;
then, one should add these substances to it as appropriate.
Having combined one part of rock salt (*saindhava*), one part of *citraka*, and likewise one part of black salt (*sauvarcala-lavaṇa*),
one should saturate [the mixture] with it again and again.
By this method, that elixir becomes properly perfected;
one should administer three *valla*s of the juice combined with sugar and clarified butter.
Boiled rice made from wheat, along with mung bean soup and *vāstuka* greens,
combined with the fruit of the *dhātrī*, destroys all fevers;
this is proclaimed by those learned in the treatises as "Dīpikā-rasa."
Mercury, green vitriol, orpiment, blue vitriol, sulfur, and borax— all these, purified and in equal parts, should be macerated for one day with the juices of *kāravallī*.
One should rub that paste and smear it on the inner surface of a copper vessel to a thickness of one-eighth of an inch; then one should cook it in what is called a bed of sand.
When the grains on his back have thus burst open in the machine,
the physician should then extract the well-cooled [medicine] from the interior of the copper vessel.
The elixir called Śītabhañjī-rasa should be powdered together with black pepper;
one should consume one *māṣa* of it with a leaf-fragment, and it will destroy fever—
whether irregular, acute, or occurring on the first, second, third, or fourth day— within three days.
One should grind equal parts of mercury, mica, and realgar in the juice of karkaṭī;
having placed that paste, reduced to the consistency of collyrium, into a copper vessel, [one should proceed].
Then, one should cook it in a sand-vat according to the prescribed method;
thereafter, the best of physicians should administer a dose of one *māṣa* with black pepper powder.
In the case of a cold-fever (śītajvara), one should drink a handful of warm water;
this is the "Cold-Breaker" (śītabhañjī) elixir, which wards off cold-fever.
Having thoroughly purified talc with the powder of *kūṣmāṇḍa* and sesame oil, and having ground it intensely with an equal amount of *suṣavī* juice,
one should form a ball with mercury produced from cinnabar inside a crucible known as a *sikatāyantra*, placed between two inverted lids.
Having covered that [substance] with a leaf and sealed the junction of the two vessels with molasses, lime, and *khaṭikā* (chalk) mixed with *śivā* (myrobalan),
the wise man should cook it over a gentle fire, setting as the limit for the cooking merely the discoloration of the rice placed atop the vessel.
Then one should give him valla mixed with *surasā*, followed by ghee, sugar, water, and honey as a drink;
to conquer virulent fevers here, one should pour a stream of very cold water over the head for the sake of calming vomiting.
Then [he saw] that jewel which is the crest-ornament of the King of Alchemy, known as "The Reviver of the Dead," by whose essence—
like the nectar of immortality— a sudden restoration to life occurs for the sick.
One *guñjā* of mercury, vermilion, and *jepāla*, increased in dose and rubbed with the juice of *dantī*, destroys fever when taken with sugar after half a day.
One should grind together purified mercury, poison, sulfur, and *dhūrtabīja* in equal parts,
along with *vyoṣa* in four equal parts, and store the resulting powder.
It may be given in a vessel of ivory or a horn, but never on wood;
it should be administered in cases of fever caused by wind (vāta), phlegm (śleṣman), their combination, or all three humors (tridoṣaja).
With the juice of ginger or alternatively of jambīra, one should take two guñjās; once this has been digested, one should consume curd with boiled rice.
This elixir named Mahājvarāṅkuśa, proclaimed by Śambhu, shall destroy fevers according to the sequence of the humors within one, two, or three days.

Having ground together *tāla*, copper dust, mercury, *gagana*, and Nepalese *gandhaka*—each weighing one *dīnāra*—along with *śilājatu* and *mākṣika* each weighing half a *ṭaṅka*, and two *dīnāras* of *viṣa* (aconite) and peacock bile, that which is cooked with these juices is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) for conquering floods of fever; it is known by the name *Mṛtyuñjaya*.

Equal parts of *tāla* (orpiment), copper, iron filings, *capalā*, *tuttha*, mica, *kāntaka*, and lead, along with well-pounded *paunarnava* root, should be made into a paste with the juices of *bhṛṅgī*, *kāsaharī*, *punarnavā*, and the leaves of *mahāmandāra*. When cooked in a *vālukāyantra*, this [preparation] brings an end to all fevers.
A fragrance equal to *tuttha* produced from *śiva* should be rubbed with the juice of *jambīra*;
mix it for three days, and with that, an equal amount of *vyoṣa*, whereupon *candrasūrya* is perfected.
To overcome the poison, one should apply a leaf from the creeper known as *bhujaga* hanging over the uneven terrain;
milk mixed with the juice of ginger is beneficial here, and it should be employed for cooling purposes.
But for fever with internal complications and colic, buttermilk is beneficial; the remedy mentioned immediately above [should be taken] with grape water.
For colic, *rodhra* should be taken with the water of *varā*, and *varā* with the juice of *jambīra* or with water.
In cases of epilepsy (apasmṛti), an ointment made from *bimba* and *payobhava* should be applied here;
ghee with boiled rice should be used for food, and this [mixture] destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*) when taken with the juice of *jambīra*.

In cases of splenic enlargement (plīhodara), one should administer [medicines] with the juice of *hiṅgu*, *amlīkā*, and *nimbu*, followed by a meal of rice with buttermilk. To achieve firmness [of the spleen], milk with sugar should be given; molasses should be employed for the pacification of vomiting.
Poison should not be given to one who is eighty years of age, nor to one whose wealth has been exhausted; if it were given, it would cause harm.
One should prepare equal parts of these: *megha*, *pārada*, *gandhāśman*, *viṣa*, *vyoṣa*, *paṭu*, and the two types of *jīraka*.
One should also grind it for seven nights with the juice of *sinduvāra*, the juice of garlic, and the juice of *apāmārga*.

When that has been processed in a sand-bath apparatus (vālukāyantra), one should administer a dose of one guñjā, along with betel leaf and black pepper; thereafter, one should have the patient drink cold water.
The elixir named Umāprasādana removes cold fevers;
it destroys quartan and tertian fevers—how much more so others?
One should prepare equal parts of borax, mercury, and sulfur;
having added double the amount of Nepalese copper, one should grind them together within the mortar.
One should massage it gently until it attains smoothness;
[then add] rock salt, black pepper, conch shell, and the alkali of tamarind, together with honey.
Having made this equal to that, one should then rub it with lime juice;
one should consume a pill the size of a chickpea for three days.
It destroys all fevers— those occurring every day, every two days, every three days, and every four days— and is thus known as the "Goad for Fever" (Jvarāṅkuśa).
Having taken one *tolaka* each of mica, sulfur, and mercury, and half a *tolaka* of poison and half a *tolaka* of tamarind fruit;
Having made all this equal, one should grind it within the mortar;
one should grind it slowly until it attains a fine consistency.
Having dug a pit six finger-breadths deep in both width and circumference,
a person should cast the leaves of the *phaṇivallī* plant into the interior of that pit.
One should place that paste of the leaves firmly in a pit;
one should then fill the opening of the pit over the paste with those same leaves.
Then, one should place the powder into a pit along with wild blue lotuses;
once it is known that it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should extract it thereafter.
One should grind the paste together with leaves smeared with lac in a mortar,
adding half a *tola* of *amṛta* and half a *tola* of *tintiḍī* fruit.
One should set aside the paste for a day and then administer it in a dose of one *guñjā*,
combined with ginger juice and the pungent substances *citraka* and rock salt.

It should likewise be administered in cases of fever caused by the combination of humors (saṃnipāta), by wind (vāta), or by all three humors (tridoṣa), as well as in irregular fevers (viṣamajvara), weak digestion (agnimāndya), chronic diarrhea (grahaṇī), and acute dysentery (atisāra).
One should serve food consisting of curd and boiled rice with this sauce;
then, one should pour water over it as required for the illness and other conditions.
This glorious and supreme yoga bestows life upon living beings;
it is known as the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), a mercury beautiful in every limb.

Having thoroughly rubbed the lord of mercury (sūtendra) with the five acids and the three alkalis, one should then macerate it in a bolus consisting of asafoetida, great medicinal herbs (mahauṣadha), and *asurī*, using fermented grain-water (*dhānyodaka*).

Then, it should be treated with the juices derived from *nirguṇḍī*, water, fire-powder (*hutāśamantha*), *tilaparṇī*, *unmatta*, *bhṛṅga*, fresh ginger, *kāmātā*, *girikarṇikā*, *plavada*, and *pañcāṅgula*.

Having thoroughly ground it with equal parts of *sūtendra* (mercury) and innate *pittas*, one should then impregnate it with the bile of fanged animals, goats, hyenas, fish, and peacocks; this will conquer *saṃnipāta*.
Renowned on earth as the *Lokanātha-guṭikā*, it should be taken in a dose the size of a jujube fruit (*mārīca*). Curd and sugarcane pieces are beneficial for it, and its potency becomes cooling.
One *niṣka* each of the ashes of diamond (*vajra*) and vaikrānta,
two *niṣkas* of *śṛṅgīviṣa*, and three *niṣkas* of *cūlikāpaṭu*.
One should combine five niṣkas of agnijāra with everything else in one place;
one should grind it for three days until it becomes as fine as ash.
One should saturate the group of drugs beginning with śārṅgaṣṭā with alkaline water twenty-three times, having both macerated and dried them.
Then, having kneaded it for a day, one should place it in a tooth-casket;
this is the mercury known as Mṛtasañjīvana, an ornament for the needle.
For one who is about to die due to a violent complication of the humors and has fallen to the ground,
one should then pierce the palate and inject this elixir.
Then, having pierced it with an extremely fine needle that has been thoroughly cleansed with water,
and having smeared it with oil, one should place it in a windless location.
Then, after half a watch had passed, having voided his urine and excrement, he regained consciousness; though filled with vigor, he shook his head repeatedly.
One should recognize that the venerable one has indeed changed from one state to another;
then, one should place him in a cauldron filled with cold water.
There, having removed the boiled water, one should add another;
then, to that person who is begging, one should subsequently give milk mixed with sugar to drink.
Or one should give curd mixed with sugar, coconut water, and plantain fruits; otherwise, he will surely die.
When he had regained consciousness and was speaking and begging for fruit and such,
[the king] dragged him away from that place, rubbed him with oil, and squeezed out the oil.
One should apply ointments of fragrant substances and camphor from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head;
thus, one should treat the patient with such cooling substances for seven nights.
One should repeatedly apply the juice derived from the root of the *dardurī* plant to the ears, eyes, nose,
and mouth of the child’s vessel on the arrival of the eighth day.
One should administer it with sugar to bring down the morbid humor;
once the humor has been brought down, one may thereafter eat food and curd as desired.
Accompanied by inhalation and exhalation, and other signs of life remaining,
one should place [the body] in a cauldron filled with water for the sake of attaining awakening.
Having drawn that one who has attained awakening [into the heart], one should treat him as before;
he lives for the duration of his lifespan and dies immediately thereafter.
Even Brahmā cannot find the end of that Dharma which rescues one sinking in the most terrible confluence, the ocean of death.
A person who has been liberated from the great fear of death caused by the convergence of humors should honor their physician even with the gift of all their possessions.
"Otherwise, one remains in hell for as long as the duration of a kalpa;
this is the command of Śaṅkara, proclaimed by Śambhu. (VRṢ 12.88)
The manifestation rooted in the crossing over of aesthetic flavor (rasa) must never be performed.
The dull-witted, out of a desire for wealth, offer it without the authority of the scriptures.
Having obtained the grace of the Guru, let it be employed during the ritual assembly (saṃnipāta).
Śārṅgaṣṭā, as well as vyāghrī, karīra, tilaparṇikā,
indravāruṇikā, mustā, haridrā, and the root of aṅkola.
Apāmārga, kaṇā, gold, kaṭutumbī, and tintiḍī—
this group beginning with śārṅgaṣṭā is a supreme remedy for *saṃnipāta*.
Having made a firm paste of equal parts of mercury, sulfur, talaka, realgar, orpiment, borax, blue vitriol, jepāla, poison, and ṭaṅkaṇa, along with honey and madhuphala;

having prepared this collyrium, one should saturate it with the bile of a serpent of virulent poison, and having cast it into a lead crucible, it is known by the name Sūcīmukha, the best of mercurial preparations.

At the gateway of Brahmā, when drops of blood are scattered, one should administer a dose the size of a single guñjā seed; having given it during a wind-disorder caused by a bowstring tied in a sealed packet, accompanied by fever and branch-like tremors, one instantly conquers cough, asthma, loss of appetite, delirium, trembling, those afflicted by hiccups, muteness, deafness, insanity, epilepsy, and fainting.
Mercury, sulfur, copper, and mica; lāṅgalī, vahnī, and asafoetida; and the leaves of vandhyā, paṭola, nirguṇḍī, sugandhā, and nimba.
One should grind together the three alkalies (pāṭhā, akṣa, and yavakṣāra), kṣveḍa, bola, dhattūra, taṇḍula, śṛṅgī, and the essence of madhuka with the acidic juice of jambīra.
One should indeed prepare pills with a measure of one niṣka;
that pill subdues fever accompanied by sweating and burning sensations, acting as a goad for the elephant of *saṃnipāta*.
The Vaiṣṇava army is indeed in the cycle of transmigration; it is immovable, adorned with the *kādi* [consonants] as its bracelets, endowed with passion like Rudra, mature, and graced with a crown.
One should know that there are three parts of orpiment and one part of mercury; half of that [mercury] is sulfur, and half of that again is realgar.
One should grind that for three praharas with the juice of *kāravallī* leaves;
when cooked in a *vālukāyantra*, this elixir (*rasa*) removes quartan fever.
Sulfur, when combined with mercury, becomes exceedingly beautiful;
it should be tripled with *hiyāvalī* and rubbed with the juice of *nirguṇḍī*.
That [powder] should be used seven times with the juice of fresh ginger;
it destroys continuous and other types of fever, acting as a goad for the elephant of quartan fever.
Realgar, orpiment, red arsenic, manahshila, copper, and sulphur, along with mercury, should be rubbed with the juice of musali; when cooked in a kukkuti-puṭa,
it is known as Mṛtyuñjaya.
One should employ two *vallās* of this great elixir (*mahārasa*) as desired along with a meal of curd; it destroys acute fever and *saṃnipāta*. (VRs 12.103)
One should grind purified mercury, poison, sulphur, black pepper, borax,
and *kaṇā* with the juice of *dhūrta* and *jadrā* for one day, and then dry it.
The five-faced substance called *rasa*, weighing two *guñjās*, conquers the *saṃnipāta* fever;
one should administer it with a decoction of *arka* root along with *tryūṣaṇa*.
Curd-rice is beneficial in this case, and one should also employ the application of water.
One should grind mercury and sulphur in equal parts with the juice of *dhattūra* fruits for one day, and then add an equal amount of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*). This elixir,
known by the name *unmatta*, conquers *saṃnipāta* when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*).
One should grind ten niṣkas of seeds of *jepāla* (Cassia tora) from which the husks have been removed;
one should then mix with it one niṣka each of black pepper, long pepper, and mercury.
It should be diligently soaked for seven days in juices extracted from citron fruits;
when used as an ointment, it quickly destroys *saṃnipāta* fever and is known as "Auspicious" (*śiva*).
Having powdered two *pratiniṣkas* each of *madanaphala*, *viḍalavaṇa*,
and mustard seeds, along with *ṭaṅkaṇa*, one should drink it with a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
In cases of leprosy, fever, jaundice, throat diseases, and indigestion,
one should take a single seed of *girikarṇī* with cold water as a nasal drop (*nasya*).
Having prepared a beautiful ink from two palas each of pure mercury and sulphur, one should add three *prakuñcas* of *mlecchalulāya*, *locana*, *manaḥśilā*, and *dhātrī*;
three *badara*-sized pieces of *pathyā*, the three pungents (*tri-kaṭu*) at six *śāṇas* each, *vacā*, *dharmiṇī*, *vellā*, *ambhodhara-pattraka*, *dvirada-kiñjalka*, and *aśvagandhā*.

Having ground all these ingredients together in equal proportions and measuring one *karṣa* of the total, one should place them in a mortar and rub them thoroughly with half a *karañja* fruit, *amṛtā*, *agasti*, and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*); then, with a steady mind, one should perform seven successive saturations (*bhāvanā*) using *bhūdhātrī*, *vijayā*, the fruit of the ocean-born tree (*saritpatiphala*), *jvālāmukhī*, and *mārkava*, each used in turn.

Then, having prepared five types of *pitta* with the five [ingredients], the excellent physician should next apply the fumigation of *karañja* leaves and *amṛta*; thereafter, he should fashion a pill in the shape of a grain of rice using the fresh juice of ginger.

One part of *deya* (the base ingredient) should be given in cases of *saṃnipāta*; with *pratihataviṣaya*, it is used for those suffering from delusion and sleep disorders; with *ajamodā*, it is for *gulma*; and with *tryūṣaṇa*, it is for disorders of *vāyu* and *grahaṇī*.
To protect the lives of elephants, horses, and men, Vaidyanātha has declared that this *rasaka* should be administered along with *jīraka*, as it is equal in potency to the ocean of the body.
The mercury, equal in weight to sulphur and mica, rubbed with the juice of *vārāhī* and cooked in a *vālukāyantra* with *triphalā*, *vyoṣa*, and *citraka*, [attains its perfection].
It is combined with the three alkalis, the five salts, asafoetida, guggulu, dīpyaka, cumin, and indrayava,
each equal in quantity to the juice.
A dose of one māṣa, taken with two palas of warm water as an after-drink, is for those suffering from feverish exhaustion,
loss of digestive fire, disorders of the grahaṇī, anemia, or abdominal tumors.
One should perform the preservation of life; therefore, he is remembered as the Lord of Life (Prāṇeśvara).
When the disease increases, its application twice is approved by physicians.
Rasa, iron, the three pungents (vyoṣa), kaṅkuṣṭha, realgar, orpiment, mica, abhraka, cinnabar, kumbhī, agni, bhṛṅga, mārī, taṇḍulīyaka, and honey; VRs 12.119.
Having ground equal parts of hastiśuṇḍī and half as much śivagandhaka with moist water for three days, one should place it in a sealed jar and heat it over a sand-fire.
One should add water from the *jaya*, *jambīra*, *nirguṇḍī*, and *cāṅgerī* plants;
having boiled it for fourteen days, one should grind it while moist and dry it.
This elixir named Mṛtasaṃjīvana, when consumed in the measure of one *valla*,
will swiftly conquer all diseases, including *saṃnipāta* and others.
One part of mercury (rasa) is prescribed, and sulphur (gandhaka) is considered to be double that amount;
[along with] poison (viṣa), orpiment (tālaka), kaṅkuṣṭha, realgar (śilā), vermilion (hiṅgula), and iron (lohaka).
Fire, the three pungents, bhṛṅgarāja, gold, honey, mica, hastiśuṇḍī, poison, kumbhī, taṇḍulīyaka, and copper; 12.124.
Taking one part of each of these individually,
one should powder them and macerate the mixture with the juice of fresh ginger for three days.
The juice of the jambīra fruit, measured at three palas, should be taken,
along with three palas each of triphalā and nirguṇḍī.
One *pala* of the juice of *cāṅgerī* is prescribed;
having placed it in a glass flask and inserted it into the apparatus, one should proceed with diligence.
Having extracted [the juice] and rubbed it with fresh ginger extracts, one should dry it;
this elixir known on earth as "The Reviver of the Dead" should be administered in a dose of two *guñjā* seeds to dispel *saṃnipāta* fevers.
One should grind together equal parts of tin, lead, mercury, Nepalese sulphur, copper, and poison with fresh mercury.
Furthermore, this mercury, rubbed with the juice of *nirguṇḍī* and *cāṅgerī*,
when administered in a dose of one *valla*, destroys *saṃnipāta*.
Having prepared a kajjalī by mixing one karṣa each of purified sulphur and mercury together, one should then form it into a pill.
Having placed it in a new vessel, one should cover it with a copper dish;
having sealed that vessel firmly, one should then set it upon the fire.
When the swelling has subsided as much as the bursting of a grain of rice and the fever has cooled in one's own limbs,
one should administer the juice known as *parpaṭika* in cases of acute fever (*navajvara*).
The physician should firmly cover the fever patient with three balls made of ginger juice for three days, until perspiration arises.
For a person freed from fever, rice with buttermilk (takrabhakta) is wholesome;
this elixir called Navajvarāri is exceedingly rare.
This elixir is considered generally effective, and especially so for fever caused by Vāta.
Take equal parts of borax, mercury, sulfur, and black pepper;
grind them all together with the juice of *jambīra* for three days.
Having dried it and mixed it with sugar, one should saturate it with fish bile;
once saturated, that juice should be processed for three days with the fresh juice of ginger.
Three *valla* measures of cool water should be given for drinking;
buttermilk with rice, combined with eggplant (*vṛntāka*), is wholesome.
This *jalamañjarī* elixir destroys all types of acute fevers (*navajvara*). (VR 12.138)
One should cause the ashes of vessels that have been pierced by the neck of a beloved [animal] to be made;
mercury equal to that amount, along with sulphur and ṭaṅkaṇa, [should be mixed] with nimba-water.
Then, having ground that paste, one should rub it for three days again.
One should infuse this with fish bile equal in quantity to the juice;
this perfected *kāntarasa* should be administered in cases of acute fever by the best of physicians in appropriate doses, accompanied by a draught of ginger.
Having mixed mercury with equal parts of mercury-oxide, sulfur,
tin, and mica, one should then grind the mercury together with an equal amount of tin.
There, having combined [the ingredients] and ground them with *jambīra* juice in a vessel of fragrant clay,
one should apply the general *puṭa* [method] to the mercury prepared seven times.
Then, having processed it seven times with *kumārī*,
*citraka*, jaggery, and cumin, one should administer it when the chronic fever has subsided.
Through the application of a decoction of triphalā, it cures cough and asthma;
through the application of a decoction of amṛtā, it cures insanity and dhanurvāta.
Thus, this elixir named Candrodaya is the destroyer of diseases.
Lead, tin, mercury, copper, sulfur, and likewise borax, as well as Nepalese poison and yellow orpiment, all in equal measure.
Having ground everything together with the milky sap of the banyan tree (*vaṭa*), one should form it into a ball (*golaka*);
that ball should then be cooked inside a vessel over the flame of a lamp.
Having cooled that pill, one should rub it with *bhṛṅgarāja*;
one should also rub it repeatedly with the juice of fresh ginger.
One should administer *vaṭakas* (pills) the size of a chickpea, moistened with juice;
this, in a dose of two *guñjās*, removes chronic fever.
Equal parts of mercury,
sulfur, and realgar should be ground together and combined with the juice of *karkoṭikā*.
Murāri,
taken as one *valla* with sugar and followed by a post-digestive drink (*anupāna*) of *taṇḍulīya* juice or even with sugar,
destroys new fevers by force when administered in a dose of two *guñjās*. (VR 12.150)
When pitta is vitiated by the excessive consumption of foods that are bitter, sour, pungent, salty, hot, burning, and dry,
it corrupts the blood; then, circulating through both pathways, it discharges blood in great quantities from the spleen, liver, and the site of the blood vessels.
One should combine mercury and cinnabar with the juice of a hen’s egg and ṭaṅkaṇa alkali using an *ūrdhvayantra*. 13.2.
Likewise, one should grind a portion of sulphur with clarified butter;
having prepared this elixir, one should administer it with goat's urine.
Taken for three days along with a *māṣa* bean, it conquers disorders of the *grahaṇī* and blood;
it destroys fever and burning sensations, and cures *rakta-pitta*.
Having weighed out mercury and copper ash individually by the weight of one *tola* each,
one should form them into pills and cast them into the fire for three days.
Then, having taken that which has been dried, one should grind it once again;
having prepared a collyrium (kajjalikā) with all those identical fragrant substances, [one should proceed].
With water from musta, pomegranate, and dūrvā grass; with the sap from the breasts of the ketakī flower; and with the water of sahadevī, kumārī, and parpaṭa.
Having diligently processed [the powder] day by day separately with the waters of *rāmaśītalikā* and the juice of *śatāvarī*, one should apply it.
Equal quantities of the bitter essence of *guḍūcī*, *parpaṭī*, *uśīra*, *māgadhī*, *śṛṅgāṭa*, and *sārivā* should be made into a fine powder.
One should saturate it seven times with a decoction of grapes and other such fruits; then, having placed it into a cloth strainer, pills the size of chickpeas should be prepared.
This mercury, renowned by the name Candrakalā,
is celebrated as the destroyer of all bile-related diseases and the remover of disorders arising from wind and bile.
Capable of utterly destroying both internal and external great fevers,
it is especially praised during the summer season and particularly so in the autumn.
It does not cause sluggishness of the digestive fire, but removes high fever with great heat;
it quickly dispels fatigue and fainting, as well as the excessive flow of blood in women.
It destroys upward and downward hemorrhaging, especially vomiting of blood, and all types of dysuria; of this there is no doubt.
Powdered *paṭola* mixed with an equal amount of mercury (*sūtendra*),
rubbed together with the group of drugs known as *lohāri*, is a supreme remedy for hemorrhaging (*raktapitta*).
A person who licks one *karṣa* of the fresh juice of *vṛṣādalā*, combined with mercury, *guñjā*, and honey-sugar at dawn, shall destroy the terrible *raktapitta* that is a source of suffering.
Combined with patola and asafoetida, and taken with honey, it cures raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders).
One should eat fresh butter, sugar, parched grain, and grapes together.
And one should apply ghee to the head; it is the supreme remedy for curing raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders).
One should drink a decoction of ten thousand grapes boiled with *vāsā*, sweetened with sugar.

One afflicted by *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) should conquer thirst, burning sensations, and fever by consuming either *vāsārasa* (the juice of *vāsā*) with sugar and honey, or parched grain (*lājā*) mixed with an equal amount of sugar.
One should consume the powder of *dhātrī* mixed with sugar to alleviate *rakta-pitta*.
The humors (doṣas), agitated by wasting, mental distress, and fever, produce cough; consequently, the patient expectorates yellow, foul-smelling phlegm resembling pus, with eyes turned upward.

Desiring both cold and heat, eating excessively without cause, with a glossy and serene countenance, yet suffering from pain in the flanks, loss of strength, and emaciation—the symptoms may also manifest in the opposite manner.
Abhraka (mica) processed with *sārka*, *tīkṣṇa* (iron), and the juices of *agastya*, *kāsamarda*, and *varā*,
and then ground with the acid of *vetasa* and formed into a pill, destroys cough.
Having added four times as much yellow orpiment (haritāla) as the ground stone (piṣṭaśilā),
one should grind it with the juices of vāsā and gokṣura for two praharas.
Sweated in a sand-pot (vālukāyantra) in a dose of two guñjās,
it removes cough when combined with the powder of the roots of trikaṭu and nirguṇḍī.
The essence of bhūnāga and abhraka, kāntaloha, gold, abhraka, silver, pearls, gems, tāpya, and vaikrānta; VRs 13.27.
All this has been reduced to ashes; it is considered to be measured separately by a single *māṣa*, while the pure dust of *rājāvarta* is likewise measured by a single *niṣka*.
Having ground all this together with *amlavetasa* and combined it evenly,
one should seal it inside the belly of a crucible (*mūṣā*) and heat it in a furnace until the sky is visible [through the opening].
Having thus ground it with *amlavetasa* and heated it one hundred times,
one should then add two *śāṇa* measures of pearl-ash once this has been powdered.
Having added five *śāṇa* measures of black pepper and having ground them with effort,
one should place them in a beautiful casket and set it aside immediately thereafter.
This very jewel-casket, a supreme elixir that transmutes honey and ghee, shall destroy dyspnea, fever, chronic diarrhea, cough, and the disease of hiccups;

it shall also cure colic, consumption, abdominal enlargement, and various types of leprosy. It is strengthening, aphrodisiac, the best stimulant of the digestive fire, suitable for those in good health, and possesses great potency.
One part of pure mercury, one part of pure sulfur,
three parts of killed copper, and five parts of black pepper.
One should add one part of mercury to four parts of dead mica, and one part of *bhūtāṅkuśa*;
then grind everything together with sour gruel.
One *yāma* of the substance called Bhūtāṅkuśa, or one *māṣa* of the bark of the *vibhītaka* fruit, conquers cough caused by wind (*vāta*). One should lick it with honey as an after-drink;
it destroys bile-cough (*pitta-kāsa*), loss of appetite, asthma, and cough due to wasting (*kṣaya*).
Mercury ash and poison in equal parts, with sulphur considered double that amount;
along with bola, talaka, vāhlīka, karkoṭī, mākṣika, and niśā.
Having powdered kaṇṭakārī, yavakṣāra, lāṅgalī, kṣāra, saindhava salt,
and the essence of madhūka, one should soak them for seven days in the juice of fresh ginger.
One should consume this pill, shaped like a jujube fruit, for the removal of phlegm and cough; this mercury, bound with bola, also conquers asthma and jaundice.
A powder consisting of mercury, sulphur, long pepper, myrobalan, and *akṣavāsaka*,
increased by sixfold [successive] qualities, should be saturated with a decoction of *babbūla*.
Having dried it twenty-one times, one should reduce it to powder;
if one consumes it with honey, this "fire-essence" (agnirasa) indeed cures cough.

The three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), cardamom (elā), nutmeg (jātīphala), and cloves (lavaṅgaka)— of these taken in equal parts, the previously mentioned juice should be an equal amount.
Having filled [the vessel] and stirred it with honey, two niṣkas each should be consumed;
this is "Agnirasa" by name, which destroys consumption and cough.
Indeed, one should hold a bolus made of *bhṛṅgarāja* leaves powdered with honey in the mouth for the alleviation of cough and constipation.
And by drinking the juice of the leaves of *arka* and *eraṇḍa*, one conquers cough.
Or one should inhale the smoke of dantī root or of nirguṇḍī to overcome it.
One afflicted by wasting cough should consume one niṣka each of the root of indravāruṇikā along with bhṛṅgī, kṛṣṇā, and sesame seeds for the sake of pacification.
When the wind (pavana) is excessively vitiated and obstructed by phlegm (śleṣman), it further corrupts the channels carrying water and food;
situated in the stomach (āmāśaya) and moving crookedly within the bodies of living beings, it produces this dyspnea (śvāsa).
One should eat the root of *indravāruṇī*, *devadāru*,
and the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*) together with sugar to pacify upward-breathing (*ūrdhvaśvāsa*).
One should grind mercury and sulphur in equal parts for one *yāma* with the juice of *kanyākā*;
then, one should mix an equal amount of copper leaf with this preceding paste.
Having cooked it for one day in a *haṇḍikā* vessel, one should reduce it to powder; this juice of *sūryāvarta*, taken in a dose of two *guñjā*s, becomes a conqueror of asthma.

Take sixteen *sūtas* (mercury), an equal amount of *dinakara* (iron), half that portion of *bali* (sulphur), and an amount of *sindhu* (rock salt) equal to that; these should be ground very finely along with six powdered *pippalīs*. This mixture, rubbed with the juice of *jambīra* (citron) and heated until well-cooked, should be licked; it destroys cough, asthma, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), colic, abdominal enlargement, and anemia.
I shall now describe the universal pill (vaṭaka); listen to it according to the truth:
take one pala each of mercury and sulfur.
One should add three *palas* each of the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) and one *pala* of tin (*vaṅga*);
having combined everything together in one place, one should grind it for three days.
Likewise, one should rub it for three days with cow urine;
then, one should prepare pills the size of an *akṣa* fruit and dry them in the shade.
Taking one *vaṭaka* daily for exactly thirty days removes asthma,
cough, and fever, and cures sluggish digestion and loss of appetite.
One part of mercury (rasa) is required, and sulphur (gandhaka) is considered to be double that amount;
three parts of long pepper (pippalī) should be taken, and four parts of myrobalan (harītakī).
Vibhītaka should be taken in five parts, vāsā sixfold, and bhārṅgī sevenfold; one should prepare all these as a powder.
Having taken a decoction of *babbūla*, one should saturate it twenty-one times;
then, one should prepare pills the size of a *vibhītaka* with honey.
One should consume one pill named "Seven Nectars" every morning;
it destroys diseases such as asthma and cough at that very moment.

Having ground together mercury, lead, excellent iron, *bali*, *amṛta*, the "three triads," *reṇukā*, *abdam*, *gaṇḍīra*, and *kesarāgni*, combined with double the amount of jaggery, one should fashion very beautiful boluses (*vaṭakas*) the size of a *kola* stone. By eating them at the beginning of the day while following a wholesome diet, this preparation named *Nīlakaṇṭha* utterly destroys all diseases.
Grind mercury with an equal amount of sulphur, realgar, and orpiment using the juices of *āṭarūṣa*, *surasā*, and fresh ginger; then form it into a pill.
Then, having wrapped the ball with clay, one should cook it for two watches (six hours) in an earthen furnace;
thereafter, one should treat it with an equal amount of sulfur and then process it with *aṭarūṣaka* and *kaṭuka*.
A wise person should consume the juice of the *vallī* plant, which is a lion to the elephants of asthma and cough.
Equal parts of mercury, sulphur, copper, mica, pippalī, ginger, and trikaṭu,
along with one part of bhūta and one part of poison, constitute "Sūrya," which destroys cough and other ailments.
One should drink sulphur with black pepper and clarified butter to remove asthma and phlegm.
One should lick one karṣa each of realgar, asafoetida, viḍaṅga, black pepper, kuṣṭha, and rock salt, mixed with honey and clarified butter, to cure asthma, cough, and phlegm.
By foods that cause burning sensations, heaviness, constipation, dryness, or excessive secretions;

by cold drinks, food, and environments; by dust, smoke, sunlight, and wind; by physical exercise, labor, carrying heavy loads, walking long distances, suppression of natural urges, and fasting; [the vata humor becomes aggravated].

Hiccups, dyspnea, and cough arise in men. [The remedy consists of] mercury, sulfur, paddy-rice ash, mica, talc, sulphur, and bitumen, each increasing by one part in sequence, combined with vacā, kuṣṭha, haridrā, akṣa, kṣāra, and citraka. (VR 13.66)
Equal parts of pāṭhā, lāṅgalī, the three pungents (vyoṣa), rock salt (saindhava), and akṣaviṣa,
processed with the juice of bhṛṅga, cures hiccup, hoarseness, and cough.
Juice ground with ripe copper is beneficial for those who are strong and suffer from hiccups.
Having placed the powder of *pāṭhā* and *indravāruṇī* in a vessel, one should then add realgar (*kunaṭī*) on top of that;
upon its surface, one should apply purified mercury along with a portion of realgar.
Half a *sūta* (mercury) of *kunaṭī* powder, and half of that amount of the aforementioned root-herb powder—
having added this powder, one should cook it on a stove for eight *yāmas* over a gentle fire.
This preparation, known as *śilāpūtarasa*, destroys hiccup when taken in a dose of three *guñjās*.
One should powder equal parts of dead mercury, dead copper, asafoetida, root of *puṣkara*, rock salt, sulfur, orpiment, and *kaṭuka*.
One should grind [the mercury] firmly for one day with the juices of *devadālī*, *punarnavā*, *nirguṇḍī*, *meghanāda*, and bitter *koṣātakī*.
One should lick a dose of one *māṣa* of the juice of Manthānabhairava with honey for the purpose of pacifying diseases of phlegm; thereafter, one should drink a decoction of nimba.

The leaf arising from the *kīrapriya* plant—which is the night-blooming flower emerging from the three [parts] beginning with *viśva*—and that which resides in the throat of the blue-necked one (Śiva), known as the third eye of the Lord of the Gods;
these, along with water from *nirguṇḍikā*, equal in measure to a mass of scholars and a rival to worms, should be made into pills the size of chickpeas, which cure asthma and cough.
One should cause him to drink a decoction of rāsnā, bṛhatī, agni, and balā, along with milk.
One should cause the patient to inhale smoke produced from the leaves of the *śikhinī* plant.
One should drink one karṣa of purified sulphur with ghee and warm water;
indeed, this Pañcavaktra-rasa, taken with honey, destroys phlegm.

When the bodily humors—wind and the others—are provoked by speaking too loudly, grief, excessive study, physical injury, or corruption, they enter the channels that carry the voice and destroy its stability; thus, the voice becomes afflicted in six ways.
Having ground the mercury with twice its quantity of sulphur and *bhṛṅgarāja*,
one should melt it in an iron vessel smeared with ghee over a fire of jujube wood.
Having applied cow dung above and below, one should shape it into the form of a *parpaṭa* (pancake) using tender plantain leaves and a smooth iron ladle.
Cast into an iron vessel, it becomes an iron tablet;
cast into a copper vessel, it becomes a copper tablet.
Regarding the statement "double the amount of *parpaṭī* juice":

having ground [the mercury] together with *bhṛṅgarāja* juice, one should heat it until it is liquefied and pour it onto a plantain leaf placed over cow dung using a smooth iron ladle. Then, placing an inverted plantain leaf on top of that and applying cow dung, [one should press it down] with the palm of the hand or similar means.
Having pressed it, one should make it into the shape of a parpaṭa (thin wafer).
If it is placed upon a smooth iron plate in place of a plantain leaf, it becomes an iron parpaṭika. Alternatively, if it is placed upon a smooth copper plate, it becomes a copper parpaṭika.
Furthermore, one should place plantain leaves and the like over the liquid.
One should also employ a quarter-part of poison in diseases that are to be treated by it,
as well as [the juices] of surasā, jayantī, kanyā, and āṭarūṣaka.
It should be soaked daily with the juices of triphalā, munī, bhārṅgī, muṇḍī, trikaṭu, citrā, bhṛṅgarāja, and vahnī.
One should then saturate it seven times with the juice of fresh ginger;
this excellent *parpaṭa* extract should then be gently warmed over charcoal embers.
One should give him eight *guñjā* seeds combined with betel leaf;
one should also have him drink a decoction of ten *pippalī* fruits and *nirguṇḍī*.
This *rasa* should always be employed in cases of hoarseness, phlegm, and asthma.
Having finely crushed the roots of *trikaṇṭaka* and ginger,
one should add them to goat’s milk mixed with half as much water and boil until the milk remains.
One should drink that milk at night, and also with one's meals, along with rice;
however, one should avoid pumpkin, tamarind, eggplant, and even the karkaṭī gourd.
One should avoid fermented gruel, oil, and sexual intercourse;
and one should consume [the prescribed regimen] for three months for the cessation of cough and asthma.
A meat broth prepared with cumin, asafoetida, and the three pungents (vyoṣa) will cure *grahaṇī*;
likewise, it cures vāta-fever with a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and kapha with *trikaṭu*.
One should treat fever of every origin with the essence of *madhuka* and the five spices (*pañcakola*);
consumption (*yakṣman*) with honey and long pepper; and hemorrhoids with cow’s urine.

A plaster of *śūla* (the root of *śūla*) with castor oil cures anemia and swelling; with *guggulu*, it cures leprosy (*kuṣṭha*); and [a plaster] of *bhṛṅga*, *bhallātaka*, *vākucī*, and the five parts of the neem tree (*pañcanimbaka*) likewise [cures leprosy].
Combined with the seeds of *dhattūra*, it destroys urinary disorders and insanity;
together with *vyoṣa* and the leaves of *nimbu*, it quickly destroys epilepsy.
This juice is exceedingly beneficial for infants who are still nursing;
furthermore, by means of powders such as *pathyā* and *akṣa*, it overcomes other diseases that are otherwise very difficult to cure.
One should administer the juice of parpaṭī with nutmeg and cold water;
in the case of pitta-type indigestion, one should also sprinkle his head with cold water.
One should administer nasal medication, expectoration, sharp medicinal smoke, emesis, and purgation;
as well as food that is dry, small in quantity, sharp, and hot, and characterized by pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes;
and wine that has stood for a long time—for a patient suffering from disorders of *kapha*.
Sluggish digestion, fever, coldness, vomiting of blood and pus,
loss of mental vigor, and debility are the symptoms of the king’s disease (rājaroga).
One should prepare gold ash with an equal portion of mercury;
likewise, [one should prepare] realgar, sulfur, blue vitriol, pyrite, zinc, and mica.
One should employ tuttha in equal proportion with the rasa; once it has been reduced to ash, one should place this mayūrakasututthaka, likewise reduced to ash, into the fire.
Having added a small amount of borax and combined it with cat-viśa,
one should first roast it with curd and a second time with honey.
First, one should purify the mineral calamine by cooking it with the alkali of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds;
thereafter, one should cook it thoroughly in oil or purify it in its powdered form.
One should purify sulfur in milk, mercury in human urine,
and copper pyrite combined with rock salt should be cooked in the juice of citron.
One should cook the mineral (śilā) ground with the juice of *jayantī* in that very [liquid];
then, having combined everything, one should rub it with the milk of the *arka* plant.
One should take each of these— jayantī, bhṛṅgarāja, vāsā, pāṭhā, kṛśānu, agasti, and lāṅgalī— gradually, one by one, every day.
Then, having formed a ball (golaka), one should cook it as previously described;
thereafter, having properly pulverized it, one should saturate it with ginger-water.
The juice known as Kanakasundara is prepared by boiling it seven times with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and exudations;
two or three *guñjā* seeds of this [medicine] serve to dispel pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣmā*).

The physician, who understands the specific variations in the patient's strength and condition, should have the patient lick a preparation of long pepper and black pepper mixed with honey and ghee. (VR 14.11)
A wise person should administer either the ashes of *jayapāla* or ginger smeared with cow’s ghee to one suffering from colic, and especially to one suffering from abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
One should consume wholesome food that is pleasing to the heart and strengthening, as previously described, with the exception of [foods beginning with] the letter *ka*.
In cases of *sannipāta* (combined derangement of the humors), one should administer this [medicine] combined with the juice of fresh ginger;
guggulu processed with decoctions of *guḍūcī* and *triphalā* is excellent.
[The Mercury-Rasāñjana Elixir: Three parts of mercury-ash, one part of gold-ash, one part of killed copper, along with realgar, sulfur, and orpiment; VR 14.14.

Having combined the two pure parts of the *pratibha* and powdered them together, one should fill cowrie shells (*varāṭa*) with that powder; likewise, one should fill [shells] with borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*) using goat's milk.
Having ground [the ingredients] with that [liquid], one should seal the mouth [of the vessel] and confine it within an earthen pot;
one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire once purified, and powder it when it has cooled naturally.
This mercury, known as Rājamṛgāṅka, consisting of four guñjās, destroys consumption.
For the pacification of the king of diseases (consumption), the physician should administer it with ten long peppers, honey, and nineteen black peppers, along with clarified butter.
[The Mercury of Śaṅkheśvara]:
One niṣka from the coil of a conch shell, four niṣkas of cowrie shells, half a niṣka of blue vitriol, and an amount of sulfur equal to the sum of all these. VR 14.18.
Equal parts of sulphur (gandha), mercury (nāga),
and borax (rasa)— the mercury being equal to the borax— should be rubbed and cooked like the moon (mṛgāṅka).
This is known by the name Śaṅkheśvara and is considered a destroyer of pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman).
[The Mercury-Compound of Mṛgāṅkapoṭalī: One should grind conch-shell navel with sixteen niṣkas of cow’s milk;
with that, a crucible (mūṣā) should be fashioned, and within it, the mercury-ash (bhasmasūtaka).
Having powdered half a niṣka of sulphur and three [niṣkas] of [the other substance], one should cast them [into the crucible];
having sealed it, one should wrap it in cloth and apply a coating of clay on the outside.
Having dried it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* with a crucible (*mūṣā*) and then reduce it to powder.
Taken in a dose of one *guñjā* as an after-drink, it destroys consumption (*kṣaya*) like the moon (*mṛgāṅka*).
[The Mercury-Embryo Patola Juice]:
Two *niṣkas* of mercury ash, one *niṣka* of gold ash,
and two *niṣkas* of purified sulfur, having been powdered together with the juices of *citraka*, [should be processed].
Then, having dried it for two watches of the night, one should fill cowrie shells with that [substance];
having sealed the cowries inside an earthen vessel, one should cook them in a *gajapuṭa* fire.

Then, having ground it until it is cool to the touch of one's own body, one should swallow a four-rupee-weight (caturguñja) dose of this gold-encased medicinal ball (*poṭalī*), shaped like the moon; it cures consumption (*rājayakṣman*).
One should personally consume three niṣkas of agnirasa; it cures consumption caused by the king (rājayakṣman).

[The Essence of the Five Nectars: Equal parts of ash, mercury, mica, iron, bitumen, and poison, along with guggulu processed with decoctions of *guḍūcī* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). VR 14.27.
One should employ dead copper from Nepal in place of mercury;
having combined them, one should consume two guñjas of this mixture to destroy pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman).
The after-drink is indeed called the essence of the five nectars, as before.
Or *jayantī* taken with milk and *ajagandhā* removes consumption.

[The Essence that Pacifies Consumption: Equal parts of mercury (pārada) and sulfur (gandhaka), along with the powder of the three pungents (trikaṭuka); equal to those should be conch-shell ash, and equal to the mercury should be the ash of cowrie shells (kaparda) and borax (ṭaṅkaṇa).

To all these combined, black pepper (marica) equal to one-fourth part should be added. One should lick this gradually with clarified butter (sājyaka) until it amounts to one niṣka; by doing so daily for a month, consumption (kṣaya) is pacified.
One should prepare gold with the ash of mercury (rasa) using a one-fourth portion [of the ash];
having added double the amount of sulfur (gandhaka), one should grind it with the juice of *citraka*.
Having filled the mouth of the vessel containing the moving and non-moving [substances] with ṭaṅkaṇa and sealed it,
one should then place it in a jar smeared with powder and close it with clay.
Having dried it, one should place it in a pit one *aratni* deep and roast it in the afternoon;
then, having removed it when it has cooled to the touch of one's own body and ground it into powder, one should store it away.
This is the one named Lokeśvara, who increases nourishment and vigor;
four *guñjā* seeds, combined with ghee and black pepper, [should be used].
One should consume this with supreme devotion for the sake of the All-Seeing Lord of the World;
it is effective for emaciation of the limbs, sluggish digestion, cough, and hiccups.
For three days, one should administer black pepper mixed with ghee;
during that time, one should avoid salt and eat food prepared with ghee and curd.
For twenty-one days, one should drink black pepper with ghee; wholesome food should be given like that prescribed for the Moon regimen, and one should sleep with the feet raised upward.
Once the emesis has commenced, one should take a decoction of *guḍūcī* and have the patient drink it together with honey; furthermore, one should have them eat roasted eggplant.
One should bathe with cool water and pour a stream over the head;
however, when a disorder of phlegm has arisen, one should take the fruit of the plantain tree.
Having fried that [ginger] together with black pepper, one should eat it to alleviate phlegm;
or else, fresh ginger mixed with honey, or even jaggery and fresh ginger.
Having fried coriander and dehusked mung beans, one should then grind them into powder;
mixed with sugar and ghee, this should be administered to alleviate loss of appetite.
Having properly fried cumin seeds in ghee, one should drink it with sugar;
likewise, one should take cardamom combined with black pepper until the vomiting has subsided.
One should administer ajamoda and viḍaṅga ground with buttermilk,
or a decoction of vātaghna and musta, for the purpose of pacifying the provocation of intestinal worms.
Having prepared *dugdhikā* over fire, one should employ it for purgation;
likewise, having slightly fried the powder of *jayā*, one should consume it at night with honey.
Having massaged the patient's limb with ghee at the joints,
the physician should bathe the patient with warm water while recollecting the Lord of the World, the Elixir (Rasa).
[Vaidyanātharasa:
One *niṣka* of conch-shell bangle, four *niṣkas* of cowrie shells,
one *karṣa* portion each of blue vitriol (*nīlatuttha*), orpiment (*tāla*), sulphur (*gandhāśman*), and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*).
One should likewise roast half a niṣka of tuttha and nāgarasa and seal it as before;
then one should cook it with a coating of powdered cowrie shells and prepared maṇḍūra.
One should lick half a māṣaka of this, half a māṣaka of black pepper, and [the powder] impregnated with the juice of the betel vine;
these, smeared upon its leaves, should be licked with honey or with *haiyaṅgavīna* ghee.
Once it has emerged through the channel-path, one should consume very little wholesome food as instructed by the Lord of the World;
doing so every watch until the end of the mandala, this Lord of Physicians is proven to be an immediate conqueror of consumption.
One and a half *niṣkas* of mercury (*rasanātha*), one part each of *rasatuttha* and sulphur (*gandhaka*) weighing one *karṣa* each,
one *karṣa* of conch shell, two *karṣas* of purified copper, and nine cowries— these should be placed together within a sealed crucible (*sampuṭa*).
Having cooked [the previous ingredients], one should cook them again until moistened with the juice of *arka* leaves; then, add half a part of dried cow-dung (*karīṣa*).
One should lick this preparation with ghee, taking half a quarter-part (one-eighth) of it, along with half a part of black pepper and one *niṣka* of *gandhāśman* (realgar).
One should consume wholesome food as before for twenty-one days;
this is the "Essence of the Lord of the World" (Lokanātharasa) by name, which cuts through the king of diseases.
Twenty niṣkas of iron powder, processed with one āḍhaka of *bhṛṅga* juice and moistened with the juices of *dhattūra*,
*bhārṅgī*, and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), should be cooked in *puṭa* vessels together with an equal portion of copper.

Having cooked mercury, one part of niṣka, an equal portion of tuttha, two pieces of sulphur, and four cowries in a *puṭa* fire, one should likewise cook the powders of the base metals mixed with the aforementioned juices.

In this powder, one should mix seven units of black pepper and ten units each of blue vitriol (tuttha) and borax (ṭaṅkaṇa); this is declared by the Lord of Life (Prāṇanātha) as being equal to one niṣka of mercury taken separately.

Those suffering from consumption (rājayakṣman), wasting diseases, abdominal enlargements, hemorrhoids, malabsorption disorders, fever, tumors, and other such afflictions, should consume half a portion of this [preparation] with honey alone. (VR 14.57)

One *karṣa* of *vajrarasa* and one *karṣa* of the essence of *kharpara*, when introduced into six *niṣkas* of mercury that has been liquefied in gold for six months, and then into eight *niṣkas* of *gandhāśman* (sulphide ore), [achieve the desired result].
The powder of coral and pearls, with equal parts of gold, along with two, three, and four *niṣkas* respectively of iron, lead, and copper; (VRs 14.59)
It should be ground for three *yāmas* with the sour juice of *cāṅgerī* and then powdered separately;
[one should take] two *niṣkas* each of blue *vaṭaka*, *vyoma*, magnetite (*ayaskānta*), and *tālaka*.
From *aṅkolla*, *kaṅguṇī* seeds, and *tuttha*, take four [parts] each separately;
eight from *ṭaṃkaṇa* salt, and twenty cowries' weight of [mercury].
One should grind [the ingredients] with two *prasthas* of great *jambīra* juice;
this should be mixed with eight *śarāvas* of pure husked rice.

Then, one should cook two *māṣa* weights [of mercury] with a load of dried cow dung; likewise, one-fourth part of this amount of sulfur, as well as black pepper that has been processed [with the same], should be added.
One should lick [the preparation] mixed with honey and smeared on betel leaves;
once a ghaṭikā has passed, one should eat wholesome food at every watch of the night.
If the fire is not ignited, it will burn the bodily constituents (dhātus) in an instant; therefore, having used this for one day, one should abandon it and leave the other maṇḍala.
Thereafter, eating as he pleases, he shall live happily for twelve years; having consumed a great elixir once every year, he shall remain so for each day.
At the beginning of the year, one should discard what is to be discarded; by conquering decay over twelve years, this is known as Vajrarasa, which shatters the mountain of consumption (kṣaya).
[The Mahāvīra-rasa:
Two niṣkas of tuttha, one niṣka of well-processed mercury,
one niṣka of poison, two niṣkas of tīkṣṇa, and a karṣa each of sulphur and pearl.
One should cook [the substance] ground with the juices of *agniparṇī*, *harilatā*, *bhṛṅga*, fresh *surasā*, and *rasa* inside a sealed vessel (*sampuṭa*) smeared with the bulb of *lāṅgalī*.
One should lick half a *poṭalī* of [the plant], two *kākinyas* of poison,
and a powder of black pepper equal in measure to the *poṭalī*, together with honey.
The Mahāvīra meat-juice is excellent and beneficial for those suffering from consumption, dysentery, diarrhea, weakness of the digestive fire, cough, anemia, and abdominal tumors.
For one who is excessively obese, provided there is no vomiting of pus, blood, or phlegm and no wasting away,
one should not administer milk or meat broths, because that would contradict the principles of the sequential treatment.
[The general remedy: One should eat the roots of *mātuluṅga*, parched rice flour, and rock salt,
combined with long pepper (*pippalī*) and honey, for the pacification of vomiting.
One should drink a *niṣka* of *rajanī*, *śaṅkha*, and *pūga* to destroy vomiting; or else, one should drink half a *niṣka* of *ṭaṅkaṇa* with the juices of *kākamācī*.
One should drink or eat fragrant substances for the complete pacification of all types of vomiting;
lac-resin mixed with honey is the supreme remedy for the expulsion of blood.
[The Tṛṣṇāhara-rasa: Iron, realgar, and gold pyrite, combined with a paste of sulphur, are reduced to ash through the proper method; this prevents thirst and vomiting. (VR 14.76)
[The juice of *rājāvarta*:
The juice of *rājāvarta*, copper, and honey-gold (*mākṣika*), cooked in ghee and combined with honey, clarified butter, and sugar, destroys all forms of alcoholism (*madātyaya*). (VR 14.77)
Copper combined with the essence of rājāvarta and placed within the womb of mercury,
rubbed with the juices of yaṣṭīmadhu and cooked in the midst of ghee.
Combined with honey, clarified butter, and sugar, it cures all types of alcoholism.
[Bhairavanāthī Pañcāmṛta Parpaṭī]:
Gold, silver, copper, sattva, mica, and magnetite—all these increased in sequence; then iron, lead, and tin.
Having melted everything together and then solidified it,
one should proceed by placing the fragrant substances, each weighing one *pala*, along with realgar (*śilāla*).
Having placed everything into a mortar, one should grind it with the group of acidic substances (amlavarga);
then, one should add powdered calamine, blue vitriol, orpiment, realgar, and sulphur.
Having added [the ingredients] repeatedly, one should heat it for twenty cycles;
then, with twice as much mercury as the iron, and twice as much sulfur as that mercury.
Having prepared a smooth kajjalī and placed it in an iron vessel,
one should melt it with mild *badara* coals and then pour it out.
Then one should stir the ashes of the five metals, beginning with gold;
thereafter, one should place them upon a leaf of the *kadalī* tree set in cow dung.
Having covered it with another leaf, one should carefully flatten it;
upon that, one should immediately sprinkle a small amount of cow dung.
Having gathered naturally cool [water] and prepared a powder of cloth, one should then place it in an upward-pointing vessel (pālikā).
As before, one should slowly melt [the substance] with mild jujube-wood coals;
[one should take] half a pala of equal parts of *alaka*, realgar, and sulphur, which has been impregnated with poison.
One should repeatedly digest [the mercury], which is equal to or slightly less than a *parpaṭikā* tablet,
within the crucible so that the *parpaṭikā* is not consumed by fire.
The oil-extraction machine is designated as a *paliketi*;
once the powder of *tāla* and other substances has been digested, a cloth-powder (*paṭacūrṇa*) should be prepared.
A decoction made from five *palas* each of *pūtīkarañja*, *ṣaṭkoḷa*, *vyāghrī*, *saubhāñjana*, and the root of [*gokṣura*], reduced to one-sixteenth of its original volume; ||| VRs_14.91 |||
Having steamed it with that decoction, one should dry it seven times with juices extracted from the fruit of the *viṣatindu* and with juices of *nirguṇḍī*.
Having visualized [the deity] and placed [the substance] in the middle of a crucible, one should apply a slight heat using a jujube-wood fire and preserve it with great care.
Thus has the *pañcāmṛtaparpaṭī* been described by Bhairavanātha;
it should be licked, measured in the size of a *guñjā* seed, together with the three pungent spices (*vyoṣa*) and clarified butter.
Complete with all its characteristics, it destroys wasting diseases,
asthma, cough, cholera, urinary disorders, and abdominal ailments.
It also cures incurable anorexia, excessive salivation, vomiting arising from the heart,
hemorrhoids caused by all three doshas, colic, and skin diseases without exception.
It cures fever caused by wind, constipation, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and diseases of the limbs arising from phlegm;
it also cures other major ailments originating from one, two, or all three humors.
This Parpaṭī formulation certainly and specifically cures sluggish digestion (agnimāndya);
thus, having combined the ingredients in this manner, it should be administered by the best of physicians for various diseases.
Through formulations that alleviate various specific diseases and by means of appropriate adjuncts for those respective ailments,
the Pañcāmṛtaparpaṭī shall become a destroyer of all diseases, including consumption (kṣaya) and others.
One should avoid sesame, mustard, bilva, sour [fruits], kāravelaka, and safflower;
likewise, one should renounce the flesh of the pigeon, eggplant, and the cock.
Now, regarding hemorrhoids: flesh-like thorns arise either externally or internally within the anus.
For hemorrhoids are well known as the cause of all diseases for men.
Those which discharge blood are proclaimed to be born of bile (pitta).
Those born of wind, arising from exhaustion, produce upward movement of the bodily humors (udāvarta).
Those born from phlegm (kapha) produce swelling; those born from all three humors (tridoṣaja) produce all [of these symptoms].
[The Mercury-Extract for Hemorrhoids:
One *pala* of purified mercury, two *palas* of purified sulfur, three *palas* of calcined copper, and three *palas* of calcined iron—each taken individually. VRs 15.5.
One should add two palas each of trikaṭu, lāṅgalī, dantī, piruka, and likewise citraka, as well as yavakṣāra and ṭaṅkaṇa.
Both [the two substances] should be combined in five-pala portions, along with five palas of rock salt (saindhava),
thirty-two palas of cow’s urine, and an equal amount of snuhī milk.
One should cook everything in a pot over a mild fire until it is well-kneaded into a mass.
One should always eat two *māṣa* measures of this; for this elixir is indeed an axe to the hemorrhoids (*arśas*).
It may be taken with buttermilk, pomegranate juice, or with cooked tubers.
Equal parts of dead mercury, copper, gold, mica, iron, muṇḍa, sulphur, maṇḍūra, and mākṣika should be ground together with the juice of kanyā for one day.
It should be cooked for three days in an andhamūṣā crucible using a fire of chaff;
once powdered, one should eat a māṣa with sugar to conquer bile-type hemorrhoids.
[The Essence that is the Support of All Worlds:
One *pala* of purified mercury, half a *pala* of sulfur, half of that [sulfur] each of orpiment and pyrite, and *rasaka* (zinc) equal to half a portion of the orpiment. VR 15.11.
One should prepare a kajjalī (potion) from these by grinding them firmly for one day;
then, indeed, one should grind them for three days after adding nimba water.
Having formed it into pills and dried them, one should then place them inside a glass vessel,
carefully covering its opening with a leaf of *arka* weighing one *niṣka*.
Having smeared it with clay to a height of one and a half finger-breadths,
he should then place it upon a third of a vessel filled with sand.
Having placed sand upon the top, one should fill it with sand;
having sealed its opening, one should kindle a fire beneath it for half a day.
Having drawn that liquid from a glass jar while it was cooled by its own body-heat, one should then prepare a powder of cloth; then, [add] two *pala* of copper and mica.
Half a pala of *palāśa* and one *catuṣpala* each of *amṛta* and black pepper, having combined all these together, one should place them in a coconut vessel.

This excellent mercury (rasavara), the refuge of all the world, when combined with ghee and two *guñjā* measures, removes diseases arising from wind and phlegm, ailments produced in the rectum, consumption (*śoṣa*), and jaundice (*pāṇḍu*).

It also cures tuberculosis, wind-pain, fever in its entirety, sluggish digestion, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and the accumulation of all diseases through formulations that destroy those specific ailments; it acts as a digestive stimulant (*dīpana*) instantaneously.
[The Purgative Pill for Hemorrhoids] O auspicious son, listen as I describe the hemorrhoid-curing pill (*arśoghna-vaṭaka*).
[It consists of] long pepper (*pippalī*), the root of long pepper (*pippalīmūla*), wild ginger (*vanasūraṇa*), and leadwort (*citraka*). (VRs 15.19)
Māricā, kaṇṭakārī, and raktapuṣpī, taken in equal parts—
one pala each of all— should be finely ground on a stone slab.
One should pour the urine of elephants, goats, and sheep into an auspicious vessel and cook it over a gentle fire until everything is reduced to the state of powder.
One should add one pala of the three salts right there;
thus, one should prepare pills the size of an akṣa fruit, each separately.
For thirty days, the wise man should provide a meal consisting of equal parts ghee and buttermilk, which is an excellent digestive stimulant and a destroyer of parasites.
[The Arśoghnī Vaṭikā]: Having ground sulphur, silver, and copper together into a paste,
one should add an equal amount of mica and iron (tīkṣṇa), along with a fifth part of the sulphur.
One sixteenth part of poison and two parts of mercury,
having combined these with effort, should be rubbed with the juice of *jambīra* fruit.
Having placed it in an earthen vessel, one should saturate it with a decoction of the best *akvā* (liquorice);
indeed, it should be cooked gradually in a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and *śatāvarī*.
Then, having carefully removed it, the wise one should have it made into pills the size of three *guñjā* seeds; this cures colic and hemorrhoids.
[The Mercury of the Root-Axe]:
Having melted together excellent lead, as well as calamine, copper, and steel, and having added a small amount of alum in very slight measure; VR 15.28.
One should shake it incessantly until the mercury becomes truly three times the size of the seed-vessel (tālaka);
then, having rubbed it with that [substance], one should prepare a paste (piṣṭī) with the mercury.
Then, one should dig it up from within the root of a Bhallātaki tree;
after a month, having extracted that powder, one should place it in cow's milk.
Then, having extracted the oil of *bhallātaka* from a subterranean machine,
he placed that paste into a smooth iron vessel.
One should indeed digest that oil, measuring one *prastha*, with great care;
having been processed with perfumes impregnated by that oil, it will be reduced to ashes when subjected to the *puṭa* process.
Then, having repeatedly rubbed the mercury with the juices extracted from *koraṇṭa* petals produced in the month of Kārttika, and having placed it in the heat, one should kill it.
One should mix that ash with an equal portion of the previously mentioned ash,
along with *vanasūraṇa*, *nirguṇḍī*, *mahārāṣṭrī*, and *bhakaṇṭikā*.
One should grind these with the juices of *vajravallī* and *śikhī* and dry them;
having dissolved them three times with the juices of *mārkava*, one should dry them again.
Then, having carefully reduced them to powder, one should place them in a glass vessel.

This very "Root-Axe" (mūlakuṭhāraka), an excellent elixir combined with dīpya, agni, and the best of vella, taken along with ghee in a dose of one *valla*, destroys hemorrhoids (*arśāṃsi*) of the mouth, nose, eyes, and anus— even those causing most intense pain— as well as splenic disorders (*plīhāna*), malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), liver disease (*yakṛt*), sluggishness of digestion, and skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
Three *pala* of sulfur that has been swallowed and then vomited out by mercury,
and one *karṣa* each of dead mercury, mica, copper, and iron, [are to be taken] separately.
One pala of vermilion powder, three palas of honey,
one pala of kampillaka, and likewise half a pala of poison.
One should grind everything for seven days, repeatedly adding powdered water;
then, having formed it into a ball, one should place it in the sun for seven days.
One should apply a thick paste made from jaggery powder and realgar powder;
then, having added three palas of sulfur, one should place it into a ball within a *krauñcī* [crucible].
And one should place three palas of tāla upon the globule;
having sealed it with great effort, one should indeed apply the gajapuṭa fire.
Having brought forth the *golaka* while it is still cool from one's own body,
one should grind it seven times together with ointments derived from the fruit of the *viṣatindu* tree.
Then, having dried it in the sun with liquid substances, one should place it in a beautiful casket;
one should then add thirty parts of vaikrānta ash to it.
For this is the distinguished elixir taught by Nandīśvara, which indeed destroys disease;
its power remains unassailed against all ailments, and it is named Mahodayapratyayasāra.
It destroys all diseases of the rectum, consumption, leprosy, weak digestion, the ailments of colic and flatulence, phlegm, and asthma;
it cures insanity, epilepsy, all wind-born pains, various types of great fevers, as well as the accumulation of great diseases arising from wind and phlegm, and the disorder of malignant *grahaṇī*.
[Kanakasundararasa: One should take purified mercury, green vitriol (mākṣika), magnetite, mica, lead, and gold,
each in equal parts, along with an amount of sulfur equal to all of them combined.
Having placed it in a mechanical device for the Vidyādharas, one should cook it with wild blue lotuses;
then, having removed it while still cool to the touch, one should mix it with the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa).
In cases of hemorrhoids, pain in the waist, and severe eye pain;
in the disorder of the three humors (sannipāta), wasting, cough, asthma, weak digestion, and fever.
One should employ it for earache, headache, and toothache;
for chronic catarrh, splenic enlargement, heart pain, and severe glandular swelling (granthivāta).
It cures paralysis of a single limb, wind disorders of the bowels, tremors, fainting, all types of irregular fevers, and numerous other diseases.
The mercury known as *kanakasundara*, when administered according to the regimen of wholesome diet and practice,
should be given in a dose of one *guñjā*, accompanied by appropriate adjuncts.
Combined with ghee, it should be administered in Vata-type fever; with honey, in Pitta-type fever; with long pepper (pippalī), in Kapha-type fever; and with sandalwood, in fever arising from Pitta.
In cases arising from phlegm and wind, it should be taken with buttermilk; in cases of wind and bile, it should be mixed with ghee;
in cases of phlegm and bile, with *ārdra* ginger; and in cases of the combination of all three (*sānnipātika*), with *nirguṇḍī*.
One should administer the three fruits in cases of colic and irregular fevers;
or else, one may give ginger, especially in cases of impaired digestive fire.
In cases of excessive secretions (abhiṣyanda), headache, and fainting due to kapha and vāta, [one should take] gāyatrī combined with bola and mixed with the meat of birds.

In cases of paralysis of a single limb (ekāṅga) and dhanurvāta, milk should be used; likewise for chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), consumption (kṣaya), cough (kāsa), and jaundice (kāmalā), ghee prepared with black pepper (marica) is prescribed.

With *ajamodā* and *viḍaṅga*, it conquers abdominal pain, dullness of digestion, dry fever, and loss of appetite; when combined with plantain fruit, it is to be administered. With *bola*, it is prescribed by Nāgabodhi for pain in the lower back. (VR 15.57)
One should combine mercury, sulphur, the three salts, and iron filings— one *pala* each of the first four and three *palas* of the latter—

and grind them all for three days. Thereafter, having applied that mixture, one should perform twenty-five *puṭa*-firing sessions using the juices of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), fire (*agni*), and *vetasa*.

Then, one creeper of this [plant] grown from jaggery, taken with water in these five stages, destroys all types of hemorrhoids when accompanied by *sūraṇa* and ghee; its food in this case is beneficial.
"The sun should be avoided," said the sage Śrī Vāsudeva, along with the fruit of the *kūṣmāṇḍī*, black gram, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), excessive exercise, and the heat of the sun. (VR 15.59)
[The Tīkṣṇamukharasa]:
Mercury, gold, copper, cat’s eye (biḍālaka), bola, brass, iron, impurities,
mica, sulphur, and mākṣika— this mixture, when rubbed with the juice of kanyā and cooked in a *puṭa*, constitutes the Tīkṣṇamukha, which is effective for hemorrhoids.
